M2 from element in standard state

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write equations, with state symbols, for the standard enthalpy change of atomisation of (i) sodium and (ii) chlorine.
parts.answer: (i) Na(s) → Na(g) (ii) ½Cl₂(g) → Cl(g)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the enthalpy change of atomisation of chlorine is half the Cl–Cl bond energy.
parts.answer: One mole of Cl atoms comes from half a mole of Cl₂ molecules, so only half a mole of Cl–Cl bonds is broken.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)
stem: Data (kJ/mol): ΔHf⦵ MgO(s) −602; ΔHat⦵ Mg +148; 1st IE Mg +738; 2nd IE Mg +1451; ΔHat⦵ O (½O₂ → O) +249; 1st EA O −141; 2nd EA O +798.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the lattice energy of magnesium oxide.
parts.answer: −3845 kJ/mol
parts.working:
M1 sum of steps from elements to gaseous ions = 148 + 738 + 1451 + 249 − 141 + 798 = +3243
M1 LE = −602 − 3243
A1 −3845 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why magnesium oxide is used to line the inside of furnaces.
parts.answer: Its very exothermic lattice energy (strong attraction between 2+ and 2− ions) gives it a very high melting point.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)
stem: Calcium chloride is used to melt ice on roads. Data (kJ/mol): ΔHf⦵ CaCl₂(s) −796; ΔHat⦵ Ca +178; 1st IE Ca +590; 2nd IE Ca +1145; ΔHat⦵ Cl (½Cl₂ → Cl) +122; 1st EA Cl −349.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the lattice energy of calcium chloride.
parts.answer: −2255 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the two ionisation energy equations included in the cycle.
parts.answer: Ca(g) → Ca⁺(g) + e⁻; Ca⁺(g) → Ca²⁺(g) + e⁻

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)
stem: Data (kJ/mol): ΔHf⦵ KBr(s) −394; ΔHat⦵ K +89; 1st IE K +419; ΔHat⦵ Br (½Br₂(l) → Br(g)) +112; 1st EA Br −325.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the lattice energy of potassium bromide.
parts.answer: −689 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: The Br–Br bond energy is 193 kJ/mol. Explain why the enthalpy change of atomisation of bromine (+112 kJ/mol) is greater than ½ × 193.
parts.answer: Bromine is a liquid in its standard state, so atomisation also includes vaporisation (overcoming London dispersion forces between Br₂ molecules) as well as breaking half a mole of Br–Br bonds.
parts.working:
M1 standard state is liquid
M2 energy needed to vaporise / overcome intermolecular forces

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)
stem: Data (kJ/mol): ΔHat⦵ Li +159; 1st IE Li +520; ΔHat⦵ F (½F₂ → F) +79; 1st EA F −328; lattice energy LiF −1046.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data to calculate the standard enthalpy change of formation of lithium fluoride.
parts.answer: −616 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the equation for the standard enthalpy change of formation of lithium fluoride.
parts.answer: Li(s) + ½F₂(g) → LiF(s)

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)
stem: Lattice energies (kJ/mol): NaF −918; NaCl −787; NaBr −747.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the trend in lattice energy from NaF to NaBr.
parts.answer: The anion radius increases from F⁻ to Br⁻, so the distance between ion centres increases and the electrostatic attraction becomes weaker; the lattice energy becomes less exothermic.
parts.working:
M1 anion size increases (same charge)
M2 weaker attraction, less exothermic

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the lattice energy of MgO (−3845 kJ/mol) is much more exothermic than that of NaF.
parts.answer: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ have double the charges of Na⁺ and F⁻ (and Mg²⁺ is smaller), so the attraction between the ions is much stronger.
parts.working:
M1 higher charges on both ions
M2 stronger electrostatic attraction (Mg²⁺ smaller)

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)
stem: Data (kJ/mol): ΔHf⦵ CaO(s) −635; ΔHat⦵ Ca +178; 1st IE Ca +590; 2nd IE Ca +1145; ΔHat⦵ O +249; 1st EA O −141; lattice energy CaO −3454.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data to calculate the second electron affinity of oxygen.
parts.answer: +798 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the second electron affinity of oxygen is endothermic.
parts.answer: The electron is being added to a negative ion, O⁻, so energy is needed to overcome the repulsion between the O⁻ ion and the incoming electron.
parts.working:
M1 adding electron to negative ion
M2 repulsion must be overcome

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)
stem: Data (kJ/mol): ΔHat⦵ Mg +148; 1st IE Mg +738; 2nd IE Mg +1451; ΔHat⦵ Cl +122; 1st EA Cl −349.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔHf⦵ for the hypothetical compound MgCl(s), taking its lattice energy as −753 kJ/mol.
parts.answer: −94 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate ΔHf⦵ for MgCl₂(s), whose lattice energy is −2526 kJ/mol.
parts.answer: −643 kJ/mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why magnesium forms MgCl₂ and not MgCl, even though forming Mg²⁺ needs much more energy than forming Mg⁺.
parts.answer: The much more exothermic lattice energy of MgCl₂ (2+ ion, smaller and more highly charged) more than compensates for the second ionisation energy, so MgCl₂ is far more energetically stable (ΔHf much more negative).
parts.working:
M1 LE of MgCl₂ far more exothermic, outweighs IE2
M2 ΔHf(MgCl₂) much more negative, so MgCl₂ is more stable

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why MgCl₃ does not form.
parts.answer: The third electron would be removed from an inner (2p) shell, so the third IE (about 7700 kJ/mol) is too large to be recovered by the lattice energy.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)
stem: Aluminium oxide is mined as bauxite. Data (kJ/mol): ΔHf⦵ Al₂O₃(s) −1676; ΔHat⦵ Al +326; IE of Al: 1st +578, 2nd +1817, 3rd +2745; ΔHat⦵ O +249; 1st EA O −141; 2nd EA O +798.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the lattice energy of aluminium oxide.
parts.answer: 2Al³⁺(g) + 3O²⁻(g) → Al₂O₃(s)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the lattice energy of aluminium oxide.
parts.answer: −15 326 kJ/mol

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)
stem: Data (kJ/mol): ΔHf⦵ SrO(s) −592; 1st IE Sr +550; 2nd IE Sr +1064; ΔHat⦵ O +249; 1st EA O −141; 2nd EA O +798; lattice energy SrO −3276.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data to calculate the enthalpy change of atomisation of strontium.
parts.answer: +164 kJ/mol
parts.working:
M1 ΔHf = ΔHat(Sr) + IE1 + IE2 + ΔHat(O) + EA1 + EA2 + LE
M1 ΔHat(Sr) = −592 − 550 − 1064 − 249 + 141 − 798 + 3276
A1 +164 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the lattice energy of SrO is less exothermic than that of CaO (−3454 kJ/mol).
parts.answer: Sr²⁺ is larger than Ca²⁺, so the ions are further apart and attract less strongly.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)

parts.label: a
parts.text: List, in order, the enthalpy changes in a Born–Haber cycle that lead from K(s) and ½Cl₂(g) to K⁺(g) and Cl⁻(g), giving an equation for each.
parts.answer: atomisation of K: K(s) → K(g); 1st IE of K: K(g) → K⁺(g) + e⁻; atomisation of Cl: ½Cl₂(g) → Cl(g); 1st EA of Cl: Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g) (atomisation steps may come in either order before the ionisation/EA steps)
parts.working: B1 each step with correct equation

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which of the steps in (a) are exothermic.
parts.answer: Only the first electron affinity of chlorine

parts.label: c
parts.text: Given ΔHf⦵ KCl = −437, ΔHat K = +89, IE K = +419, ΔHat Cl = +122 and EA Cl = −349 (all kJ/mol), calculate the lattice energy of KCl.
parts.answer: −718 kJ/mol

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)
stem: Data (kJ/mol): ΔHf⦵ MgF₂(s) −1124; ΔHat⦵ Mg +148; 1st IE Mg +738; 2nd IE Mg +1451; ΔHat⦵ F +79; 1st EA F −328.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the lattice energy of magnesium fluoride.
parts.answer: −2963 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: The lattice energy of MgO is −3845 kJ/mol. Predict which of MgO and MgF₂ has the higher melting point and explain your answer.
parts.answer: MgO: O²⁻ has twice the charge of F⁻, so stronger attraction between ions; more energy needed to separate them.
parts.working:
B1 MgO
B1 O²⁻ double charge → stronger ionic attraction / more exothermic lattice energy

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)
stem: Data (kJ/mol): ΔHf⦵ CsCl(s) −443; ΔHat⦵ Cs +76; 1st IE Cs +376; ΔHat⦵ Cl +122; lattice energy CsCl −668.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data to calculate the first electron affinity of chlorine.
parts.answer: −349 kJ/mol
parts.working:
M1 cycle: ΔHf = ΔHat(Cs) + IE(Cs) + ΔHat(Cl) + EA(Cl) + LE
M1 EA = −443 − 76 − 376 − 122 + 668
A1 −349 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the first ionisation energy of caesium is low, and explain why the lattice energy of CsCl (−668 kJ/mol) is less exothermic than that of NaCl (−787 kJ/mol).
parts.answer: Cs has its outer electron in the 6th shell, far from the nucleus with a lot of shielding, so little energy is needed to remove it. Cs⁺ is much larger than Na⁺ (same charge), so the distance between ion centres is larger and the attraction between Cs⁺ and Cl⁻ is weaker.
parts.working:
M1 outer electron far from nucleus / much shielding, so low IE
M2 Cs⁺ larger than Na⁺, ions further apart, weaker attraction → less exothermic lattice energy

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the standard enthalpy change of hydration of an ion.
parts.answer: The enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous ions dissolves in water to form an infinitely dilute solution (one mole of aqueous ions), under standard conditions.
parts.working:
M1 one mole of gaseous ions
M2 dissolved in (excess) water to form aqueous ions

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define the standard enthalpy change of solution.
parts.answer: The enthalpy change when one mole of a solute dissolves in enough solvent to form an infinitely dilute solution, under standard conditions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write equations, with state symbols, for (i) the enthalpy change of hydration of K⁺ and (ii) the enthalpy change of solution of NaCl.
parts.answer: (i) K⁺(g) + aq → K⁺(aq) (ii) NaCl(s) + aq → Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)
stem: Data (kJ/mol): lattice energy NaCl −787; ΔHhyd⦵ Na⁺ −419; ΔHhyd⦵ Cl⁻ −364.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe, in words, an energy cycle linking the lattice energy, the hydration enthalpies and the enthalpy change of solution of NaCl.
parts.answer: NaCl(s) → Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g) (reverse of lattice energy, +787) → Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) (sum of hydration enthalpies); this equals NaCl(s) → Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) (ΔHsol).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the enthalpy change of solution of NaCl.
parts.answer: +4 kJ/mol
parts.working:
M1 ΔHsol = −LE + ΔHhyd(Na⁺) + ΔHhyd(Cl⁻) = 787 − 419 − 364
A1 +4 kJ/mol

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)
stem: Hydration enthalpies (kJ/mol): Li⁺ −519; Na⁺ −419; K⁺ −322; Mg²⁺ −1920.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the trend in hydration enthalpy from Li⁺ to K⁺.
parts.answer: Ionic radius increases from Li⁺ to K⁺ (same charge), so charge density falls and the attraction between the ion and the δ− oxygen of water molecules becomes weaker; hydration is less exothermic.
parts.working:
M1 ionic radius increases / charge density decreases
M2 weaker attraction to (O of) water molecules

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the hydration enthalpy of Mg²⁺ is much more exothermic than that of Na⁺.
parts.answer: Mg²⁺ has twice the charge and a smaller radius, so a much higher charge density and stronger attraction for water molecules.
parts.working:
M1 higher charge and smaller
M2 stronger ion–dipole attraction

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how water molecules are arranged around a cation and around an anion.
parts.answer: Around a cation the δ− oxygen atoms point towards the ion; around an anion the δ+ hydrogen atoms point towards the ion.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)
stem: Data (kJ/mol): enthalpy change of solution of KCl +17.2; lattice energy KCl −703; ΔHhyd⦵ K⁺ −322.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the hydration enthalpy of the chloride ion. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: −364 kJ/mol
parts.working:
M1 ΔHsol = −LE + ΔHhyd(K⁺) + ΔHhyd(Cl⁻)
M1 ΔHhyd(Cl⁻) = 17.2 + (−703) − (−322)
A1 −364 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict whether the temperature rises or falls when KCl dissolves in water.
parts.answer: Falls (ΔHsol is positive / endothermic).

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)
stem: A student investigates instant cold packs used by sports teams. 8.00 g of ammonium nitrate is added to 50.0 g of water in a polystyrene cup. The temperature falls from 21.5 °C to 10.3 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the heat energy absorbed from the water. [c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the enthalpy change of solution of ammonium nitrate, in kJ/mol, including its sign. [Mr: NH₄NO₃, 80.0]
parts.answer: +23.4 kJ/mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two assumptions made in your calculation.
parts.answer: The solution has the same specific heat capacity (and density) as water; mass of solid is ignored (mass of solution = 50.0 g); no heat is gained from the surroundings / cup has negligible heat capacity.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one improvement to the method that would make the result more accurate.
parts.answer: Insulate the cup (lid, second cup) or take readings over time and extrapolate the cooling curve back to the time of mixing.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)
stem: Data (kJ/mol): lattice energy MgCl₂ −2526; ΔHhyd⦵ Mg²⁺ −1920; ΔHhyd⦵ Cl⁻ −364.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the enthalpy change of solution of magnesium chloride.
parts.answer: −122 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the chloride hydration enthalpy must be multiplied by 2 in this calculation.
parts.answer: One mole of MgCl₂ produces two moles of Cl⁻ ions.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)
stem: Data (kJ/mol): enthalpy change of solution of LiF +4.9; ΔHhyd⦵ Li⁺ −519; ΔHhyd⦵ F⁻ −506.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the lattice energy of lithium fluoride from these data. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: −1030 kJ/mol
parts.working:
M1 ΔHsol = −LE + ΔHhyd(Li⁺) + ΔHhyd(F⁻)
M1 LE = −519 + (−506) − 4.9
A1 −1030 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Lithium fluoride is only slightly soluble in water, but lithium chloride is very soluble. Suggest an explanation in terms of the enthalpy changes involved.
parts.answer: F⁻ is very small, so the lattice energy of LiF is very exothermic; the large hydration enthalpies of Li⁺ and F⁻ only just balance it (ΔHsol slightly positive). For LiCl the lattice energy falls more (larger Cl⁻) than the hydration enthalpy, so ΔHsol is negative.
parts.working:
M1 LiF lattice energy very large (small ions)
M2 for LiCl lattice energy decreases more than hydration enthalpy, so dissolving is more favourable

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)
stem: Data (kJ/mol): lattice energy MgSO₄ −2833, BaSO₄ −2469; ΔHhyd⦵ Mg²⁺ −1920, Ba²⁺ −1360, SO₄²⁻ −1059.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the enthalpy change of solution of MgSO₄ and of BaSO₄.
parts.answer: MgSO₄ −146 kJ/mol; BaSO₄ +50 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the data to explain why the solubility of the Group 2 sulfates decreases down the group.
parts.answer: The sulfate ion is large, so the lattice energy changes only a little as the cation gets bigger (−2833 to −2469, a change of 364). The hydration enthalpy of the cation falls much more (−1920 to −1360, a change of 560). So ΔHsol becomes less exothermic / more endothermic down the group and the sulfates become less soluble.
parts.working:
M1 lattice energy decreases only slightly (large SO₄²⁻ dominates the inter-ionic distance)
M1 cation hydration enthalpy decreases much more
M1 ΔHsol becomes more endothermic → less soluble

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)
stem:
A student dissolves different masses of potassium nitrate, KNO₃, in 50.0 g portions of water and records the temperature fall.
mass of KNO₃ / g: 2.02, 4.04, 6.06, 8.08
temperature fall / °C: 3.2, 6.5, 8.1, 13.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result and suggest one reason for it.
parts.answer: 6.06 g (ΔT 8.1 °C), which is well below the trend (about 9.8 °C expected); e.g. not all the solid dissolved, or the minimum temperature was missed.
parts.working:
B1 6.06 g result
B1 sensible reason

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the result for 8.08 g to calculate the enthalpy change of solution of potassium nitrate. [Mr: KNO₃, 101.1; c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹]
parts.answer: +34.0 kJ/mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: The data-book value is +34.9 kJ/mol. Suggest why the experimental value is lower and how this error could be reduced.
parts.answer: Heat is gained from the surroundings while the solution is below room temperature, so the measured ΔT is too small. Use a lid/insulation, or plot temperature against time and extrapolate to find the true minimum.
parts.working:
M1 heat gained from surroundings
M2 insulation / extrapolation of cooling curve

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the hydration enthalpy of F⁻ (−506 kJ/mol) is more exothermic than that of Cl⁻ (−364 kJ/mol).
parts.answer: F⁻ is smaller than Cl⁻ (same charge), so it has a higher charge density and attracts the δ+ hydrogen atoms of water molecules more strongly.
parts.working:
M1 F⁻ smaller / higher charge density
M2 stronger attraction to δ+ H of water

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the type of interaction between an ion and the water molecules around it.
parts.answer: Ion–dipole attraction

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)
stem: Data (kJ/mol): ΔHf⦵ NaCl(s) −411; ΔHat⦵ Na +107; 1st IE Na +496; ΔHat⦵ Cl +122; 1st EA Cl −349; enthalpy change of solution of NaCl +3.9; ΔHhyd⦵ Cl⁻ −364.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the lattice energy of NaCl.
parts.answer: −787 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence calculate the hydration enthalpy of Na⁺. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: −419 kJ/mol
parts.working:
M1 ΔHhyd(Na⁺) = ΔHsol + LE − ΔHhyd(Cl⁻) = 3.9 + (−787) − (−364)
A1 −419 kJ/mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the enthalpy change for Na(s) + ½Cl₂(g) → Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq).
parts.answer: −407 kJ/mol

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)
stem: Data (kJ/mol): lattice energy CaCl₂ −2255; ΔHhyd⦵ Ca²⁺ −1650; ΔHhyd⦵ Cl⁻ −364.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the enthalpy change of solution of calcium chloride.
parts.answer: −123 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: 5.55 g of anhydrous CaCl₂ is dissolved in 100 g of water. Using your answer to (a), calculate the expected temperature rise. [Mr: CaCl₂, 111.1; c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹; assume the solution has mass 100 g]

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the first electron affinity of an element.
parts.answer: The enthalpy change when one electron is added to each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1− ions.
parts.working:
M1 one mole of gaseous atoms each gaining one electron
M2 forming gaseous 1− ions

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the equation for the first electron affinity of oxygen.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the first electron affinity of oxygen is exothermic.
parts.answer: The incoming electron is attracted by the nucleus (effective nuclear charge), so energy is released.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)
stem: First electron affinities (kJ/mol): F −328; Cl −349; Br −325; I −295.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the general trend from chlorine to iodine.
parts.answer: The atoms get larger with more shielding, so the incoming electron is further from the nucleus and attracted less strongly; less energy is released.
parts.working:
M1 larger atom / more shielding
M2 weaker attraction for added electron

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why fluorine's first electron affinity is less exothermic than chlorine's.
parts.answer: F is very small, so the added electron is repelled strongly by the electrons already in the small, crowded 2p sub-shell.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The second electron affinity of sulfur is +640 kJ/mol. Calculate the enthalpy change for S(g) + 2e⁻ → S²⁻(g) given that the first electron affinity of sulfur is −200 kJ/mol.
parts.answer: +440 kJ/mol

author: HomiLabs

topic: Chemical energetics (A Level: lattice energy, Born–Haber, hydration)
stem: Data (kJ/mol): 1st IE Mg +738; 2nd IE Mg +1451; 1st EA O −141; 2nd EA O +798.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the enthalpy change for O(g) + 2e⁻ → O²⁻(g).
parts.answer: +657 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total enthalpy change for Mg(g) + O(g) → Mg²⁺(g) + O²⁻(g).
parts.answer: +2846 kJ/mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: Forming the gaseous ions is very endothermic, yet magnesium burns vigorously in oxygen to form MgO. Explain why.
parts.answer: The lattice energy of MgO is very exothermic (small, doubly charged ions attract strongly), which more than compensates for the energy needed to form the ions, so ΔHf of MgO is very negative.
parts.working:
M1 very exothermic lattice energy
M2 outweighs the endothermic steps so overall ΔHf negative

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student in a Lahore college laboratory pipettes 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution into a conical flask and titrates it with 0.100 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid using phenolphthalein. The mean titre is 21.35 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation, with state symbols, for the reaction of sodium hydroxide with sulfuric acid.
parts.answer: 2NaOH(aq) + H₂SO₄(aq) → Na₂SO₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l)
parts.working: B1 correct formulae, balancing and state symbols.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of sulfuric acid used in the mean titre.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the concentration, in mol/dm³, of the sodium hydroxide solution. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 0.171 mol/dm³

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A food-quality analyst tests a brand of white vinegar sold in Karachi. 25.0 cm³ of the vinegar is diluted to 250 cm³ with distilled water in a volumetric flask. 25.0 cm³ portions of the diluted solution are titrated with 0.0950 mol/dm³ NaOH(aq).
Titre results (cm³): rough 19.10; run 1 18.60; run 2 18.95; run 3 18.70.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the concordant titres and calculate the mean titre.
parts.answer: 18.60 and 18.70 cm³; mean = 18.65 cm³
parts.working: B1 uses only titres within 0.10 cm³ of each other (rough and 18.95 cm³ excluded).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the concentration, in mol/dm³, of ethanoic acid in the diluted solution.
parts.answer: 0.0709 mol/dm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of ethanoic acid in the original vinegar, in g/dm³. [Mr of CH₃COOH = 60.0]
parts.answer: 42.5 g/dm³
parts.working: M1 dilution factor 250/25.0 = 10, so 0.709 mol/dm³; A1 × 60.0 = 42.5 g/dm³.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the vinegar was diluted before titration.
parts.answer: So that a sensible titre (within one burette filling) is obtained / the undiluted acid would need too large a volume of NaOH.
parts.working: B1 any one: titre would exceed 50 cm³ burette; reduces percentage error from a very large titre.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A 0.500 g antacid tablet bought from a pharmacy in Peshawar contains calcium carbonate as its only base. The tablet is added to 50.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid (an excess). When reaction stops, the excess acid needs 22.40 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ NaOH(aq) for neutralisation. [Mr of CaCO₃ = 100.1]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount of HCl added to the tablet and the amount left over after the reaction.
parts.answer: added 0.0100 mol; left over 0.00224 mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of calcium carbonate in the tablet. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: M1 HCl reacted = 0.007760 mol; M1 CaCO₃ = ÷2 = 0.003880 mol (CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂); A1 mass = 0.388 g → 77.7 %.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a back titration is used here rather than titrating the tablet directly with acid.
parts.answer: CaCO₃ is insoluble and reacts slowly, so the end point of a direct titration would be unclear.
parts.working: B1 insoluble solid / slow reaction / no sharp end point.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
25.0 cm³ of sodium carbonate solution is titrated with 0.150 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid using methyl orange. The end point is reached after 20.0 cm³ of acid.
Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂
What is the concentration of the sodium carbonate solution?
A 0.0300 mol/dm³
B 0.0600 mol/dm³
C 0.120 mol/dm³
D 0.240 mol/dm³
parts.answer: B 0.0600 mol/dm³
parts.working: mol HCl = 0.150 × 0.0200 = 0.00300; mol Na₂CO₃ = 0.00150; ÷ 0.0250 = 0.0600 mol/dm³. C ignores the 1:2 ratio.

stem:
An iron supplement tablet is dissolved in dilute sulfuric acid and the solution made up to 100 cm³. 25.0 cm³ of this solution needs 14.60 cm³ of 0.00500 mol/dm³ potassium manganate(VII) for complete reaction.
MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount of MnO₄⁻ ions used in the titration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of iron, in mg, in one tablet. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. [Ar of Fe = 55.8]

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why no indicator is added to this titration.
parts.answer: MnO₄⁻ is purple and Mn²⁺ is almost colourless, so the first permanent pale pink colour shows the end point.
parts.working: B1 KMnO₄ acts as its own indicator.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
How many atoms in total are present in 0.25 mol of ammonia, NH₃? [L = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹]
A 1.51 × 10²³
B 4.52 × 10²³
C 6.02 × 10²³
D 2.41 × 10²⁴
parts.working: 0.25 mol molecules × 4 atoms per molecule = 1.0 mol atoms = 6.02 × 10²³. A counts molecules only.

stem: Aluminium sulfate is used as a coagulant at water treatment plants such as those supplying Islamabad.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the relative formula mass of aluminium sulfate, Al₂(SO₄)₃.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of 0.0350 mol of aluminium sulfate.

parts.label: c

parts.answer: 0.0401 mol/dm³

stem: One sachet of oral rehydration salts (ORS), widely used in Pakistan for treating diarrhoea, is dissolved in water to make 1.00 dm³ of solution. It contains: 2.6 g NaCl, 1.5 g KCl, 2.9 g trisodium citrate dihydrate (Na₃C₆H₅O₇·2H₂O) and 13.5 g glucose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentration, in mmol/dm³, of Na⁺ ions in the solution. [Mr: NaCl 58.5; Na₃C₆H₅O₇·2H₂O 294.0]
parts.answer: 74.0 mmol/dm³
parts.working: M1 NaCl: 2.6/58.5 = 0.0444 mol; M1 citrate: 2.9/294.0 = 0.00986 mol → Na⁺ = 3 × that = 0.0296 mol; A1 total 74.0 mmol/dm³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the concentration, in mmol/dm³, of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆.
parts.answer: 75.0 mmol/dm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the concentration, in mmol/dm³, of Cl⁻ ions in the solution. [Mr KCl = 74.6]
parts.answer: 64.6 mmol/dm³
parts.working: M1 Cl⁻ from both NaCl and KCl: 0.0444 + 0.0201; A1 64.6 mmol/dm³.

stem: A sample of bromine contains two isotopes: ⁷⁹Br (isotopic mass 78.92, abundance 50.69 %) and ⁸¹Br (isotopic mass 80.92, abundance 49.31 %).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term relative atomic mass.
parts.answer: The weighted average mass of the atoms of an element compared with 1/12 of the mass of an atom of carbon-12.
parts.working: B1 weighted mean/average mass of atoms (of naturally occurring isotopes); B1 relative to 1/12 the mass of a ¹²C atom.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the relative atomic mass of bromine. Give your answer to 4 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage abundance of ⁶⁹Ga in the sample. Take the isotopic masses as 69.0 and 71.0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one way in which the atoms of ⁶⁹Ga and ⁷¹Ga are the same and one way in which they differ.
parts.answer: Same: number of protons (31) and electrons / same chemical properties. Different: number of neutrons (38 and 40).
parts.working: B1 same proton number/electron configuration; B1 different number of neutrons.

stem: Chlorine has two isotopes, ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl, in the abundance ratio 3 : 1. A sample of chlorine gas, Cl₂, is analysed in a mass spectrometer. Take the isotopic masses as 35 and 37.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the m/z values of the three molecular-ion peaks for Cl₂⁺.

parts.text: Use your ratio to calculate the mean relative molecular mass of chlorine molecules.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A sample of element X contains three isotopes: ²⁴X (79.0 %), ²⁵X (10.0 %) and ²⁶X (11.0 %). Taking the isotopic masses as whole numbers, what is the relative atomic mass of X?
A 24.1
B 24.3
C 24.5
D 25.0
parts.working: (24 × 79.0 + 25 × 10.0 + 26 × 11.0)/100 = 24.32 → 24.3. D is the unweighted mean of the mass numbers.

stem: In a lime kiln in Punjab, limestone (calcium carbonate) is heated strongly to make quicklime (calcium oxide).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate.
parts.answer: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass, in kg, of calcium oxide formed from 5.00 kg of calcium carbonate. [Mr: CaCO₃ 100.1; CaO 56.1]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the volume, in dm³, of carbon dioxide released, measured at room temperature and pressure. [molar volume = 24.0 dm³/mol]
parts.answer: 1200 dm³

author: HomiLabs

stem: 0.360 g of magnesium ribbon is added to 25.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. [Ar Mg = 24.3; molar gas volume 24.0 dm³ at r.t.p.]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show by calculation which reactant is in excess.
parts.answer: Magnesium is in excess: 0.0148 mol Mg needs 0.0296 mol HCl but only 0.0250 mol HCl is present.
parts.working: M1 mol Mg = 0.360/24.3 = 0.0148; mol HCl = 0.0250; A1 HCl needed 0.0296 > 0.0250 so Mg in excess.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the volume of hydrogen, in cm³, produced at room temperature and pressure.
parts.answer: 300 cm³
parts.working: M1 mol H₂ = 0.0250/2 = 0.0125 (from limiting HCl); A1 × 24 000 = 300 cm³.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
20 cm³ of a gaseous hydrocarbon CₓHᵧ is mixed with 150 cm³ of oxygen (an excess) and exploded. After cooling to room temperature (water is a liquid), the gas volume is 110 cm³. After passing the gas through NaOH(aq), 50 cm³ of gas remains. All volumes are measured at the same temperature and pressure.
CₓHᵧ + (x + y/4)O₂ → xCO₂ + (y/2)H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide formed and the volume of oxygen that reacted.
parts.answer: CO₂ = 60 cm³; O₂ reacted = 100 cm³
parts.working: B1 CO₂ = 110 − 50 = 60 cm³ (absorbed by NaOH); B1 O₂ left = 50 cm³, so O₂ used = 150 − 50 = 100 cm³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Deduce the molecular formula of the hydrocarbon. Show your working.
parts.answer: C₃H₈

author: HomiLabs

stem: Compound Y, a sweet-smelling liquid used as a solvent in nail-varnish remover, contains 54.5 % carbon, 9.1 % hydrogen and 36.4 % oxygen by mass.

parts.text: Calculate the empirical formula of Y.
parts.answer: C₂H₄O

parts.answer: C₄H₈O₂

author: HomiLabs

stem: 0.360 g of an organic compound Z, containing only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, is burned completely in oxygen. It forms 0.528 g of carbon dioxide and 0.216 g of water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the masses of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen in the sample.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Deduce the empirical formula and, given Mr = 60.0, the molecular formula of Z.
parts.answer: CH₂O; C₂H₄O₂

author: HomiLabs

stem: 2.32 g of a black iron oxide found in sand from a beach near Gwadar is heated in a stream of hydrogen until only iron remains. The mass of iron is 1.68 g. [Ar: Fe 55.8; O 16.0]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the empirical formula of the oxide.
parts.answer: Fe₃O₄

parts.label: b
parts.text: This oxide contains both Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ ions. Deduce the ratio of Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ ions.
parts.working: M1 total positive charge must be +8 for 4 O²⁻; A1 one Fe²⁺ and two Fe³⁺ (2 + 6 = 8).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student heats 2.46 g of hydrated magnesium sulfate (Epsom salt), MgSO₄·xH₂O, until all the water is removed. 1.20 g of anhydrous magnesium sulfate remains.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of x in MgSO₄·xH₂O. [Mr: MgSO₄ 120.4; H₂O 18.0]
parts.working: M1 mass water 1.26 g → 0.0700 mol; M1 mol MgSO₄ = 1.20/120.4 = 0.00997; A1 ratio 7.02 → 7.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the student could check that all the water had been removed.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Hydrated barium chloride, BaCl₂·xH₂O, is heated in a crucible.
Mass of empty crucible / g: 15.62
Mass of crucible + hydrated salt / g: 18.06
Mass after 1st heating / g: 17.74
Mass after 2nd heating / g: 17.70
Mass after 3rd heating / g: 17.70

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the crucible was heated three times.
parts.answer: To make sure all water of crystallisation was removed – the last two masses agree (constant mass).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of water lost and the mass of anhydrous barium chloride.
parts.answer: water 0.36 g; BaCl₂ 2.08 g

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the value of x. [Mr: BaCl₂ 208.3; H₂O 18.0]
parts.working: M1 mol H₂O 0.0200, mol BaCl₂ 0.00999; A1 ratio 2.00 → 2.

parts.label: d
parts.text: If some solid spat out of the crucible during heating, state and explain the effect on the value of x.
parts.answer: x would be too high
parts.working: M1 mass loss too large / recorded as water; A1 calculated water too high so x too high.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
1.43 g of washing soda crystals, Na₂CO₃·xH₂O, is dissolved in water and made up to 250 cm³. 25.0 cm³ of this solution needs 20.0 cm³ of 0.0500 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid for complete reaction.
Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount of Na₂CO₃ in the 250 cm³ of solution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the Mr of the hydrated crystals and hence the value of x. [Mr of Na₂CO₃ = 106.0]

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What volume of oxygen, measured at room temperature and pressure, is needed for the complete combustion of 0.10 mol of butane, C₄H₁₀? [molar gas volume = 24.0 dm³]
A 9.6 dm³
B 10.8 dm³
C 15.6 dm³
D 31.2 dm³
parts.answer: C 15.6 dm³
parts.working: C₄H₁₀ + 6½O₂ → 4CO₂ + 5H₂O; 0.10 × 6.5 = 0.65 mol × 24.0 = 15.6 dm³. D uses 13 mol O₂ per mol butane.

stem: 0.0100 mol of a metal M reacts exactly with 0.0300 mol of hydrochloric acid, forming hydrogen and a solution containing only ions of M and chloride ions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Deduce the charge on the ion of M formed. Explain your answer.

parts.text: Write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the reaction of M with the acid.
parts.answer: 2M(s) + 6H⁺(aq) → 2M³⁺(aq) + 3H₂(g)

parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction of solid ammonium sulfate with sodium hydroxide solution on warming.
parts.answer: (NH₄)₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2NH₃ + 2H₂O

author: HomiLabs

stem: 3.312 g of lead(II) nitrate is heated until no further change. The solid residue is 2.232 g of lead(II) oxide. 480 cm³ of nitrogen dioxide and 120 cm³ of oxygen are collected (volumes at r.t.p.; molar gas volume 24.0 dm³).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amounts, in mol, of Pb(NO₃)₂ heated, PbO formed, NO₂ formed and O₂ formed. [Mr: Pb(NO₃)₂ 331.2; PbO 223.2]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answers to deduce the balanced equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: 2Pb(NO₃)₂ → 2PbO + 4NO₂ + O₂

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that the equation is consistent with the conservation of mass, using the masses given.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
6.00 g of ethanoic acid is heated with excess ethanol and a little concentrated sulfuric acid. 5.28 g of ethyl ethanoate is obtained.
CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Chloroethane can be made by two routes.
Route A: C₂H₄ + HCl → C₂H₅Cl
Route B: C₂H₆ + Cl₂ → C₂H₅Cl + HCl (in ultraviolet light)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the atom economy of each route. [Mr: C₂H₄ 28.0; HCl 36.5; C₂H₆ 30.0; Cl₂ 71.0; C₂H₅Cl 64.5]
parts.answer: Route A 100 %; Route B 63.9 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: In route B, 10.0 g of ethane gives a 40.0 % yield of chloroethane. Calculate the mass of chloroethane obtained.

parts.text: Give two reasons, other than atom economy, why route A is preferred.
parts.answer: Route B gives a mixture of further-substituted products (e.g. dichloroethanes) so low yield and separation needed; route B needs UV light and produces corrosive HCl waste.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: multiple substitution / mixture of products; lower yield; HCl by-product; A is a single product addition.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the formula of chromium(III) sulfate?
A CrSO₄
B Cr₂SO₄
C Cr₂(SO₄)₃
D Cr₃(SO₄)₂
parts.answer: C Cr₂(SO₄)₃
parts.working: Cr³⁺ and SO₄²⁻: two Cr³⁺ (+6) balance three SO₄²⁻ (−6). D swaps the numbers of each ion.

stem: Fertilisers, hard water and photographic chemicals contain a range of ions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the formula of each compound: (i) ammonium phosphate (ii) calcium hydrogencarbonate (iii) iron(II) hydroxide (iv) sodium thiosulfate.
parts.answer: (i) (NH₄)₃PO₄ (ii) Ca(HCO₃)₂ (iii) Fe(OH)₂ (iv) Na₂S₂O₃

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the formula, including charge, of: (i) the nitrite ion (ii) the manganate(VII) ion.
parts.answer: (i) NO₂⁻ (ii) MnO₄⁻

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A and B react in solution. Initial rates were measured at constant temperature.
Expt 1: [A] = 0.10, [B] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, rate = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
Expt 2: [A] = 0.20, [B] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, rate = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
Expt 3: [A] = 0.10, [B] = 0.30 mol dm⁻³, rate = 1.8 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text: Deduce the order of reaction with respect to A and with respect to B. Explain your reasoning.
parts.answer: First order in A; second order in B
parts.working: B1 expts 1→2: [A] doubles, rate doubles → first order in A; B1 expts 1→3: [B] ×3, rate ×9 → second order in B.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the rate equation and calculate the rate constant, k, including its units.
parts.answer: rate = k[A][B]²; k = 0.20 dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹
parts.working: B1 rate equation; M1 k = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ ÷ (0.10 × 0.10²) = 0.20; A1 units dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the initial rate when [A] = 0.25 mol dm⁻³ and [B] = 0.040 mol dm⁻³.
parts.answer: 8.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Propanone reacts with iodine in acid solution:
CH₃COCH₃ + I₂ → CH₃COCH₂I + HI
The rate equation is rate = k[CH₃COCH₃][H⁺]. With [CH₃COCH₃] = 0.40 mol dm⁻³, [H⁺] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³ and [I₂] = 0.0020 mol dm⁻³, the initial rate is 3.4 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the rate equation tells you about the role of iodine in the rate-determining step.
parts.answer: Iodine is not involved in the rate-determining step (it reacts in a later, fast step).
parts.working: B1 zero order → I₂ not in / after the RDS.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate constant and give its units.
parts.answer: k = 4.25 × 10⁻⁴ dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the initial rate when [CH₃COCH₃] = 0.60 mol dm⁻³, [H⁺] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³ and [I₂] is doubled.
parts.answer: 2.55 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest how the rate of this reaction could be followed.
parts.answer: Use a colorimeter to measure the decrease in the brown/yellow iodine colour over time.
parts.working: B1 colorimetry (or titrating quenched samples with thiosulfate).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the units of the rate constant for a reaction that is (i) zero order overall (ii) first order overall (iii) second order overall.
parts.answer: (i) mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ (ii) s⁻¹ (iii) dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the shape of a graph of concentration of reactant against time for a reaction that is zero order with respect to that reactant.
parts.answer: A straight line with negative gradient (constant rate).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the shape of a graph of initial rate against concentration of a reactant for a reaction that is second order with respect to it.
parts.answer: A curve upwards through the origin (rate ∝ [X]², a parabola).

stem:
Nitrogen monoxide reacts with oxygen: 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g). The rate equation is rate = k[NO]²[O₂].
Expt 1: [NO] = 0.020, [O₂] = 0.010 mol dm⁻³, rate = 6.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
Expt 2: [NO] = 0.010, [O₂] = 0.040 mol dm⁻³, rate = X
Expt 3: [NO] = Y, [O₂] = 0.010 mol dm⁻³, rate = 0.054 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate constant, k, with units, using experiment 1.
parts.answer: k = 1500 dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the missing value X (rate in experiment 2).
parts.answer: X = 0.0060 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the missing value Y ([NO] in experiment 3).
parts.answer: Y = 0.060 mol dm⁻³

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the rate equation suggests the reaction might occur in a single step, and why this is unlikely in practice.
parts.answer: Rate eq matches the stoichiometry 2NO + O₂ (a termolecular collision); a three-particle collision with correct orientation and energy is very improbable.
parts.working: B1 orders match equation coefficients; B1 simultaneous collision of three particles very unlikely.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student investigates the reaction S₂O₈²⁻ + 2I⁻ → 2SO₄²⁻ + I₂ using an iodine clock. Each mixture contains 10.0 cm³ of K₂S₂O₈(aq), 5.0 cm³ of Na₂S₂O₃(aq), 1 cm³ of starch, a volume V of KI(aq) and enough water to make the total volume 26.0 cm³. The time t for the blue-black colour to appear is recorded.
V / cm³: 10, 8, 6, 4, 2
t / s: 22.0, 27.5, 36.7, 55.0, 110.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the total volume of each mixture is kept the same.
parts.answer: So that the volume of KI solution is proportional to [I⁻] in the mixture.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate 1000/t for each experiment, giving values to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: B2 all five correct (B1 for three or four).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why 1/t can be used as a measure of the initial rate.
parts.answer: Each run stops when the same fixed amount of iodine has been formed (just enough to use up all the thiosulfate), so rate ∝ amount/t ∝ 1/t.
parts.working: B1 same (fixed) amount of I₂ formed/reacted before the blue-black colour appears in every run.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Use your values to deduce the order of reaction with respect to iodide ions. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: First order
parts.working: M1 1/t is directly proportional to volume of KI (e.g. halving volume halves 1/t; graph straight line through origin); A1 first order.

parts.label: e
parts.text: State two variables, other than total volume, that must be kept constant.
parts.answer: Temperature; concentration/volume of peroxodisulfate (and of thiosulfate and starch).

author: HomiLabs

stem: For the reaction X + 2Y → Z, the rate equation is rate = k[X][Y]².

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the order of reaction with respect to X, with respect to Y, and overall.
parts.answer: X: 1; Y: 2; overall 3
parts.working: B1 X and Y; B1 overall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the factor by which the rate changes when the concentrations of both X and Y are doubled.
parts.answer: 8 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the factor by which the rate changes if [X] is tripled and [Y] is halved.
parts.answer: 0.75 (rate falls to three-quarters)

author: HomiLabs

stem: The decomposition of dinitrogen pentoxide, 2N₂O₅(g) → 4NO₂(g) + O₂(g), is first order with a constant half-life of 24 minutes at a certain temperature.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the fraction of the original N₂O₅ remaining after 96 minutes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate constant, in min⁻¹, using k = 0.693/t½.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the half-life would change if the initial concentration of N₂O₅ were doubled. Explain.
parts.answer: No change – the half-life of a first-order reaction is independent of the starting concentration.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Hydrogen peroxide decomposes in the presence of a catalyst. The concentration of H₂O₂ is measured over time.
t / s: 0, 100, 200, 300, 400, 600
[H₂O₂] / mol dm⁻³: 0.800, 0.566, 0.400, 0.283, 0.200, 0.100

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data to show that the reaction is first order with respect to H₂O₂.
parts.answer: Successive half-lives are constant: 0.800→0.400 in 200 s, 0.400→0.200 in 200 s, 0.200→0.100 in 200 s.
parts.working: M1 two or more half-lives found from data; A1 they are equal (200 s), so first order.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate constant, k, using k = 0.693/t½, and give its units.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the initial rate of reaction.
parts.answer: 2.77 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ (accept 2.78 × 10⁻³)

author: HomiLabs

stem: 2-chloro-2-methylpropane is hydrolysed by water in a first-order reaction: rate = k[(CH₃)₃CCl], with k = 4.62 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ at 25 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the half-life of the reaction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for the concentration of 2-chloro-2-methylpropane to fall to 12.5 % of its initial value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the concentration of water does not appear in the rate equation, even though water is a reactant.
parts.answer: Water is the solvent and in large excess, so its concentration is effectively constant; and/or it is not involved in the slow step (SN1 – RDS is ionisation of the C–Cl bond).
parts.working: B1 water in large excess/constant; B1 RDS involves only the halogenoalkane.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Ammonia decomposes on the surface of a hot tungsten wire: 2NH₃(g) → N₂(g) + 3H₂(g).
t / s: 0, 100, 200, 300, 400
[NH₃] / 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³: 2.00, 1.60, 1.20, 0.80, 0.40

parts.label: a
parts.text: Deduce the order of reaction with respect to ammonia. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Zero order
parts.working: M1 concentration falls by the same amount (0.40 × 10⁻³) in each 100 s – constant rate/straight line; A1 zero order.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate constant and give its units.
parts.answer: 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the time for the first half-life and the time for the next half-life (from 1.00 × 10⁻³ to 0.50 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³).
parts.answer: 250 s and 125 s

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the rate does not depend on the concentration of ammonia in this experiment.
parts.answer: The tungsten surface is fully covered with adsorbed ammonia (all active sites occupied), so extra NH₃ cannot react faster.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A medicine is removed from the body by a first-order process with a half-life of 6.0 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of the drug remaining in the body 24 hours after a 400 mg dose.
parts.answer: 25 mg

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the first-order rate constant, in h⁻¹.
parts.answer: 0.116 h⁻¹ (accept 0.115 h⁻¹)

parts.label: c
parts.text: The drug is effective only while at least 60 mg remains. A doctor says a second dose is needed after 12 hours. Use a calculation to show whether this advice is sensible.
parts.answer: Sensible: after 12 h (2 half-lives) 100 mg remains, still above 60 mg; after 18 h only 50 mg would remain (< 60 mg), so the level falls below 60 mg between 12 h and 18 h (at about 16.4 h) and a second dose at 12 h keeps the drug effective.
parts.working: M1 amounts at 12 h (100 mg) and 18 h (50 mg); A1 conclusion.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysis.
parts.answer: Homogeneous: catalyst in the same phase as the reactants; heterogeneous: catalyst in a different phase.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Classify each of the following as homogeneous or heterogeneous: (i) iron in the Haber process (ii) Fe²⁺ ions in the reaction of S₂O₈²⁻ with I⁻ (iii) platinum/rhodium in a catalytic converter (iv) NO₂ in the oxidation of atmospheric SO₂.
parts.answer: (i) heterogeneous (ii) homogeneous (iii) heterogeneous (iv) homogeneous

stem: Peroxodisulfate ions oxidise iodide ions: S₂O₈²⁻ + 2I⁻ → 2SO₄²⁻ + I₂. The reaction is catalysed by Fe²⁺(aq).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the uncatalysed reaction between S₂O₈²⁻ and I⁻ ions is slow.
parts.answer: Both ions are negatively charged, so they repel each other and collisions with enough energy are rare (high Ea).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write two equations to show how Fe²⁺ ions catalyse the reaction.
parts.answer: S₂O₈²⁻ + 2Fe²⁺ → 2SO₄²⁻ + 2Fe³⁺; 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Fe³⁺ ions can catalyse this reaction equally well.
parts.answer: The two steps occur in reverse order: Fe³⁺ first oxidises I⁻ to make Fe²⁺, which then reduces S₂O₈²⁻ – the catalyst is regenerated either way.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the property of iron that allows it to act as this catalyst.
parts.answer: It has variable oxidation states (+2 and +3).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Cars on the roads of Lahore are fitted with catalytic converters containing platinum and rhodium.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction between carbon monoxide and nitrogen monoxide in a catalytic converter.
parts.answer: 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the steps by which the solid catalyst speeds up this reaction.
parts.answer: Reactant molecules adsorb onto active sites on the metal surface; bonds in reactants weaken and molecules are held close together in suitable orientation, so reaction occurs; products desorb, freeing the sites.
parts.working: B1 adsorption; B1 bonds weakened/lower Ea/correct orientation; B1 desorption.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the catalyst is spread as a thin coating on a ceramic honeycomb.
parts.answer: Gives a large surface area so more active sites, and uses less expensive metal.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Over industrial cities, sulfur dioxide from burning fuel is oxidised in the air faster when nitrogen dioxide from vehicle engines is present.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write two equations to show how nitrogen dioxide catalyses the oxidation of sulfur dioxide to sulfur trioxide in the atmosphere.
parts.answer: SO₂ + NO₂ → SO₃ + NO; NO + ½O₂ → NO₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the oxidation numbers of nitrogen in NO₂ and in NO, and of sulfur in SO₂ and in SO₃.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this is described as homogeneous catalysis and how the overall equation shows that NO₂ is a catalyst.
parts.answer: All species are gases (same phase); NO₂ is used in the first step and regenerated in the second, so it does not appear in the overall equation SO₂ + ½O₂ → SO₃.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State why this reaction contributes to acid rain.
parts.answer: SO₃ reacts with water to form sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The reaction between nitrogen dioxide and carbon monoxide occurs in two steps:
Step 1 (slow): NO₂ + NO₂ → NO₃ + NO
Step 2 (fast): NO₃ + CO → NO₂ + CO₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the overall equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: NO₂ + CO → NO + CO₂
parts.working: B1 add steps and cancel NO₃ and one NO₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Deduce the rate equation. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: rate = k[NO₂]²
parts.working: M1 step 1 is slow/rate-determining; A1 involves two NO₂, CO not in RDS.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the intermediate in this mechanism.
parts.answer: NO₃

author: HomiLabs

stem: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide. The rate equation is rate = k[(CH₃)₃CBr].

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the order of reaction with respect to hydroxide ions and explain what this shows about the mechanism.
parts.answer: Zero order; OH⁻ is not involved in the rate-determining step, which is the slow ionisation of the C–Br bond.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the two-step mechanism, naming the intermediate.
parts.answer: Step 1 (slow): (CH₃)₃CBr → (CH₃)₃C⁺ + Br⁻ (heterolytic fission); Step 2 (fast): (CH₃)₃C⁺ + OH⁻ → (CH₃)₃COH. Intermediate: tertiary carbocation.
parts.working: B1 slow step forming carbocation; B1 fast attack by OH⁻.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the effect on the initial rate of doubling [(CH₃)₃CBr] and halving [OH⁻] at the same time.
parts.answer: Rate doubles

author: HomiLabs

stem: Hydrogen reacts with iodine monochloride: H₂(g) + 2ICl(g) → I₂(g) + 2HCl(g). The experimentally determined rate equation is rate = k[H₂][ICl].

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest a two-step mechanism consistent with the rate equation. Show which step is slow and identify the intermediate.
parts.answer: Step 1 (slow): H₂ + ICl → HI + HCl; Step 2 (fast): HI + ICl → HCl + I₂. Intermediate HI.
parts.working: B1 slow step contains one H₂ and one ICl; B1 fast step uses second ICl, steps add to overall equation; B1 HI intermediate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rate equation cannot be deduced from the overall equation.
parts.answer: Orders come from the rate-determining step, which need not match the stoichiometry; they must be found by experiment.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The [H₂] is tripled and [ICl] is reduced to one-third. State the effect on the rate.
parts.answer: No change

author: HomiLabs

stem: A mixture of gases reacts with activation energy Ea.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Boltzmann distribution curve for a gas at temperature T₁. Refer to the axes and the start of the curve.
parts.answer: y-axis: number/proportion of molecules; x-axis: energy. Curve starts at the origin, rises to a peak (most probable energy) and falls gradually, never touching the energy axis.
parts.working: B1 axes labelled; B1 starts at origin, single peak, asymptotic to x-axis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the curve changes at a higher temperature T₂.
parts.answer: Peak moves to higher energy and is lower; curve is broader with more molecules at high energy; area under curve unchanged.
parts.working: B1 peak lower and to the right; B1 same area / more molecules beyond Ea.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the Boltzmann distribution to explain why the rate of reaction increases with temperature.
parts.answer: A larger proportion of molecules have energy ≥ Ea, so more frequent successful collisions (also slightly more frequent collisions).
parts.working: B1 more molecules with E ≥ Ea; B1 more successful/effective collisions per unit time.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The temperature of a sample of gas is increased. Which statement about its Boltzmann distribution is correct?
A The total area under the curve increases.
B The peak becomes higher and moves to lower energy.
C The peak becomes lower and moves to higher energy.
D The activation energy moves to a lower value.
parts.answer: C The peak becomes lower and moves to higher energy.
parts.working: At higher temperature the most probable energy increases and the peak falls; the area (total number of molecules) stays the same, so A is wrong; Ea is unchanged by temperature.

stem:
Marble chips (calcium carbonate, in excess) are added to hydrochloric acid in a conical flask on a balance. The loss in mass, caused by carbon dioxide escaping, is recorded.
t / s: 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180, 210, 240
loss in mass / g: 0.00, 0.44, 0.78, 1.02, 1.18, 1.26, 1.30, 1.32, 1.32

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of carbon dioxide produced in total.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of reaction, in g s⁻¹, over the first 30 s and over the period 60 s to 90 s.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain, in terms of particles, why the rate decreases during the reaction.
parts.answer: Concentration of acid falls (and chip surface shrinks), so fewer particles per unit volume and fewer collisions per second.
parts.working: B1 concentration decreases; B1 collision frequency falls.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why a loose plug of cotton wool is placed in the neck of the flask.
parts.answer: Lets CO₂ escape but stops acid spray being lost (which would add to the mass loss).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plans to find how the concentration of hydrochloric acid affects the rate of its reaction with magnesium ribbon, collecting the hydrogen in a 100 cm³ gas syringe.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent variable, the dependent variable and two control variables.
parts.answer: Independent: concentration of HCl; dependent: volume of H₂ (with time); control: mass/length of Mg, volume of acid, temperature.
parts.working: B1 independent; B1 dependent; B1 two control variables.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A tangent drawn to the curve at t = 20 s passes through the points (0 s, 12 cm³) and (40 s, 52 cm³). Calculate the rate at 20 s.
parts.answer: 1.0 cm³ s⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one source of error in measuring the volume of gas at the start, and an improvement.
parts.answer: Gas lost while inserting the bung after adding Mg; place Mg in a small tube inside the flask and tip it over after sealing (or use a divided flask).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about the effect of a catalyst on a reversible reaction is correct?
A It increases the enthalpy change of the forward reaction.
B It lowers the activation energy of the forward reaction only.
C It increases the rates of the forward and backward reactions equally.
D It increases the equilibrium yield of products.
parts.answer: C It increases the rates of the forward and backward reactions equally.
parts.working: A catalyst provides an alternative route with lower Ea for both directions, so equilibrium is reached faster but its position is unchanged. B is wrong because the reverse Ea is lowered by the same amount.

stem: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes: 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g), ΔH = −98 kJ per mol of H₂O₂. The activation energy is 75 kJ mol⁻¹ without a catalyst and 23 kJ mol⁻¹ with the enzyme catalase (found in potato and liver).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the activation energy of the reverse reaction for the uncatalysed and the catalase-catalysed reactions.
parts.answer: 173 kJ mol⁻¹ and 121 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the Boltzmann distribution to explain how a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction.
parts.answer: Catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower Ea; on the Boltzmann curve the lower Ea lies further to the left; so a greater proportion of molecules have E ≥ Ea and more collisions are successful per unit time.
parts.working: B1 alternative route lower Ea; B1 more molecules have energy ≥ Ea (shaded area larger); B1 more effective collisions per unit time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the catalyst affects the enthalpy change of the reaction.
parts.answer: No effect – ΔH stays −98 kJ mol⁻¹.

author: HomiLabs

stem: For a reaction, k = 2.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ at 300 K and k = 8.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ at 320 K.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the Arrhenius equation and explain what happens to k as temperature increases.
parts.answer: k = Ae^(−Ea/RT); as T increases, −Ea/RT becomes less negative so k increases (exponentially).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using ln k = ln A − Ea/RT, calculate the activation energy, in kJ mol⁻¹. [R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹]
parts.answer: 55.3 kJ mol⁻¹

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The rate constant of a reaction was measured at five temperatures.
T / K: 290, 300, 310, 320, 330
k / s⁻¹: 0.00154, 0.00353, 0.00767, 0.0159, 0.0315

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ln k and 1/T for the experiments at 290 K and 330 K.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A graph of ln k against 1/T is a straight line. Calculate its gradient using your values from (a).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the gradient to calculate the activation energy in kJ mol⁻¹. [R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹]
parts.answer: 60.0 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: d
parts.text: State how the graph could be used to find the pre-exponential factor A.
parts.answer: Extrapolate to find the y-intercept, which equals ln A; A = e^(intercept).

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a fertiliser factory near Multan, the rates of several gas and solution reactions are controlled carefully.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why increasing the pressure increases the rate of a reaction between two gases.
parts.answer: Same number of molecules in a smaller volume / more molecules per unit volume; so collisions are more frequent (more successful collisions per second).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why powdered zinc reacts faster with dilute sulfuric acid than the same mass of zinc granules.
parts.answer: Powder has a larger surface area exposed to acid; so more frequent collisions between acid particles and zinc atoms.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why increasing concentration does not change the proportion of collisions that are successful.
parts.answer: Concentration does not change the energy of the particles, so the fraction with E ≥ Ea is unchanged.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change increases the frequency of collisions between reacting particles but does NOT change the fraction of collisions that have energy greater than the activation energy?
A adding a catalyst
B increasing the temperature
C increasing the concentration of a reactant in solution
D using a reactant with a lower activation energy
parts.answer: C increasing the concentration of a reactant in solution
parts.working: Higher concentration means more particles per unit volume, so more frequent collisions, but the energy distribution is unchanged. B raises both the collision frequency and the fraction with E ≥ Ea.

stem: Milk turns sour because of reactions caused by bacterial enzymes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term activation energy.
parts.answer: The minimum energy that colliding particles must have for a reaction to occur.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A rough rule says the rate of a reaction doubles for every 10 °C rise. Calculate the factor by which the rate increases when the temperature of milk rises from 5 °C (in a fridge) to 35 °C (on a hot day).
parts.answer: 8 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a small rise in temperature causes a large increase in rate, even though the mean kinetic energy of the particles rises only a little.
parts.answer: The Boltzmann distribution shifts so that the number of particles with energy ≥ Ea increases by a large proportion; only these particles react, so the number of successful collisions per second increases greatly.
parts.working: B1 many more particles with E ≥ Ea; B1 more successful collisions per unit time.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Hydrogen and iodine are sealed in a flask at 450 °C: H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the rates of the forward and backward reactions change from the moment H₂ and I₂ are mixed until equilibrium is reached.
parts.answer: Forward rate is greatest at the start and decreases as [H₂] and [I₂] fall; backward rate starts at zero and increases as [HI] rises; at equilibrium the two rates are equal (and non-zero).
parts.working: B1 forward decreases; B1 backward increases from zero; B1 equal at equilibrium.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect of adding a catalyst on (i) the rates of the forward and backward reactions (ii) the position of equilibrium (iii) the time taken to reach equilibrium.
parts.answer: (i) both increase by the same factor (ii) no change (iii) decreases

parts.label: c
parts.text: The forward reaction is exothermic. Explain why raising the temperature decreases the equilibrium yield of HI even though both rates increase.
parts.answer: The backward (endothermic) reaction has the larger Ea, so its rate increases by a greater proportion; equilibrium shifts left.
parts.working: B1 endothermic direction favoured/its rate increases more; B1 equilibrium shifts to the left.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which mechanism, SN1 or SN2, is mainly followed in the hydrolysis of (i) 1-bromobutane (ii) 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.
parts.answer: (i) SN2 (ii) SN1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why tertiary halogenoalkanes react mainly by the SN1 mechanism.
parts.answer: Tertiary carbocation is the most stable because three alkyl groups donate electrons (positive inductive effect) and stabilise the positive charge; the three bulky alkyl groups hinder (steric hindrance) attack by a nucleophile from the side opposite the halogen, so SN2 is difficult.
parts.working: B1 tertiary carbocation stable; B1 alkyl groups electron-donating/inductive effect; B1 steric hindrance prevents SN2 attack.

stem: 1-bromobutane is warmed with aqueous sodium hydroxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the SN2 mechanism for the reaction of 1-bromobutane with hydroxide ions. Describe in words where each curly arrow starts and ends, and describe the transition state.
parts.answer: Arrow from a lone pair on O of OH⁻ to the δ+ carbon bonded to Br; arrow from the C–Br bond to Br; transition state [HO···C···Br]⁻ with partial bonds and a negative charge, OH and Br on opposite sides of carbon; products butan-1-ol and Br⁻.
parts.working: B1 C–Br dipole (Cδ+, Brδ−); B1 arrow from OH⁻ lone pair to C; B1 arrow from C–Br bond to Br; B1 transition state with partial bonds and overall negative charge.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the rate equation for this reaction.
parts.answer: rate = k[CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂Br][OH⁻]

author: HomiLabs

stem:
An isomer of C₄H₉Br reacts with aqueous hydroxide ions. Initial rates at 25 °C:
Expt 1: [C₄H₉Br] = 0.050, [OH⁻] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, rate = 3.6 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
Expt 2: [C₄H₉Br] = 0.100, [OH⁻] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, rate = 7.2 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
Expt 3: [C₄H₉Br] = 0.050, [OH⁻] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³, rate = 3.6 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text: Deduce the orders with respect to C₄H₉Br and to OH⁻, and write the rate equation.
parts.answer: First order in C₄H₉Br, zero order in OH⁻; rate = k[C₄H₉Br]
parts.working: B1 orders from data; B1 rate equation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate constant, with units.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Deduce the mechanism and hence the structural formula of this isomer of C₄H₉Br. Explain.
parts.answer: SN1, so the isomer is tertiary: (CH₃)₃CBr, 2-bromo-2-methylpropane
parts.working: M1 rate independent of [OH⁻] → SN1; A1 tertiary isomer (CH₃)₃CBr.

author: HomiLabs

stem: 2-bromobutane, CH₃CHBrCH₂CH₃, can undergo nucleophilic substitution with hydroxide ions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why 2-bromobutane is chiral.
parts.answer: Carbon 2 is bonded to four different groups (H, Br, CH₃, C₂H₅).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A single enantiomer of 2-bromobutane reacts with OH⁻ by the SN2 mechanism. State and explain whether the butan-2-ol formed rotates plane-polarised light.
parts.answer: Yes – OH⁻ attacks from the side opposite Br, so the configuration is inverted and a single enantiomer of butan-2-ol forms, which is optically active.
parts.working: B1 attack opposite to leaving group/inversion; B1 single enantiomer so optically active.

parts.label: c
parts.text: If the same reaction occurred by SN1, the product would not rotate plane-polarised light. Explain why.
parts.answer: The carbocation intermediate is planar, so the nucleophile can attack equally from either side; a racemic mixture (50 : 50 enantiomers) forms and the rotations cancel.
parts.working: B1 planar carbocation, attack from both faces; B1 racemic mixture, no net rotation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which halogenoalkane is most likely to undergo hydrolysis by an SN1 mechanism?
A CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl
B CH₃CHClCH₃
C (CH₃)₃CCl
D CH₃Cl
parts.answer: C (CH₃)₃CCl
parts.working: (CH₃)₃CCl is tertiary: it forms the most stable carbocation and is sterically hindered towards SN2. B is secondary and can react by either route, but less readily by SN1.

stem:
Three test-tubes each contain 1 cm³ of ethanol, 1 cm³ of aqueous silver nitrate and three drops of a halogenoalkane, warmed in a water bath at 50 °C: 1-chlorobutane, 1-bromobutane and 1-iodobutane.
Bond energies / kJ mol⁻¹: C–Cl 340; C–Br 280; C–I 240

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the order in which precipitates appear, fastest first, and state the colour of each precipitate.
parts.answer: 1-iodobutane (yellow AgI) first, then 1-bromobutane (cream AgBr), then 1-chlorobutane (white AgCl) last.
parts.working: B1 order I > Br > Cl; B1 all colours.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the bond energies to explain the order of reactivity.
parts.answer: C–I is the weakest bond (240 kJ mol⁻¹), so it breaks most easily; C–Cl is the strongest (340 kJ mol⁻¹), so the chloroalkane is hydrolysed most slowly.
parts.working: B1 bond strength decreases C–Cl > C–Br > C–I; B1 weaker bond broken more easily so faster rate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student predicts that 1-chlorobutane should react fastest because the C–Cl bond is the most polar. Explain why this prediction is wrong.
parts.answer: Bond strength, not bond polarity, is the dominant factor controlling the rate of hydrolysis.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain the purpose of the ethanol.
parts.answer: It is a solvent in which both the halogenoalkane and aqueous silver nitrate dissolve (they mix).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the reagent and conditions needed to convert 2-bromopropane into propene.
parts.answer: NaOH (or KOH) dissolved in ethanol; heat (under reflux).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: CH₃CHBrCH₃ + NaOH → CH₃CH=CH₂ + NaBr + H₂O

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the role of the hydroxide ion in this reaction.
parts.answer: Base (removes H⁺ from the carbon next to the C–Br carbon).

stem: 2-bromobutane is heated with potassium hydroxide in ethanol. Three different alkenes are formed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name all three alkenes formed.
parts.answer: but-1-ene; cis-but-2-ene (Z); trans-but-2-ene (E)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why there are two products with the formula CH₃CH=CHCH₃.
parts.answer: Restricted rotation about the C=C bond; and each carbon of the double bond carries two different groups (H and CH₃), so cis/trans (geometrical) isomers exist.
parts.working: B1 restricted rotation; B1 two different groups on each C of C=C.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the organic product and write an equation when 1-bromopropane is heated with (i) NaOH(aq) (ii) NaOH in ethanol.
parts.answer: (i) propan-1-ol: CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + NaOH → CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + NaBr (ii) propene: CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + NaOH → CH₃CH=CH₂ + NaBr + H₂O
parts.working: 1 mark for each product name, 1 mark for each equation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the different behaviour of the hydroxide ion in (i) and (ii).
parts.answer: In water OH⁻ acts mainly as a nucleophile, attacking the δ+ carbon (substitution); in ethanol it acts mainly as a base, removing H⁺ (elimination).
parts.working: B1 nucleophile in aqueous; B1 base in ethanolic.

stem: There are four structural isomers with formula C₄H₉Br. Each is heated with ethanolic potassium hydroxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the names of the four structural isomers of C₄H₉Br.
parts.answer: 1-bromobutane; 2-bromobutane; 1-bromo-2-methylpropane; 2-bromo-2-methylpropane

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify which isomer(s) give(s) only 2-methylpropene on elimination.
parts.answer: 1-bromo-2-methylpropane and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the isomer whose elimination products include a pair of stereoisomers.
parts.answer: 2-bromobutane

parts.label: d
parts.text: Identify the isomer that gives only an unbranched alkene with the C=C at the end of the chain.
parts.answer: 1-bromobutane (gives but-1-ene only)

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which reagent and conditions convert bromoethane into ethene?
A NaOH(aq), warm
B NaOH in ethanol, heat
C concentrated H₂SO₄, 170 °C
D KCN in ethanol, heat
parts.answer: B NaOH in ethanol, heat
parts.working: Hot ethanolic hydroxide removes HBr (elimination). A gives ethanol (substitution); C is used to dehydrate ethanol, not bromoethane.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why chlorobenzene does not undergo nucleophilic substitution with NaOH(aq) under normal laboratory conditions.
parts.answer: A lone pair (p-orbital) on Cl overlaps with the delocalised π-electrons of the ring; so the C–Cl bond has partial double-bond character and is stronger/harder to break; the electron-rich ring also repels nucleophiles.
parts.working: B1 p-orbital overlap with π system; B1 stronger C–Cl bond; B1 π electron cloud repels OH⁻.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict what is seen when chlorobenzene and 1-chlorobutane are each warmed with ethanolic silver nitrate.
parts.answer: Chlorobenzene: no precipitate; 1-chlorobutane: white precipitate (slowly).

stem: Consider three chlorine compounds: benzoyl chloride (C₆H₅COCl), 1-chlorobutane (CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂Cl) and chlorobenzene (C₆H₅Cl).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Put the three compounds in order of ease of hydrolysis, most easily hydrolysed first.
parts.answer: benzoyl chloride > 1-chlorobutane > chlorobenzene

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what is observed when each compound is added to water containing AgNO₃(aq) at room temperature.
parts.answer: C₆H₅COCl: immediate white precipitate (and steamy fumes of HCl); 1-chlorobutane: no precipitate at room temperature (slow, faint on warming); C₆H₅Cl: no precipitate.
parts.working: B1 immediate precipitate with acyl chloride; B1 none/very slow for the other two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why benzoyl chloride is hydrolysed most easily.
parts.answer: The carbonyl carbon is attached to both O and Cl, two electronegative atoms, so it is strongly δ+; the planar C=O carbon is easily attacked by water (addition–elimination).
parts.working: B1 two electronegative atoms make C very δ+; B1 attack by water easy (lone pair of H₂O).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Methylbenzene reacts with chlorine under two different sets of conditions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the conditions needed to make (i) 1-chloro-4-methylbenzene (and its 2-isomer) (ii) (chloromethyl)benzene, C₆H₅CH₂Cl, from methylbenzene and chlorine.
parts.answer: (i) AlCl₃ (or FeCl₃) catalyst, room temperature, no UV (ii) UV light (or boiling)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of mechanism in each case.
parts.answer: (i) electrophilic substitution (ii) free-radical substitution

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the equation for the formation of the electrophile in (i).
parts.answer: Cl₂ + AlCl₃ → Cl⁺ + AlCl₄⁻

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the number of structural isomers of C₇H₇Cl that contain a benzene ring and name the one with Cl on the side chain.
parts.answer: 4; (chloromethyl)benzene
parts.working: B1 4 (three ring isomers + one side-chain); B1 name.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe a chemical test to distinguish (chloromethyl)benzene from 1-chloro-4-methylbenzene. Give the results.
parts.answer: Warm each with NaOH(aq); acidify with dilute HNO₃; add AgNO₃(aq). (Chloromethyl)benzene gives a white precipitate; 1-chloro-4-methylbenzene gives no precipitate.
parts.working: B1 warm NaOH(aq) then HNO₃ then AgNO₃; B1 white ppt with side-chain compound; B1 no ppt with ring-substituted.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why dilute nitric acid is added before the silver nitrate.
parts.answer: To neutralise excess OH⁻, which would otherwise form a brown precipitate of silver oxide.

stem: Equal amounts of bromobenzene, 1-bromobutane and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane are added to separate tubes of warm aqueous ethanolic silver nitrate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the order in which a cream precipitate appears in the three tubes, fastest first.
parts.answer: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, then 1-bromobutane; bromobenzene gives no precipitate

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain your order for the two halogenoalkanes.
parts.answer: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane is tertiary and reacts by SN1 via a stable tertiary carbocation, faster than the primary 1-bromobutane (SN2).
parts.working: B1 tertiary via SN1/carbocation; B1 faster than primary.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why bromobenzene gives no precipitate.
parts.answer: The C–Br bond is strengthened by overlap of a Br lone pair with the ring π system, and the π electrons repel the nucleophile, so no Br⁻ is released.
parts.working: B1 stronger C–Br bond (delocalisation); B1 nucleophile repelled.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Bromoethane, C₂H₅Br, is a useful starting material in synthesis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the reagent and conditions to convert bromoethane into (i) ethanol (ii) propanenitrile (iii) ethylamine.
parts.answer: (i) NaOH(aq), heat under reflux (ii) KCN in ethanol, heat under reflux (iii) excess concentrated NH₃ in ethanol, heat in a sealed tube (under pressure)
parts.working: 1 mark for each reagent and 1 mark for each set of conditions.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
1-bromopropane is heated under reflux with KCN in ethanol. What is the organic product?
A propanenitrile
B butanenitrile
C propan-1-ol
D propylamine
parts.answer: B butanenitrile
parts.working: CN⁻ replaces Br, adding one carbon: CH₃CH₂CH₂CN is butanenitrile. A forgets that the nitrile carbon is counted in the name.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give reagents and conditions for each step of a two-step synthesis of butanoic acid from 1-bromopropane, naming the intermediate.
parts.answer: Step 1: KCN in ethanol, heat under reflux → butanenitrile; Step 2: dilute HCl(aq) (or H₂SO₄), heat under reflux → butanoic acid.
parts.working: B1 KCN/ethanol/heat; B1 intermediate butanenitrile; B1 aqueous acid; B1 reflux.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this route is useful in synthesis.
parts.answer: It increases the length of the carbon chain by one carbon atom.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction of 1-chloropropane with excess ammonia to form propylamine.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl + 2NH₃ → CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂ + NH₄Cl

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why ammonia is used in large excess.
parts.answer: Propylamine has a lone pair and is itself a nucleophile, so it can react with more 1-chloropropane to form secondary and tertiary amines (and quaternary salts); excess NH₃ makes collision of the halogenoalkane with NH₃ more likely.
