parts.working: B1 amine product also nucleophile/further substitution; B1 excess NH₃ reduces this.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the reaction is carried out in a sealed tube.
parts.answer: Ammonia is volatile; the sealed tube keeps it in (under pressure) when heated.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give the structural formula of the secondary amine that could form as a by-product.
parts.answer: (CH₃CH₂CH₂)₂NH

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term nucleophile.
parts.answer: A species that donates a lone pair of electrons (to an electron-deficient carbon) to form a new covalent bond.

parts.label: b
parts.text: From the list, identify all the nucleophiles: OH⁻, H⁺, CN⁻, Br₂, NH₃, NO₂⁺, H₂O, AlCl₃
parts.answer: OH⁻, CN⁻, NH₃, H₂O
parts.working: B2 all four and no extras (B1 three correct).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the carbon atom bonded to the halogen in a halogenoalkane is attacked by nucleophiles.
parts.answer: The halogen is more electronegative than carbon, so the C–X bond is polar and the carbon is δ+.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe, with curly arrows described in words, the SN1 mechanism for the hydrolysis of 2-chloro-2-methylpropane by water.
parts.answer: Step 1: C–Cl bond breaks heterolytically (arrow from C–Cl bond to Cl) to give (CH₃)₃C⁺ and Cl⁻; Step 2: a lone pair on the O of H₂O attacks the carbocation (arrow from O lone pair to C⁺); Step 3: loss of H⁺ from the –OH₂⁺ group gives (CH₃)₃COH.
parts.working: B1 heterolytic fission arrow; B1 carbocation and Cl⁻; B1 arrow from O lone pair to C⁺; B1 loss of H⁺ to give 2-methylpropan-2-ol.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the rate-determining step.
parts.answer: Step 1 – formation of the carbocation.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Bromomethane reacts with hydroxide ions by the SN2 mechanism. Which statement describes the transition state?
A It is a carbocation, CH₃⁺.
B It has a partial C–O bond and a partial C–Br bond and carries a negative charge.
C It contains a full C–O bond and a full C–Br bond.
D It is uncharged, with OH and Br on the same side of the carbon atom.
parts.answer: B It has a partial C–O bond and a partial C–Br bond and carries a negative charge.
parts.working: In SN2, bond-making and bond-breaking happen together: [HO···CH₃···Br]⁻ with OH and Br opposite each other. A describes the SN1 intermediate, not a transition state.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the mechanism of the reaction between bromoethane and ammonia to form ethylamine. Describe each curly arrow in words and show the intermediate ion.
parts.answer: Lone pair on N of NH₃ attacks δ+ C of C–Br (arrow N lone pair → C); C–Br bond breaks (arrow C–Br → Br), giving CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺ and Br⁻; a second NH₃ uses its lone pair to remove H⁺ from CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺ (arrow from N lone pair to H, arrow from N–H bond to N) giving CH₃CH₂NH₂ and NH₄⁺.
parts.working: B1 dipole and attack by N lone pair; B1 C–Br breaks, Br⁻; B1 intermediate CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺; B1 deprotonation by second NH₃.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of mechanism.
parts.answer: Nucleophilic substitution (SN2)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the organic product formed when 1-iodopropane is heated with each reagent: (i) NaOH(aq) (ii) KCN in ethanol (iii) excess NH₃ in ethanol in a sealed tube.
parts.answer: (i) propan-1-ol (ii) butanenitrile (iii) propylamine (propan-1-amine)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the formula of the inorganic product in (i).
parts.answer: NaI

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the organic product when 2-bromobutane is warmed with dilute aqueous sodium hydroxide?
A butan-1-ol
B butan-2-ol
C but-2-ene
D butanone
parts.answer: B butan-2-ol
parts.working: OH⁻ replaces Br on the same carbon (C2), giving butan-2-ol. C would need ethanolic NaOH (elimination).

stem: 5.48 g of 1-bromobutane is heated under reflux with excess aqueous sodium hydroxide. 2.22 g of pure butan-1-ol is obtained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage yield of butan-1-ol. [Mr: C₄H₉Br 136.9; C₄H₉OH 74.0]

parts.label: b
parts.text: A different isomer, P, of C₄H₉Br is hydrolysed to an alcohol Q. Q does not change the colour of hot acidified potassium dichromate(VI). Identify P and Q.
parts.answer: P: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CBr; Q: 2-methylpropan-2-ol, (CH₃)₃COH
parts.working: M1 Q is a tertiary alcohol (not oxidised); A1 both names/structures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the colour change seen if butan-1-ol is warmed with acidified potassium dichromate(VI).
parts.answer: Orange to green

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give a reagent for converting propan-2-ol into 2-chloropropane, and write the equation.
parts.answer: PCl₅ (or SOCl₂, or PCl₃ with heat, or conc HCl with ZnCl₂): CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ + PCl₅ → CH₃CHClCH₃ + POCl₃ + HCl
parts.working: B1 reagent; B1 matching balanced equation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the reagent and conditions for making bromoethane from (i) ethene (ii) ethane.
parts.answer: (i) HBr(g), room temperature (ii) Br₂, ultraviolet light
parts.working: B1 HBr; B1 Br₂; B1 UV light.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why method (ii) is not a good way to make pure bromoethane.
parts.answer: Free-radical substitution gives a mixture of multi-substituted products (e.g. dibromoethanes).

stem: 2-chloro-2-methylpropane is prepared by shaking 7.40 g of 2-methylpropan-2-ol with concentrated hydrochloric acid in a separating funnel at room temperature. The upper organic layer is washed with sodium hydrogencarbonate solution, then with water, dried with anhydrous sodium sulfate and distilled. 6.94 g of product is collected.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the purpose of shaking with sodium hydrogencarbonate solution and how the pressure in the funnel is controlled.
parts.answer: Removes/neutralises the remaining HCl acid; CO₂ is produced so the tap must be opened regularly (with the funnel inverted) to release pressure.
parts.working: B1 neutralise acid; B1 release CO₂ pressure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why anhydrous sodium sulfate is added.
parts.answer: It is a drying agent that removes traces of water from the organic layer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage yield. [Mr: (CH₃)₃COH 74.0; (CH₃)₃CCl 92.5]

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one safety precaution specific to this experiment.
parts.answer: Use concentrated HCl in a fume cupboard / wear gloves (corrosive, gives off HCl fumes); keep the volatile, flammable product away from flames.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name each of the four structural isomers of C₄H₉Cl and classify each as primary, secondary or tertiary.
parts.answer: 1-chlorobutane (primary); 2-chlorobutane (secondary); 1-chloro-2-methylpropane (primary); 2-chloro-2-methylpropane (tertiary)
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct name with classification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a halogenoalkane is classified as primary, secondary or tertiary.
parts.answer: By the number of alkyl groups (carbon atoms) bonded to the carbon atom carrying the halogen: one, two or three.

stem: Water pipes and crates sold in Pakistani markets are often made from poly(propene) and poly(chloroethene).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the repeat unit of poly(propene). Use the form –CH₂–CHX– with X identified.
parts.answer: –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–
parts.working: B1 continuation bonds shown at both ends.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the structural formula and name of the monomer used to make poly(chloroethene), PVC.
parts.answer: CH₂=CHCl, chloroethene

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the type of polymerisation and why no other product forms.
parts.answer: Addition polymerisation; the C=C π bonds open and monomers join with no atoms lost, so the polymer is the only product.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A polymer has the repeat unit –CH₂–CCl₂–. What is the monomer?
A CH₂=CHCl
B CHCl=CHCl
C CH₂=CCl₂
D CCl₂=CCl₂
parts.answer: C CH₂=CCl₂
parts.working: Both Cl atoms are on the same carbon of the repeat unit, so the monomer is 1,1-dichloroethene. B would give –CHCl–CHCl–.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the structural formula of the monomer and the repeat unit of PTFE, poly(tetrafluoroethene).
parts.answer: Monomer CF₂=CF₂; repeat unit –CF₂–CF₂–

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why PTFE is very unreactive, making it suitable for non-stick cooking pans.
parts.answer: The C–F bonds are very strong (high bond energy) and the polymer is saturated (no C=C), so it resists attack by most chemicals.
parts.working: B1 strong C–F bonds; B1 saturated/non-polar overall, no reactive sites.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A molecule of poly(ethene) has Mr = 280 000. Calculate the number of monomer units in the molecule. [Mr of C₂H₄ = 28.0]

parts.label: b
parts.text: A chain of poly(chloroethene) contains 2000 monomer units. Calculate its Mr. [Mr of C₂H₃Cl = 62.5]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a sample of poly(ethene) is described by an average Mr rather than a single value.
parts.answer: Chains grow and stop at random, so the polymer contains chains of different lengths.

stem: A city council plans to reduce waste from thin plastic shopping bags made of poly(ethene) and from PVC pipes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why poly(alkene)s cause problems in landfill sites.
parts.answer: They are non-biodegradable because they are saturated/non-polar with strong C–C and C–H bonds; microorganisms cannot break them down, so they persist for many years.
parts.working: B1 non-biodegradable; B1 reason (inert, no polar bonds for enzymes to attack).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why burning PVC waste is particularly harmful.
parts.answer: Combustion releases toxic and acidic hydrogen chloride gas (and possibly toxic chlorinated compounds); HCl causes acid rain/respiratory damage.
parts.working: B1 HCl produced; B1 harmful effect.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of recycling over incineration.
parts.answer: Saves crude oil (raw material) and energy; no toxic gases released.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Part of a polymer chain is shown: –CH₂–CH(CN)–CH₂–CH(CN)–CH₂–CH(CN)–
What is the monomer?
A CH₂=CHCN
B CH₃CH₂CN
C CH₂=C(CN)₂
D CH≡CCN
parts.answer: A CH₂=CHCN
parts.working: The repeat unit is –CH₂–CH(CN)–, from propenenitrile CH₂=CHCN. B has no C=C so cannot undergo addition polymerisation.

stem: A section of a copolymer used for flexible food packaging is: –CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the two monomers used to make this polymer.
parts.answer: ethene, CH₂=CH₂, and propene, CH₂=CHCH₃

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the type of polymerisation and give the empirical formula of the polymer if the monomers are present in equal numbers.
parts.answer: Addition; CH₂
parts.working: B1 addition; B1 C₅H₁₀ per pair → CH₂.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Draw (as a text formula) the repeat unit of the polymer formed from but-2-ene, CH₃CH=CHCH₃.
parts.answer: –CH(CH₃)–CH(CH₃)–

parts.label: b
parts.text: A sample of this polymer has an average Mr of 112 000. Calculate the average number of but-2-ene monomer units in each chain. [Mr of C₄H₈ = 56.0]
parts.working: B1 112 000 ÷ 56.0 = 2000 (the repeat unit has the same formula as the monomer, ignoring end groups).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the atom economy of any addition polymerisation and explain your answer.
parts.answer: 100 %; all the atoms of the monomer end up in the polymer – it is the only product.
parts.working: B1 100 %; B1 only one product / no atoms lost.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the polymer from but-2-ene is saturated even though the monomer is unsaturated.
parts.answer: The π bond of each C=C breaks to form new C–C single bonds to neighbouring monomers.

stem: Perspex, a clear plastic used for shop signs, is an addition polymer made from methyl 2-methylpropenoate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the structural formula of the monomer, methyl 2-methylpropenoate.
parts.answer: CH₂=C(CH₃)COOCH₃

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the repeat unit of the polymer.
parts.answer: –CH₂–C(CH₃)(COOCH₃)–

parts.label: c
parts.text: The polymer is heated with aqueous sodium hydroxide. Describe the change to the side groups and name the small molecule released.
parts.answer: The ester side groups are hydrolysed to sodium carboxylate groups (–COO⁻Na⁺); methanol is released. The main carbon chain is not broken.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the polymer backbone survives this treatment while a polyester backbone would not.
parts.answer: The backbone of the addition polymer contains only C–C bonds; in a polyester, ester links are in the main chain and are hydrolysed.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A waste incinerator burns PVC pipe offcuts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of hydrogen chloride, at r.t.p., released when 1.00 kg of PVC is burned completely. Assume each repeat unit –CH₂–CHCl– gives one HCl. [Mr of C₂H₃Cl = 62.5; molar gas volume 24.0 dm³]
parts.answer: 384 dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: The HCl is removed by passing the gases through powdered calcium carbonate. Write the equation and calculate the mass of calcium carbonate needed. [Mr CaCO₃ = 100.1]
parts.answer: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂; 801 g
parts.working: B1 equation; M1 8.00 mol CaCO₃; A1 801 g.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prop-2-en-1-ol, CH₂=CHCH₂OH, can form an addition polymer. Give its repeat unit.
parts.answer: –CH₂–CH(CH₂OH)–

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the addition polymer from (a) can dissolve in water, whereas poly(propene) cannot.
parts.answer: Each repeat unit has an –OH group that forms hydrogen bonds with water molecules; poly(propene) has only non-polar C–H/C–C bonds with instantaneous dipole forces.
parts.working: B1 –OH hydrogen bonds with water; B1 poly(propene) non-polar.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain whether prop-2-en-1-ol alone could form a condensation polymer.
parts.answer: No – it has only one functional group (–OH) able to take part in condensation; a condensation polymer needs two reacting groups per monomer (or two different monomers).
parts.working: B1 only one condensing group; B1 needs two functional groups.

stem: Expanded polystyrene is used to pack electronic goods and to make disposable food boxes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the name and structural formula of the monomer of polystyrene.
parts.answer: phenylethene (styrene), C₆H₅CH=CH₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the repeat unit of polystyrene.
parts.answer: –CH₂–CH(C₆H₅)–

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why poly(alkene)s such as polystyrene are chemically unreactive.
parts.answer: They are saturated (contain no C=C in the chain) and have strong non-polar C–C and C–H bonds.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a balanced equation for the complete combustion of poly(ethene), (C₂H₄)ₙ.
parts.answer: (C₂H₄)ₙ + 3nO₂ → 2nCO₂ + 2nH₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass, in kg, of carbon dioxide produced when 14.0 kg of poly(ethene) burns completely. [Mr: C₂H₄ 28.0; CO₂ 44.0]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one reason why poly(ethene) waste should not be burned in an open fire.
parts.answer: Incomplete combustion produces toxic carbon monoxide (and soot).

stem: Nylon-6,6 is used to make fishing nets for boats in Karachi harbour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the two monomers used to make nylon-6,6.
parts.answer: hexanedioic acid and hexane-1,6-diamine (1,6-diaminohexane)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the repeat unit of nylon-6,6.
parts.answer: –NH(CH₂)₆NHCO(CH₂)₄CO–
parts.working: B1 amide link shown; B1 correct numbers of CH₂ groups.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the small molecule eliminated and the linkage formed.
parts.answer: water; amide (peptide) linkage –CONH–

author: HomiLabs

stem: Plastic drinks bottles are made from PET, poly(ethylene terephthalate).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the structural formulae of the two monomers used to make PET.
parts.answer: HOOC–C₆H₄–COOH (benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid) and HOCH₂CH₂OH (ethane-1,2-diol)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the repeat unit of PET.
parts.answer: –OC–C₆H₄–COO–CH₂CH₂–O–
parts.working: B1 ester link; B1 rest correct.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the type of polymer.
parts.answer: Polyester (condensation polymer)

author: HomiLabs

stem: In the 'nylon rope trick', nylon-6,6 is made at the interface between a solution of hexanedioyl dichloride in an organic solvent and an aqueous solution of hexane-1,6-diamine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the structural formula of hexanedioyl dichloride.
parts.answer: ClCO(CH₂)₄COCl

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the small molecule eliminated when hexanedioyl dichloride reacts with hexane-1,6-diamine.
parts.answer: hydrogen chloride (HCl)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two advantages of using the diacyl dichloride rather than hexanedioic acid in a school laboratory.
parts.answer: Reaction is fast at room temperature (no heating/catalyst needed); the reaction goes to completion (not an equilibrium).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Kevlar is a polyamide used in bulletproof vests and cricket helmets.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the structural formulae of the monomers used to make Kevlar.
parts.answer: H₂N–C₆H₄–NH₂ (benzene-1,4-diamine) and HOOC–C₆H₄–COOH (benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid) (or the diacyl dichloride)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the repeat unit of Kevlar.
parts.answer: –NH–C₆H₄–NH–CO–C₆H₄–CO–

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Kevlar is very strong.
parts.answer: Rigid, flat chains line up parallel; strong hydrogen bonds form between C=O of one chain and N–H of the neighbouring chain.
parts.working: B1 linear rigid chains packed closely; B1 hydrogen bonds between chains (C=O···H–N).

author: HomiLabs

stem: PLA is made from maize or sugar cane and is used for disposable cups.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the structural formula of 2-hydroxypropanoic acid (lactic acid).
parts.answer: CH₃CH(OH)COOH

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the repeat unit of poly(lactic acid), PLA.
parts.answer: –O–CH(CH₃)–CO–

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how one monomer can form a condensation polymer on its own.
parts.answer: Each molecule has two different functional groups (–OH and –COOH), which react with groups on neighbouring molecules to form ester links.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why PLA is biodegradable.
parts.answer: Its ester links can be hydrolysed (by water/enzymes/microorganisms).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Proteins are natural polyamides formed from amino acids.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Draw (as text formulae) the two possible dipeptides formed from one glycine (H₂NCH₂COOH) and one alanine (H₂NCH(CH₃)COOH) molecule.
parts.answer: H₂NCH₂CONHCH(CH₃)COOH and H₂NCH(CH₃)CONHCH₂COOH

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the repeat unit of poly(glycine).
parts.answer: –NH–CH₂–CO–

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the linkage formed between amino acids.
parts.answer: peptide (amide) link

author: HomiLabs

stem: A section of a polyester is: –O–CH₂CH₂CH₂–O–CO–(CH₂)₄–CO–O–CH₂CH₂CH₂–O–CO–(CH₂)₄–CO–

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the products when the polyester is heated with dilute hydrochloric acid.
parts.answer: HOOC(CH₂)₄COOH (hexanedioic acid) and HOCH₂CH₂CH₂OH (propane-1,3-diol)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the products when the polyester is heated with aqueous sodium hydroxide.
parts.answer: NaOOC(CH₂)₄COONa (sodium hexanedioate) and HOCH₂CH₂CH₂OH

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the type of reaction in (a) and (b).
parts.answer: Hydrolysis

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the Mr of the repeat unit of nylon-6,6, C₁₂H₂₂N₂O₂, is 226.0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A nylon-6,6 chain has an Mr of approximately 33 900. Calculate the number of repeat units in the chain (ignore the end groups).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Each repeat unit is formed from one diacid and one diamine molecule. Deduce how many water molecules were eliminated in forming one chain with this number of repeat units. Explain.
parts.working: M1 one H₂O per amide link; A1 300 monomers joined by 299 links.

stem: A section of a polyamide is: –NH–(CH₂)₄–NH–CO–(CH₂)₈–CO–NH–(CH₂)₄–NH–CO–(CH₂)₈–CO–

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the two monomers needed to make this polyamide. Give their structural formulae.
parts.answer: H₂N(CH₂)₄NH₂ (butane-1,4-diamine) and HOOC(CH₂)₈COOH (decanedioic acid)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one other type of monomer that could replace the dicarboxylic acid.
parts.answer: The diacyl dichloride, ClCO(CH₂)₈COCl

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two differences between addition polymerisation and condensation polymerisation.
parts.answer: Addition: monomers contain C=C, no other product, polymer has same empirical formula as monomer; condensation: monomers have two functional groups, a small molecule (e.g. H₂O or HCl) is eliminated.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two differences.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Classify each linkage: –COO– and –CONH–.
parts.answer: –COO– ester (polyester); –CONH– amide (polyamide)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the repeat unit of nylon-6, made from 6-aminohexanoic acid, H₂N(CH₂)₅COOH.
parts.answer: –NH–(CH₂)₅–CO–

parts.label: b
parts.text: A chain of nylon-6, H–[NH(CH₂)₅CO]₅₀₀–OH, has 500 repeat units. Calculate its Mr. [Mr of C₆H₁₁NO = 113.0; H₂O = 18.0]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why nylon-6 and nylon-6,6 have very similar properties.
parts.answer: Both have amide links regularly spaced along similar hydrocarbon chains, so similar hydrogen bonding between chains.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each monomer or pair of monomers, state whether it forms an addition or a condensation polymer: (i) propenamide, CH₂=CHCONH₂ (ii) hexane-1,6-diol and butanedioic acid (iii) 2-aminopropanoic acid (iv) tetrafluoroethene.
parts.answer: (i) addition (ii) condensation (iii) condensation (iv) addition

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the repeat unit of the polymer formed in (ii).
parts.answer: –O(CH₂)₆O–CO(CH₂)₂CO–

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the complete hydrolysis of one repeat unit of nylon-6,6, –NH(CH₂)₆NHCO(CH₂)₄CO–, by hot concentrated hydrochloric acid.
parts.answer: –NH(CH₂)₆NHCO(CH₂)₄CO– + 2H₂O + 2HCl → [H₃N(CH₂)₆NH₃]²⁺ 2Cl⁻ + HOOC(CH₂)₄COOH
parts.working: B1 diacid and diammonium salt products; B1 balanced (2H₂O and 2HCl).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the diamine is obtained as its salt.
parts.answer: The amine groups are basic and are protonated by the excess acid.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why nylon clothing is damaged by spills of acid.
parts.answer: The amide links in the polymer chain are hydrolysed, breaking the chains and weakening the fibres.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why polyesters and polyamides are biodegradable while poly(alkene)s are not.
parts.answer: Polyesters/polyamides contain polar ester/amide links that can be hydrolysed (by enzymes/water); poly(alkene)s have only non-polar C–C and C–H bonds that are not attacked.
parts.working: B1 ester/amide links hydrolysed; B1 poly(alkene)s non-polar/inert.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what is meant by a photodegradable polymer and give one structural feature that makes a polymer photodegradable.
parts.answer: One that breaks down when exposed to light (UV); it contains C=O groups that absorb UV and break bonds nearby.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why nylon-6,6 has a much higher melting point than poly(ethene) of similar chain length.
parts.answer: Nylon chains form hydrogen bonds between N–H and C=O of neighbouring chains; poly(ethene) has only weaker instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces, needing less energy to overcome.
parts.working: B1 hydrogen bonds in nylon; B1 only id–id forces in poly(ethene)/less energy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why low-density poly(ethene), with many side branches, is softer than high-density poly(ethene).
parts.answer: Branches stop the chains packing closely, so intermolecular forces are weaker and chains slide past each other more easily.

stem: A large city such as Karachi produces thousands of tonnes of plastic waste every day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of incinerating plastic waste.
parts.answer: Advantage: energy released can generate electricity / reduces landfill volume. Disadvantage: releases CO₂ (greenhouse gas) and toxic gases such as HCl from PVC or CO.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why mixed plastic waste is difficult to recycle.
parts.answer: Different polymers have different properties/melting points and must be sorted first.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a bag made of a polyester would break down faster in a compost heap than one made of poly(propene).
parts.answer: Ester links are hydrolysed by water/enzymes from microorganisms; poly(propene) has no such polar links.
parts.working: B1 hydrolysis of ester; B1 poly(propene) inert.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A 12.0 g cup made of poly(lactic acid), PLA, is buried in an industrial compost heap. It loses 25 % of its mass in the first 30 days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of the cup remaining after 90 days, assuming it continues to lose 25 % of its remaining mass every 30 days. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of reaction by which the PLA cup breaks down and the organic product.
parts.answer: Hydrolysis; 2-hydroxypropanoic acid (lactic acid)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the same cup would break down more slowly in a dry landfill than in moist compost.
parts.answer: Hydrolysis needs water (and microorganisms), which are scarce in a dry landfill.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the sign of the entropy change, ΔS, for each reaction and explain each answer: (i) CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g) (ii) N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g) (iii) H₂O(l) → H₂O(g) (iv) Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s)
parts.answer: (i) positive – gas formed from a solid (ii) negative – 4 mol gas → 2 mol gas (iii) positive – liquid → gas, more disorder (iv) negative – free ions in solution form an ordered solid
parts.working: 1 mark each for sign with reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the entropy, S, of a system.
parts.answer: A measure of the dispersal of energy / the number of possible arrangements of particles and their energy (disorder).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Place H₂O(s) at 0 °C, H₂O(l) at 25 °C and H₂O(g) at 100 °C in order of increasing entropy and explain.
parts.answer: H₂O(s) < H₂O(l) < H₂O(g); particles become more free to move and there are more ways of arranging them and their energy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the entropy of a perfect crystal at 0 K.
parts.answer: Zero

stem: Standard entropies, S° / J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹: N₂(g) 191.6; H₂(g) 130.6; NH₃(g) 192.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard entropy change for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g).
parts.answer: −198.4 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
parts.working: M1 ΔS = ΣS(products) − ΣS(reactants) = 2(192.5) − [191.6 + 3(130.6)]; A1 value with sign and units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the sign of your answer.
parts.answer: Negative: the number of gas molecules decreases (4 → 2), so fewer ways of arranging particles.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Methane (natural gas) from the Sui gas field is burned in home cookers.
S° / J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹: CH₄(g) 186.2; O₂(g) 205.0; CO₂(g) 213.6; H₂O(l) 69.9

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔS° for the complete combustion of methane: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l).
parts.answer: −242.8 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict how ΔS° would differ if the water were formed as steam. Explain.
parts.answer: Less negative (≈ zero): 3 mol gas would give 3 mol gas, and gaseous water has much higher entropy than liquid water.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Instant cold packs used by sports teams contain solid ammonium nitrate and a pouch of water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ammonium nitrate dissolves in water spontaneously although the process is endothermic. Explain this in terms of entropy.
parts.answer: The ordered solid lattice breaks up into freely moving aqueous ions, so ΔS of the system is large and positive; TΔS is greater than ΔH, so ΔG is negative.
parts.working: B1 ΔS positive (ions dispersed); B1 TΔS > ΔH so ΔG < 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the sign of the entropy change of the surroundings for this process and explain.
parts.answer: Negative – energy is absorbed from the surroundings (they cool), reducing their entropy.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Place the following reactions in order of increasing ΔS, without calculation. Explain your order.
W: 2NaHCO₃(s) → Na₂CO₃(s) + H₂O(g) + CO₂(g)
X: C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g)
Y: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g)
Z: 2H₂O₂(l) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g)
parts.answer: Y < X < Z < W
parts.working: B1 Y lowest/negative – amount of gas decreases (3 mol → 2 mol); B1 X ≈ 0 – 1 mol gas → 1 mol gas; B1 Z forms 1 mol gas from liquids, W forms 2 mol gas from a solid, so W is largest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why ΔG = 0 for the vaporisation of a liquid at its boiling point.
parts.answer: At the boiling point liquid and vapour are in equilibrium (neither direction is favoured).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the entropy change of vaporisation of ethanol at its boiling point, 351 K, given ΔH_vap = +38.6 kJ mol⁻¹.
parts.answer: +110 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: For water, ΔH_vap = +40.7 kJ mol⁻¹ at 373 K. Calculate ΔS_vap and suggest why it is similar to that of ethanol.
parts.answer: +109 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; both involve changing 1 mol of liquid into 1 mol of gas, giving a similar increase in disorder.

stem:
Magnesium ribbon burns with a bright white flame in fireworks.
S° / J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹: Mg(s) 32.7; O₂(g) 205.0; MgO(s) 26.9

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why, unlike standard enthalpies of formation, the standard entropy of an element such as Mg(s) is not zero.
parts.answer: Entropy is an absolute quantity; all substances above 0 K have some disorder (particle motion), so S° > 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate ΔS° for 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s).
parts.answer: −216.6 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

author: HomiLabs

stem: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g); ΔH° = +178 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔS° = +161 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔG° at 298 K and state whether the reaction is feasible at this temperature.
parts.answer: +130 kJ mol⁻¹; not feasible
parts.working: M1 ΔG = 178 − 298 × 0.161 (ΔS in kJ); A1 value and conclusion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the minimum temperature at which the reaction becomes feasible.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the expression that links ΔG, ΔH, ΔS and T, and state the condition for a reaction to be feasible.
parts.answer: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; feasible when ΔG is negative (≤ 0).

parts.label: b
parts.text: For each combination, state whether the reaction is feasible at all temperatures, at no temperature, only at high temperature or only at low temperature: (i) ΔH −, ΔS + (ii) ΔH +, ΔS − (iii) ΔH −, ΔS − (iv) ΔH +, ΔS +
parts.answer: (i) all temperatures (ii) no temperature (iii) only at low temperature (iv) only at high temperature

stem: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g); ΔH° = −92.0 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔS° = −198.4 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Ammonia is made at a fertiliser plant in Punjab.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔG° for the reaction at 298 K.
parts.answer: −32.9 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the temperature above which the reaction is no longer feasible under standard conditions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The industrial process runs at about 720 K, where ΔG° is positive. Explain why this temperature is still used.
parts.answer: At 298 K the rate is far too slow; a higher temperature gives an acceptable rate (with an iron catalyst), and high pressure keeps the equilibrium yield economic (conditions are not standard).
parts.working: B1 rate too slow at low T; B1 compromise/high pressure, non-standard conditions.

author: HomiLabs

stem: ΔG_f° / kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K: NO₂(g) +51.3; N₂O₄(g) +97.8

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔG° for 2NO₂(g) → N₂O₄(g).
parts.answer: −4.8 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the value of ΔG_f° for O₂(g) and explain.
parts.answer: Zero – an element in its standard state is not formed from anything (by definition).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict, with a reason, how the feasibility of this reaction changes as temperature rises.
parts.answer: It becomes less feasible: ΔS is negative (2 mol gas → 1 mol), so −TΔS becomes more positive and ΔG eventually becomes positive.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Zinc is extracted by heating zinc oxide with carbon.
ΔH_f° / kJ mol⁻¹: ZnO(s) −348.3; CO(g) −110.5
S° / J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹: ZnO(s) 43.6; C(s) 5.7; Zn(s) 41.6; CO(g) 197.7

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔH° and ΔS° for ZnO(s) + C(s) → Zn(s) + CO(g).
parts.answer: ΔH° = +237.8 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔS° = +190.0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the minimum temperature at which carbon can reduce zinc oxide.
parts.working: M1 T = ΔH/ΔS with consistent units; A1.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
C(diamond) → C(graphite); ΔH° = −1.9 kJ mol⁻¹.
S° / J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹: C(diamond) 2.4; C(graphite) 5.7

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔS° and ΔG° at 298 K for C(diamond) → C(graphite).
parts.answer: ΔS° = +3.3 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; ΔG° = −2.88 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why diamonds in jewellery do not turn into graphite even though the reaction is feasible.
parts.answer: The activation energy is extremely high (strong covalent bonds must break), so the rate at room temperature is negligible – diamond is kinetically stable.
parts.working: B1 very high Ea; B1 rate negligible/kinetically stable.

author: HomiLabs

stem: For a reaction, ΔG° = +20.0 kJ mol⁻¹ at 300 K and ΔG° = −10.0 kJ mol⁻¹ at 500 K.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assuming ΔH and ΔS do not change with temperature, calculate ΔS (in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) and ΔH (in kJ mol⁻¹).
parts.answer: ΔS = +150 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; ΔH = +65.0 kJ mol⁻¹
parts.working: M1 ΔG = ΔH − TΔS at both temperatures; M1 subtracting gives 30.0 = 200ΔS → ΔS = 0.150 kJ K⁻¹; A1 ΔH = 20.0 + 300(0.150) = 65.0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the temperature at which ΔG = 0.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Data for thermal decomposition, MCO₃(s) → MO(s) + CO₂(g):
MgCO₃: ΔH° = +117 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔS° = +175 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
BaCO₃: ΔH° = +269 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔS° = +172 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the minimum temperature for the thermal decomposition of each carbonate.
parts.answer: MgCO₃ 669 K; BaCO₃ 1560 K

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why ΔS° is almost the same for both reactions.
parts.answer: Both form one mole of CO₂ gas from a solid; the gas dominates the entropy change.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain, in terms of the cations, why MgCO₃ decomposes at a much lower temperature than BaCO₃.
parts.answer: Mg²⁺ is smaller than Ba²⁺ (same charge), so has a higher charge density; it polarises/distorts the carbonate ion electron cloud more, weakening the C–O bonds, so less energy is needed to decompose.
parts.working: B1 Mg²⁺ smaller/higher charge density; B1 polarises carbonate anion more; B1 C–O bond weakened, decomposes more easily.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
In the Contact process, sulfur dioxide is oxidised to sulfur trioxide.
ΔH_f° / kJ mol⁻¹: SO₂(g) −296.8; SO₃(g) −395.7
S° / J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹: SO₂(g) 248.1; O₂(g) 205.0; SO₃(g) 256.7

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔH° and ΔS° for 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g).
parts.answer: ΔH° = −197.8 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔS° = −187.8 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate ΔG° at 723 K, the temperature of the converter.
parts.answer: −62.0 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the temperature above which the reaction is no longer feasible under standard conditions.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A Daniell cell is made from Zn/Zn²⁺ and Cu/Cu²⁺ half-cells. E°cell = +1.10 V.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔG° for the cell reaction Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), using ΔG° = −nE°cellF. [F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹]
parts.answer: −212 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the sign of E°cell tells you whether the reaction is feasible.
parts.answer: Positive E°cell gives negative ΔG°, so the reaction is feasible.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell powers an electric bus. The cell reaction is H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l); ΔG° = −237.1 kJ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard cell potential of the fuel cell. [F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹]

parts.label: b
parts.text: ΔH° for the same reaction is −285.8 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the maximum percentage of the enthalpy change that can be converted into electrical work.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why ΔG° is less negative than ΔH° for this reaction.
parts.answer: ΔS° is negative (1.5 mol gas → liquid), so −TΔS is positive and ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is less negative.

author: HomiLabs

stem: For dissolving potassium chloride in water: ΔH° = +17.2 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔS° = +75.5 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔG° at 298 K for KCl(s) → K⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq).
parts.answer: −5.30 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether KCl dissolves spontaneously at 298 K and explain which term drives the process.
parts.answer: Yes – ΔG is negative; the entropy term (TΔS = 22.5 kJ mol⁻¹) outweighs the endothermic ΔH.

author: HomiLabs

stem: H₂O(s) → H₂O(l); ΔH = +6.01 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔS = +22.0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. On the glaciers of Gilgit-Baltistan, the air temperature ranges from below to above 0 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔG for the melting of ice at 263 K and at 283 K. State whether melting is feasible at each temperature.
parts.answer: 263 K: +0.22 kJ mol⁻¹, not feasible; 283 K: −0.22 kJ mol⁻¹, feasible
parts.working: M1 ΔG = 6.01 − T(0.0220); A1 263 K value and conclusion; A1 283 K value and conclusion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the temperature at which ice and water are in equilibrium.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A baker in Karachi uses baking soda, sodium hydrogencarbonate.
ΔH_f° / kJ mol⁻¹: NaHCO₃(s) −950.8; Na₂CO₃(s) −1130.7; H₂O(g) −241.8; CO₂(g) −393.5
S° / J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹: NaHCO₃(s) 101.7; Na₂CO₃(s) 135.0; H₂O(g) 188.8; CO₂(g) 213.8

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔH° and ΔS° for 2NaHCO₃(s) → Na₂CO₃(s) + H₂O(g) + CO₂(g).
parts.answer: ΔH° = +135.6 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔS° = +334.2 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the minimum temperature, in °C, at which the decomposition becomes feasible.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this reaction makes cakes rise in an oven at 180 °C.
parts.answer: Above the minimum temperature ΔG is negative, so CO₂ and steam are released, forming bubbles in the cake mixture.

author: HomiLabs

stem: ΔG_f° / kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K: Fe₂O₃(s) −742.2; CO(g) −137.2; CO₂(g) −394.4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔG° for Fe₂O₃(s) + 3CO(g) → 2Fe(s) + 3CO₂(g) at 298 K.
parts.answer: −29.4 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the blast furnace is run at a very high temperature although the reaction is feasible at 298 K.
parts.answer: At 298 K the rate is negligibly slow (high activation energy); high temperature gives a fast rate.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A gas-phase reaction has ΔH = −46.0 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = −99.0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Convert ΔS to kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and calculate ΔG at 400 K.
parts.answer: ΔS = −0.0990 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; ΔG = −6.4 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the reaction is feasible at 400 K and predict the effect of increasing temperature on feasibility.
parts.answer: Feasible (ΔG negative); becomes less feasible as T rises because −TΔS is positive and grows.
parts.working: B1 feasible; B1 less feasible at higher T.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student calculates ΔG for a reaction at different temperatures.
T / K: 300, 400, 500, 600, 700
ΔG / kJ mol⁻¹: +20.0, +8.0, −4.0, −12.5, −28.0
A graph of ΔG against T should be a straight line.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result and give the value of ΔG expected at that temperature.
parts.answer: 600 K; expected −16.0 kJ mol⁻¹
parts.working: B1 600 K point off the line; B1 −16.0 (line falls 12.0 kJ mol⁻¹ per 100 K).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the other results to determine the gradient of the line and hence ΔS, in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
parts.answer: gradient = −0.120 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; ΔS = +120 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine ΔH, the intercept on the ΔG axis at T = 0.
parts.answer: +56.0 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the temperature at which the reaction becomes feasible.

parts.label: e
parts.text: State one assumption made in this analysis.
parts.answer: ΔH and ΔS do not change with temperature.

author: HomiLabs

stem: ΔH_f°(MgO(s)) = −601.7 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔS° for 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s) is −216.6 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔG° at 298 K for 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s).
parts.answer: −1139 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why magnesium ribbon does not burn until it is heated strongly, even though ΔG° is very negative.
parts.answer: The reaction has a high activation energy (and a protective oxide layer), so at room temperature the rate is negligible; heating supplies the energy to overcome Ea.
parts.working: B1 high Ea/kinetic barrier; B1 heating gives particles enough energy.

author: HomiLabs

stem: ΔH_f°(O₃(g)) = +142.7 kJ mol⁻¹. S° / J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹: O₂(g) 205.0; O₃(g) 238.8

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔS° and ΔG° at 298 K for 3O₂(g) → 2O₃(g).
parts.answer: ΔS° = −137.4 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; ΔG° = +326.3 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this reaction is not feasible at any temperature.
parts.answer: ΔH is positive and ΔS is negative, so ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is positive at every temperature.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Ozone is nevertheless formed in the stratosphere. Explain how this is possible.
parts.answer: Energy from ultraviolet radiation is continuously supplied (O₂ is split into atoms), so the process is driven by an external energy source.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Silver oxide decomposes on heating.
ΔH_f°(Ag₂O(s)) = −31.1 kJ mol⁻¹
S° / J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹: Ag₂O(s) 121.3; Ag(s) 42.6; O₂(g) 205.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔH° and ΔS° for 2Ag₂O(s) → 4Ag(s) + O₂(g).
parts.answer: ΔH° = +62.2 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔS° = +132.8 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the minimum temperature for the decomposition.
parts.working: M1 T = ΔH/ΔS in consistent units; A1.

author: HomiLabs

stem: For the vaporisation of water: ΔH = +40.7 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔS = +109 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔG for H₂O(l) → H₂O(g) at 298 K and at 400 K.
parts.answer: 298 K: +8.22 kJ mol⁻¹; 400 K: −2.90 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the signs of your answers show.
parts.answer: At 298 K boiling (to vapour at standard pressure) is not feasible; at 400 K it is feasible.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
ΔH_f° / kJ mol⁻¹: Al₂O₃(s) −1675.7; CO₂(g) −393.5
S° / J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹: Al₂O₃(s) 50.9; C(s) 5.7; Al(s) 28.3; CO₂(g) 213.8

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔH° and ΔS° for 2Al₂O₃(s) + 3C(s) → 4Al(s) + 3CO₂(g).
parts.answer: ΔH° = +2170.9 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔS° = +635.7 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the minimum temperature at which this reaction would be feasible.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answer to explain why aluminium is extracted by electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide rather than by reduction with carbon.
parts.answer: The temperature required (about 3400 K) is impractically high/very expensive in energy and above what furnaces can sustain; electrolysis supplies the energy electrically at about 1200 K using a cryolite solvent.
parts.working: B1 temperature far too high/uneconomic; B1 electrolysis provides energy instead.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Propenenitrile, CH₂=CH–C≡N, is used to make acrylic fibres for winter shawls. How many σ bonds and how many π bonds are there in one molecule of propenenitrile?
A 6 σ and 3 π
B 6 σ and 2 π
C 9 σ and 3 π
D 5 σ and 4 π
parts.answer: A 6 σ and 3 π
parts.working: σ bonds: 3 C–H, 1 C–C and one σ in each of C=C and C≡N → 6. π bonds: 1 in C=C + 2 in C≡N → 3. Option C counts every line of every multiple bond as σ; a multiple bond contains only one σ bond.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of hybridisation of each carbon atom in ethene, C₂H₄, and the H–C–H bond angle.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the σ bond and the π bond between the two carbon atoms in ethene are formed.
parts.answer: σ: end-on (head-on) overlap of sp² hybrid orbitals, electron density on the internuclear axis. π: sideways overlap of the unhybridised p orbitals, electron density above and below the plane of the molecule.
parts.working: B1 σ by end-on/axial overlap (of sp² orbitals); B1 π by sideways overlap of p orbitals; B1 π electron density above and below the plane / not on the axis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why there is no free rotation about the C=C bond in ethene.
parts.answer: Rotation would break the sideways overlap of the p orbitals (the π bond).
parts.working: B1 rotation would destroy the p-orbital overlap / break the π bond.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the hybridisation of each carbon atom, C1 to C5, in pent-3-en-1-yne, HC≡C–CH=CH–CH₃ (C1 is the carbon of HC≡, C5 is the CH₃ carbon).
parts.answer: C1 sp, C2 sp, C3 sp², C4 sp², C5 sp³
parts.working: B1 C1 and C2 sp; B1 C3 and C4 sp²; B1 C5 sp³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total number of σ bonds and of π bonds in one molecule.
parts.answer: 10 σ bonds and 3 π bonds
parts.working: 6 C–H σ bonds + 4 C–C σ bonds (one in each carbon–carbon link) = 10 σ (B1). π: 2 in C≡C + 1 in C=C = 3 (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the bond angle around C2 and around C5.

stem: Average bond energies (kJ/mol): C–C 350; C=C 610; C≡C 840.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data to estimate the energy of the π bond in C=C, and the average energy of each π bond in C≡C.
parts.answer: π in C=C ≈ 260 kJ/mol; each π in C≡C ≈ 245 kJ/mol
parts.working: M1 subtract σ (C–C) energy: 610 − 350 = 260; A1 (840 − 350)/2 = 245 kJ/mol.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, in terms of orbital overlap, why a π bond is weaker than a σ bond.
parts.answer: Sideways overlap of p orbitals is less effective than end-on overlap, so electron density between the nuclei is lower and the electrons are less strongly attracted by both nuclei.
parts.working: B1 sideways overlap is smaller/less effective than end-on; B1 electron density lies away from the internuclear axis, so weaker attraction to the nuclei.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why alkenes are much more reactive than alkanes even though the C=C bond energy is greater than the C–C bond energy.
parts.answer: Only the weaker π bond needs to be broken in addition reactions; the exposed π electron density above and below the plane attracts electrophiles.
parts.working: B1 only the π bond (≈260 kJ/mol) breaks; B1 π electrons are exposed/high electron density so electrophiles attack.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In which molecule is a carbon atom sp hybridised?
A CO₂
B CH₃CHO
C C₂H₄
D CH₃OH
parts.answer: A CO₂
parts.working: In CO₂ the carbon forms two double bonds and no lone pairs, two regions of electron density, linear → sp. CH₃CHO has sp² (C=O carbon) and sp³ carbons but no sp carbon; C₂H₄ is sp² only; CH₃OH is sp³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the bonding between the two carbon atoms in ethyne, C₂H₂, in terms of hybrid and unhybridised orbitals. State the H–C–C bond angle.
parts.answer: Each C is sp hybridised; one σ bond from end-on overlap of sp orbitals; two π bonds from sideways overlap of the two pairs of unhybridised p orbitals, at right angles to each other; 180°.
parts.working: B1 sp hybridisation and σ from sp–sp overlap; B1 two π bonds from two sets of p orbitals at 90° to each other; B1 180°.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The C–C bond lengths in ethane, ethene and ethyne are 0.154 nm, 0.134 nm and 0.120 nm. Explain this trend.
parts.answer: More shared electron pairs between the carbons (1, 2, 3) → greater electron density between the nuclei → nuclei pulled closer; also more s character in the hybrid orbitals (sp³ → sp² → sp).
parts.working: B1 bond order increases / more electrons shared between nuclei; B1 stronger attraction pulls nuclei closer (credit increasing s character).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which species has a bond angle closest to 107°?
A H₃O⁺
B BF₃
C NH₄⁺
D H₂O
parts.answer: A H₃O⁺
parts.working: H₃O⁺ has 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair around O → pyramidal, ≈107°. NH₄⁺ has 4 bonding pairs and no lone pair → tetrahedral 109.5°; H₂O has 2 lone pairs → 104.5°; BF₃ 120°.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the information for each molecule: number of bonding pairs and lone pairs around the central atom, shape, and bond angle(s).
(i) BCl₃  (ii) PCl₅ (gas)  (iii) SF₆  (iv) OF₂
parts.answer:
(i) 3 bp, 0 lp, trigonal planar, 120°
(ii) 5 bp, 0 lp, trigonal bipyramidal, 90° and 120°
(iii) 6 bp, 0 lp, octahedral, 90°
(iv) 2 bp, 2 lp, non-linear (bent), about 104°
parts.working: B1 each row correct (OF₂ angle accept 102–105°).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the principle used to predict these shapes.
parts.answer: Electron pairs around the central atom repel each other and arrange themselves as far apart as possible (lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs).
parts.working: B1 valence-shell electron pairs repel to be as far apart as possible.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The bond angles in CH₄, NH₃ and H₂O are 109.5°, 107° and 104.5°. Explain this sequence.
parts.answer: All have four electron pairs around the central atom. Number of lone pairs is 0, 1, 2. Lone pair–bonding pair repulsion is greater than bonding pair–bonding pair repulsion, so more lone pairs squeeze the bonds closer together.
parts.working: B1 four electron pairs (tetrahedral arrangement) in each; B1 0, 1, 2 lone pairs; B1 lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the shape of an NH₃ molecule.
parts.answer: (Trigonal) pyramidal

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each ion, give the number of bonding and lone pairs around the central atom, the shape and the bond angle.
(i) NH₂⁻  (ii) PCl₄⁺  (iii) PCl₆⁻  (iv) AlCl₄⁻
parts.answer:
(i) 2 bp, 2 lp, non-linear, ≈104.5°
(ii) 4 bp, 0 lp, tetrahedral, 109.5°
(iii) 6 bp, 0 lp, octahedral, 90°
(iv) 4 bp, 0 lp, tetrahedral, 109.5°
parts.working: B1 each ion. NH₂⁻: N has 5 + 2 (from H) + 1 (charge) = 8 electrons → 4 pairs, 2 bonding. PCl₄⁺: 5 − 1 + 4 = 8 → 4 bp. PCl₆⁻: 5 + 1 + 6 = 12 → 6 bp.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Solid phosphorus(V) chloride is ionic and contains PCl₄⁺ and PCl₆⁻ ions. Suggest one way in which the shape of the phosphorus species changes when gaseous PCl₅ forms the solid.
parts.answer: Trigonal bipyramidal PCl₅ becomes tetrahedral (PCl₄⁺) and octahedral (PCl₆⁻) ions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: BF₃ and NH₃ both have three atoms bonded to the central atom. Explain why BF₃ is trigonal planar but NH₃ is pyramidal.
parts.answer: B has 3 bonding pairs and no lone pair → 120° planar. N has 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair → four pairs, tetrahedral arrangement → pyramidal.
parts.working: B1 BF₃: 3 bp, no lp; B1 NH₃: 3 bp + 1 lp, lone pair repels.

parts.label: b
parts.text: BF₃ reacts with NH₃ to form the compound H₃N–BF₃. State the shape around the boron atom and around the nitrogen atom in this compound, and the F–B–F bond angle.
parts.answer: Both tetrahedral; F–B–F about 109.5°

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which substance is most likely to have a giant ionic lattice?
A melting point 770 °C; conducts when molten but not as a solid; dissolves in water
B melting point 1410 °C; poor conductor as solid and liquid; insoluble in water
C melting point 1085 °C; conducts as solid and liquid; insoluble in water
D melting point −23 °C; does not conduct as solid or liquid; insoluble in water
parts.answer: A melting point 770 °C; conducts when molten but not as a solid; dissolves in water
parts.working: Ions are fixed in the solid but mobile when molten, so conduction only when molten; high melting point; soluble in water → giant ionic. B is giant covalent (like silicon), C is metallic, D is simple molecular.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define electronegativity.
parts.answer: The power of an atom to attract the bonding pair of electrons in a covalent bond (towards itself).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the Pauling electronegativity values H 2.2, C 2.6, O 3.4, F 4.0, Cl 3.2 to place these bonds in order of increasing polarity: C–Cl, O–H, C–H, C–F.
parts.answer: C–H < C–Cl < O–H < C–F

parts.label: c
parts.text: Tetrachloromethane, CCl₄, contains polar bonds but is a non-polar molecule, whereas trichloromethane, CHCl₃, is polar. Explain.
parts.answer: CCl₄ is a symmetrical tetrahedron, so the four equal bond dipoles cancel. In CHCl₃ one C–H bond replaces a C–Cl, so the dipoles do not cancel and there is a net dipole.
parts.working: B1 CCl₄ symmetrical, dipoles cancel; B1 CHCl₃ dipoles unequal/do not cancel → net dipole.

stem:
A student in a Faisalabad college tests four solids.
W: melting point 1710 °C; does not conduct as solid or liquid; insoluble in water and in hexane.
X: melting point 660 °C; conducts as solid and liquid; insoluble in water.
Y: melting point 114 °C; does not conduct as solid or liquid; insoluble in water, soluble in hexane.
Z: melting point 996 °C; does not conduct as solid, conducts as liquid and in aqueous solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of structure of each of W, X, Y and Z.
parts.answer: W giant covalent; X giant metallic; Y simple molecular; Z giant ionic

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a possible identity for W and for Y.
parts.answer: W: e.g. silicon(IV) oxide (sand) or diamond; Y: e.g. iodine or naphthalene (a non-polar simple molecular solid)
parts.working: B1 each, any reasonable example consistent with the data.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Aluminium fluoride melts at 1290 °C, but aluminium chloride sublimes at about 180 °C. Suggest the type of bonding in each compound and explain the difference.
parts.answer: AlF₃ is (mainly) ionic; AlCl₃ is (mainly) covalent/simple molecular. Al³⁺ is small with a high charge (high charge density) and polarises anions. Cl⁻ is larger and more easily polarised than F⁻, so its electron cloud is distorted towards Al³⁺ giving covalent character. Covalent AlCl₃ forms small molecules (Al₂Cl₆) with weak intermolecular forces, so low sublimation temperature; AlF₃ has a giant lattice with strong ionic bonds.
parts.working: B1 AlF₃ ionic, AlCl₃ covalent; B1 Al³⁺ high charge density polarises anion; B1 Cl⁻ larger/more polarisable than F⁻; B1 weak intermolecular forces between molecules vs strong electrostatic attraction in giant lattice.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest, with a reason, whether magnesium chloride or aluminium chloride would show more covalent character.
parts.answer: Aluminium chloride: Al³⁺ has higher charge and smaller radius than Mg²⁺, so it is more polarising.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which compound has the highest boiling point?
A pentane
B 2-methylbutane
C 2,2-dimethylpropane
D butane
parts.answer: A pentane
parts.working: The three C₅H₁₂ isomers have the same number of electrons, but unbranched pentane has the largest surface contact between molecules, so the strongest instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces. Branching (B, C) reduces contact; butane has fewer electrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The boiling points of the halogens are: F₂ −188 °C, Cl₂ −34 °C, Br₂ 59 °C, I₂ 184 °C. Name the intermolecular forces between halogen molecules and explain the trend.
parts.answer: Instantaneous dipole–induced dipole (London/dispersion) forces. Down the group the number of electrons per molecule increases, so larger, more easily formed instantaneous dipoles; stronger forces need more energy to overcome.
parts.working: B1 id–id forces; B1 more electrons down the group; B1 stronger forces → more energy to separate molecules.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the physical state of bromine and of iodine at 25 °C.
parts.answer: Bromine liquid; iodine solid

stem: Boiling points: butane −0.5 °C (Mr 58); propanone 56 °C (Mr 58); propan-1-ol 97 °C (Mr 60).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why propanone boils at a higher temperature than butane, even though both have Mr = 58.
parts.answer: Propanone is polar (C=O dipole), so it has permanent dipole–permanent dipole forces as well as id–id forces; butane is non-polar with id–id forces only.
parts.working: B1 propanone has pd–pd forces due to polar C=O; B1 butane only id–id, similar size so similar id–id.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why propan-1-ol has an even higher boiling point than propanone.
parts.answer: Propan-1-ol has an O–H group and forms hydrogen bonds between molecules (H bonded to O, lone pair on O); hydrogen bonds are stronger than pd–pd forces.
parts.working: B1 hydrogen bonding via O–H; B1 hydrogen bonds stronger than pd–pd.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Boiling points: HCl −85 °C; HBr −67 °C. Electronegativities: H 2.2, Cl 3.2, Br 3.0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the electronegativity difference in H–Cl and in H–Br.
parts.answer: HCl 1.0; HBr 0.8

parts.label: b
parts.text: HCl is more polar than HBr, yet HBr has the higher boiling point. Explain this.
parts.answer: HBr has more electrons (36 vs 18), so stronger instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces. The increase in id–id forces outweighs the decrease in permanent dipole–dipole forces, so more energy is needed to separate HBr molecules.
parts.working: B1 HBr more electrons; B1 stronger id–id forces; B1 id–id contribution dominates over pd–pd difference.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict, with a reason, whether HI boils above or below HBr.
parts.answer: Above (−35 °C), because it has even more electrons → stronger id–id forces.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why does magnesium have a higher melting point than sodium?
A Each magnesium ion has a higher charge and is smaller, and there are more delocalised electrons per ion.
B Magnesium atoms have more protons, so magnesium has stronger intermolecular forces.
C Magnesium has covalent bonds between its atoms but sodium has ionic bonds.
D Magnesium ions are larger, so there is more space for delocalised electrons.
parts.answer: A Each magnesium ion has a higher charge and is smaller, and there are more delocalised electrons per ion.
parts.working: Mg²⁺ (2+, smaller) and two delocalised electrons per atom give stronger electrostatic attraction between cations and the sea of electrons. B is wrong: metals have metallic bonding, not intermolecular forces.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe metallic bonding.
parts.answer: A lattice of positive metal ions in a sea of delocalised electrons; electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons.
parts.working: B1 lattice of positive ions + delocalised electrons; B1 electrostatic attraction between them.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Copper is used for electrical wiring in homes in Lahore. Explain why copper conducts electricity and why it can be drawn into wires.
parts.answer: Delocalised electrons are free to move through the structure and carry charge when a voltage is applied. Layers of ions can slide over each other without breaking the metallic bonding, because the delocalised electrons still hold the ions together (ductile).
parts.working: B1 delocalised electrons mobile; B1 layers of ions slide; B1 bonding is non-directional / attraction maintained after sliding.

stem: Melting points: potassium 63 °C; sodium 98 °C; magnesium 650 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why potassium has a lower melting point than sodium.
parts.answer: K⁺ is larger than Na⁺ (same charge, one more shell), so the attraction between the cations and the delocalised electrons is weaker and less energy is needed to overcome it.
parts.working: B1 K⁺ ion larger / outer electron further from nucleus; B1 weaker attraction between cations and delocalised electrons → less energy needed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why magnesium has a much higher melting point than sodium.
parts.answer: Mg²⁺ has a higher charge and smaller radius than Na⁺, and each atom provides two delocalised electrons instead of one, so the metallic bonding is stronger.
parts.working: B1 Mg²⁺ higher charge / smaller; B1 two delocalised electrons per atom → stronger attraction.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Aircraft bodies use an alloy of aluminium containing small amounts of copper and magnesium. Explain why the alloy is harder than pure aluminium.
parts.answer: Atoms of different sizes disrupt the regular layers of ions, so the layers cannot slide over each other easily.
parts.working: B1 different-sized atoms distort the lattice; B1 layers less able to slide.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe, in words, a dot-and-cross diagram for carbon dioxide, CO₂. State the number of bonding pairs between each pair of atoms and the number of lone pairs on each atom. Show outer electrons only.
parts.answer: O=C=O: two shared pairs (a double bond) between C and each O; carbon has no lone pairs; each oxygen has two lone pairs. Carbon has 8 outer electrons around it; each O has 8.
parts.working: B1 two double bonds (2 shared pairs each, one electron of each pair from C, one from O); B1 no lone pairs on C; B1 two lone pairs on each O.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe a dot-and-cross diagram for nitrogen, N₂.
parts.answer: Three shared pairs (triple bond) between the two N atoms, each N contributing 3 electrons; one lone pair on each N.
parts.working: B1 triple bond; B1 one lone pair on each N.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total number of outer-shell electrons in a molecule of carbon monoxide, CO.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In CO both atoms have a full outer shell. Describe the dot-and-cross diagram, showing which atom provides the electrons in each bond.
parts.answer: Triple bond: two shared pairs, each with one electron from C and one from O, plus one dative pair with both electrons from O; one lone pair on C and one lone pair on O.
parts.working: B1 three bonding pairs; B1 one of them dative from O to C; B1 one lone pair on each atom.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The cyanide ion, CN⁻, is isoelectronic with CO. State the number of outer electrons in CN⁻ and describe its bonding.
parts.answer: 10 outer electrons; C≡N triple bond (three shared pairs) with one lone pair on C and one on N; the extra electron (charge) is on carbon.
parts.working: B1 4 + 5 + 1 = 10; B1 triple bond + one lone pair on each atom.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which species contains a dative covalent (co-ordinate) bond?
A H₃O⁺
B BF₃
C C₂H₆
D HCN
parts.answer: A H₃O⁺
parts.working: In H₃O⁺ an oxygen lone pair is donated to H⁺, forming a dative bond. BF₃ is electron-deficient and could accept a pair, but in BF₃ itself all three bonds are ordinary covalent bonds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: At about 180 °C aluminium chloride vapour contains Al₂Cl₆ molecules. Explain why an AlCl₃ unit can form a dative bond and describe how two AlCl₃ units join.
parts.answer: In AlCl₃ aluminium has only 6 outer electrons (electron-deficient, an empty orbital). A lone pair on a Cl atom of one AlCl₃ is donated into the empty orbital of the Al in the other unit; this happens twice, so two bridging Cl atoms each form a dative bond.
parts.working: B1 Al has only 6 electrons / incomplete octet; B1 Cl lone pair donated to Al; B1 two dative bonds / two bridging Cl.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the arrangement of the chlorine atoms around each aluminium atom in Al₂Cl₆ and the approximate Cl–Al–Cl bond angle.
parts.answer: Tetrahedral, about 109.5°

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how many dative bonds there are in one Al₂Cl₆ molecule.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structures of diamond and graphite.
parts.answer: Diamond: each C covalently bonded to 4 others, tetrahedral, giant 3-D lattice. Graphite: each C bonded to 3 others in flat hexagonal layers; one electron per carbon delocalised; weak (id–id) forces between layers.
parts.working: B1 diamond 4 bonds, tetrahedral, 3-D; B1 graphite 3 bonds, hexagonal layers; B1 delocalised electrons in graphite; B1 weak forces between layers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why graphite is used for electrodes but diamond is used on drill tips and for cutting glass.
parts.answer: Graphite conducts because delocalised electrons move along the layers; diamond is very hard because every atom is held by four strong covalent bonds in all directions.
parts.working: B1 graphite delocalised mobile electrons; B1 diamond strong covalent bonds throughout, rigid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of silicon(IV) oxide and explain its high melting point (1710 °C).
parts.answer: Giant covalent lattice: each Si bonded to 4 O tetrahedrally, each O bonded to 2 Si. Melting requires breaking many strong covalent Si–O bonds, which needs a lot of energy.
parts.working: B1 each Si to 4 O / each O to 2 Si; B1 giant 3-D covalent lattice; B1 many strong covalent bonds must break.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A sample of pure quartz sand has a mass of 6.00 g. Calculate the amount, in mol, of Si–O bonds in the sample. (Mr SiO₂ = 60.1)
parts.working: M1 n(SiO₂) = 6.00/60.1 = 0.0998 mol; A1 × 4 = 0.399 mol (each Si forms four Si–O bonds).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a hydrogen bond between two water molecules. Include the partial charges, the atoms involved and the bond angle at the hydrogen atom.
parts.answer: δ+ H of one molecule (bonded to the very electronegative O) is attracted to a lone pair on the δ− O of another molecule; O–H···O approximately linear, 180°.
parts.working: B1 δ+ on H and δ− on O; B1 lone pair on O involved; B1 O–H···O angle 180°.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why ice floats on water, for example in the frozen lakes of Gilgit-Baltistan.
parts.answer: In ice each molecule forms hydrogen bonds to four others in an open tetrahedral lattice, so molecules are further apart than in liquid water; ice is less dense.
parts.working: B1 open (rigid) lattice held by hydrogen bonds; B1 molecules further apart → lower density.

stem: 0.250 g of ethanoic acid vapour occupies 82.3 cm³ at 400 K and 101 kPa. R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the apparent relative molecular mass of ethanoic acid in the vapour. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The formula mass of CH₃COOH is 60.0. Explain why the value in (a) is larger, and describe the species responsible.
parts.answer: Ethanoic acid molecules form dimers held by two hydrogen bonds (C=O···H–O between two molecules), so many particles have Mr 120 and the average is between 60 and 120.
parts.working: B1 dimers via hydrogen bonds; B1 two hydrogen bonds between C=O of one molecule and O–H of the other.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Assume the vapour contains only monomers and dimers. Calculate the percentage of CH₃COOH units that are present as dimers. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.working: M1 apparent M = 60.0/(1 − x/2) where x = fraction of units in dimers; A1 x = 2(1 − 60.0/100) = 0.80 → 80 %.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which Period 3 oxide reacts with both dilute hydrochloric acid and aqueous sodium hydroxide?
A Al₂O₃
B MgO
C SO₂
D Na₂O
parts.answer: A Al₂O₃
parts.working: Al₂O₃ is amphoteric: it forms AlCl₃ with HCl and Na[Al(OH)₄] with NaOH. MgO is basic and reacts only with acids; SO₂ is acidic; Na₂O is basic.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A colourless liquid chloride of a Period 3 element is added to water. Steamy fumes are given off, a white solid forms and the pH of the mixture is about 2. What is the chloride?
A SiCl₄
B AlCl₃
C MgCl₂
D NaCl
parts.answer: A SiCl₄
parts.working: SiCl₄ is a liquid at room temperature and is fully hydrolysed: SiCl₄ + 2H₂O → SiO₂ + 4HCl, giving white SiO₂ and a strongly acidic solution. AlCl₃ is a solid at room temperature, so it does not fit the description of a liquid.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which oxide does not react with water but reacts with hot, concentrated aqueous sodium hydroxide?
A SiO₂
B P₄O₁₀
C MgO
D Na₂O
parts.answer: A SiO₂
parts.working: SiO₂ is insoluble in water (giant covalent) but is acidic: SiO₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂SiO₃ + H₂O. P₄O₁₀ is also acidic but reacts vigorously with water to form H₃PO₄.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In which compound does the Period 3 element have an oxidation number of +6?
A SO₃
B SO₂
C PCl₅
D P₄O₁₀
parts.answer: A SO₃
parts.working: In SO₃, S = +6 (3 × −2 = −6). SO₂ has S +4; PCl₅ and P₄O₁₀ both have P +5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of each oxide with water: (i) Na₂O (ii) P₄O₁₀ (iii) SO₂ (iv) SO₃.
parts.answer:
(i) Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH
(ii) P₄O₁₀ + 6H₂O → 4H₃PO₄
(iii) SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃
(iv) SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄
parts.working: B1 each balanced equation (state symbols not required).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest the approximate pH of the solution formed from Na₂O and from SO₃.
parts.answer: Na₂O: about 13–14; SO₃: about 0–1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Magnesium oxide is added to water and the pH is tested. Suggest the pH and explain.
parts.answer: About 9: MgO is only slightly soluble, forming a little Mg(OH)₂ (weakly alkaline).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write equations to show that aluminium oxide is amphoteric, using hydrochloric acid and aqueous sodium hydroxide.
parts.answer:
Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O
Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH + 3H₂O → 2NaAl(OH)₄
parts.working: B1 each (accept ionic equations, e.g. Al₂O₃ + 2OH⁻ + 3H₂O → 2[Al(OH)₄]⁻).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Aluminium oxide does not dissolve in water. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Its lattice energy is very high (strong ionic bonding with some covalent character), so it is insoluble.
parts.working: B1 strong bonding in the lattice / high lattice energy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which other Period 3 oxide reacts with sodium hydroxide but not with dilute hydrochloric acid, while also being insoluble in water? Write the equation.
parts.answer: SiO₂: SiO₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂SiO₃ + H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is seen, and give the approximate pH of the solution, when each chloride is added to water: NaCl, MgCl₂, AlCl₃, SiCl₄, PCl₅.
parts.answer: NaCl: dissolves, pH 7. MgCl₂: dissolves, pH about 6.5. AlCl₃: reacts (steamy fumes with little water), pH about 3. SiCl₄: violent reaction, steamy fumes of HCl, white solid, pH about 1–2. PCl₅: violent reaction, steamy fumes, pH about 1–2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write equations for the reactions of SiCl₄ and PCl₅ with water.
parts.answer:
SiCl₄ + 2H₂O → SiO₂ + 4HCl
PCl₅ + 4H₂O → H₃PO₄ + 5HCl

stem: A student adds 2.085 g of phosphorus(V) chloride to water and makes the solution up to 250.0 cm³. A 25.0 cm³ portion is titrated with 0.500 mol/dm³ NaOH(aq). Assume all three hydrogen atoms of H₃PO₄ react with the alkali. Ar: P 31.0, Cl 35.5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of PCl₅ with water.
parts.answer: PCl₅ + 4H₂O → H₃PO₄ + 5HCl

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in mol, of PCl₅ in the 25.0 cm³ portion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the volume of 0.500 mol/dm³ NaOH needed for complete neutralisation of the 25.0 cm³ portion.
parts.answer: 16.0 cm³
parts.working: M1 1 PCl₅ → 5 HCl + 1 H₃PO₄ → 5 + 3 = 8 mol NaOH; n(NaOH) = 0.0080 mol; A1 V = 0.0080/0.500 = 16.0 cm³.

author: HomiLabs

stem: 3.40 g of silicon tetrachloride is added to an excess of water: SiCl₄ + 2H₂O → SiO₂ + 4HCl. Ar: Si 28.1, Cl 35.5; Mr SiO₂ = 60.1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of silicon(IV) oxide formed. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount of hydrogen chloride formed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a technician opening an old bottle of SiCl₄ in a humid Karachi laboratory sees white fumes.
parts.answer: SiCl₄ reacts with water vapour in the air, producing HCl gas (which forms droplets with moisture) and fine SiO₂.
parts.working: B1 hydrolysis by moisture in air releasing HCl.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Magnesium chloride solution has a pH of about 6.5, whereas sodium chloride solution has a pH of 7. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Mg²⁺ is smaller and more highly charged than Na⁺ (higher charge density), so it polarises the water molecules around it; a little H⁺ is released, so slightly acidic. Na⁺ does not do this.
parts.working: B1 Mg²⁺ higher charge density; B1 polarises/hydrolyses water, releasing H⁺.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the type of bonding in MgCl₂ and in SiCl₄ and use it to explain why one dissolves while the other is hydrolysed.
parts.answer: MgCl₂ ionic: ions are hydrated and simply dissolve. SiCl₄ covalent (simple molecular): water molecules attack the Si atom, breaking Si–Cl bonds (hydrolysis).
parts.working: B1 MgCl₂ ionic dissolves; B1 SiCl₄ covalent, Si–Cl bonds broken by water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the structure and bonding of: Na₂O, Al₂O₃, SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₃.
parts.answer: Na₂O giant ionic; Al₂O₃ giant ionic (with some covalent character); SiO₂ giant covalent; P₄O₁₀ and SO₃ simple molecular (covalent).
parts.working: B1 ionic pair; B1 SiO₂ giant covalent; B1 P₄O₁₀ and SO₃ simple molecular.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the acid–base nature of the oxides changes across Period 3 and link it to the structure.
parts.answer: From basic (Na₂O, MgO, ionic, contain O²⁻ that accepts H⁺) through amphoteric (Al₂O₃) to acidic (SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₂, SO₃, covalent oxides of non-metals that react with water/bases).
parts.working: B1 basic → amphoteric → acidic; B1 ionic oxides basic (O²⁻ ions), covalent oxides acidic.

stem: X is a Period 3 element. Its oxide is a white solid with a high melting point that is insoluble in water but dissolves in both dilute HCl and NaOH(aq). Its chloride is a white solid that sublimes at about 180 °C, fumes in moist air, and exists as a dimer in the vapour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify element X.
parts.answer: Aluminium

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write equations for: (i) X burning in oxygen; (ii) X heated in chlorine to form its chloride; (iii) the formation of the dimer of the chloride.
parts.answer:
(i) 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃
(ii) 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃
(iii) 2AlCl₃ → Al₂Cl₆

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the chloride of X forms steamy fumes in moist air.
parts.answer: It is hydrolysed by water vapour, releasing HCl gas.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest the pH of a solution of the chloride of X in a large volume of water.
parts.answer: About 3

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Smog in Lahore contains sulfur dioxide from burning high-sulfur fuel. Write equations for: (i) SO₂ dissolving in rain water; (ii) the formation of SO₃ from SO₂ in the air; (iii) SO₃ reacting with water.
parts.answer:
(i) SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃
(ii) 2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃
(iii) SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of sulfur in H₂SO₃ and in H₂SO₄.
parts.answer: +4 and +6

parts.label: c
parts.text: Farmers sometimes add powdered magnesium oxide to acidic soil. Write an equation for MgO reacting with sulfuric acid.
parts.answer: MgO + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the complete neutralisation of P₄O₁₀ by aqueous sodium hydroxide, forming sodium phosphate.
parts.answer: P₄O₁₀ + 12NaOH → 4Na₃PO₄ + 6H₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of NaOH needed to neutralise 2.84 g of P₄O₁₀ completely.

parts.label: c
parts.text: P₄O₁₀ is used as a drying agent for some gases. Suggest one gas it could not be used to dry, and why.
parts.answer: Ammonia: P₄O₁₀ is acidic and would react with the basic gas.
parts.working: B1 a basic gas, e.g. NH₃, with reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of aluminium chloride with a small amount of water.
parts.answer: AlCl₃ + 3H₂O → Al(OH)₃ + 3HCl

parts.label: b
parts.text: In a large volume of water, aluminium chloride forms [Al(H₂O)₆]³⁺ ions. Explain why this solution is acidic.
parts.answer: Al³⁺ is small and highly charged (high charge density). It polarises the O–H bonds of the co-ordinated water molecules, weakening them, so an H⁺ is released: [Al(H₂O)₆]³⁺ ⇌ [Al(H₂O)₅(OH)]²⁺ + H⁺.
parts.working: B1 high charge density of Al³⁺; B1 polarises/weakens O–H bond in water ligand; B1 equation or statement that H⁺ is released.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the pH of aqueous NaCl is 7 while that of aqueous AlCl₃ is about 3.
parts.answer: Na⁺ has a low charge density and does not polarise water, so no H⁺ is released.

stem: 0.310 g of sodium oxide is dissolved in water and the solution is made up to 500 cm³. Ar: Na 23.0, O 16.0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of hydroxide ions in the solution.
parts.answer: 0.0200 mol/dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of 0.100 mol/dm³ HCl needed to neutralise 25.0 cm³ of this solution.
parts.answer: 5.00 cm³
parts.working: M1 n(OH⁻) in 25.0 cm³ = 0.00050 mol = n(HCl); A1 V = 5.00 cm³.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of magnesium oxide with dilute hydrochloric acid.
parts.answer: MgO + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of sulfur dioxide with excess aqueous sodium hydroxide.
parts.answer: SO₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₃ + H₂O

parts.label: c
parts.text: Classify MgO and SO₂ as acidic, basic or amphoteric.
parts.answer: MgO basic; SO₂ acidic

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why sodium hydroxide solution can be used to remove SO₂ from waste gases at a cement plant.
parts.answer: SO₂ is an acidic oxide, so it is neutralised (absorbed) by the alkali.

stem:
Five chlorides of Period 3 elements, A to E, are tested.
A: white solid, m.p. 801 °C, dissolves in water to give pH 7.
B: white solid, m.p. 714 °C, dissolves to give pH 6.5.
C: white solid, sublimes at 178 °C, pH 3 in water.
D: colourless liquid, b.p. 58 °C, reacts violently with water giving a white solid and pH 1–2.
E: pale yellow solid, sublimes at about 160 °C, reacts violently with water; the solution contains two acids.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify each of chlorides A to E.
parts.answer: A NaCl; B MgCl₂; C AlCl₃; D SiCl₄; E PCl₅

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why chloride D has a low boiling point but chloride A has a high melting point.
parts.answer: D (SiCl₄) is simple molecular with weak intermolecular (id–id) forces; A (NaCl) is giant ionic with strong electrostatic attraction between many ions.
parts.working: B1 D simple molecular, weak intermolecular forces; B1 A giant ionic, strong attractions throughout.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement explains why atomic radius decreases from sodium to chlorine?
A Nuclear charge increases while shielding stays about the same, so outer electrons are pulled closer.
B Number of electron shells decreases across the period.
C Shielding increases across the period because more electrons are added.
D The outer electrons are in sub-shells of higher energy across the period.
parts.answer: A Nuclear charge increases while shielding stays about the same, so outer electrons are pulled closer.
parts.working: Across Period 3 electrons enter the same (third) shell; proton number rises, shielding by inner shells is almost constant, so effective attraction increases. B is wrong: all have three shells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State and explain the general trend in first ionisation energy across Period 3.
parts.answer: Increases: nuclear charge increases, same shell / similar shielding, so outer electron more strongly attracted and smaller radius.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the first ionisation energy of aluminium is lower than that of magnesium.
