parts.text: 1.48 g of magnesium nitrate (Mr 148.3) is heated until there is no further change. Calculate the mass of the solid residue. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The gases are passed through aqueous sodium hydroxide, which absorbs all the nitrogen dioxide. Calculate the volume of gas, in cm³ at room conditions, that leaves the sodium hydroxide.
parts.answer: 120 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the residue from heating magnesium nitrate is used to line some furnaces.
parts.answer: MgO has a very high melting point (giant ionic lattice with strong attraction between small, doubly charged ions)

parts.label: a
parts.text: 3.00 g of a Group 2 nitrate, M(NO₃)₂, is heated until decomposition is complete, leaving 1.469 g of the oxide MO. Show that the Ar of M is given by the equation 1.469(Ar + 124) = 3.00(Ar + 16).
parts.working: B1 Mr of M(NO₃)₂ = Ar + 124.0 and Mr of MO = Ar + 16.0. B1 equal amounts in mol leads to the equation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Solve the equation to find Ar and identify M.
parts.answer: Ar = 87.6; strontium

subtopic: Group 2 solubility & thermal stability trends (A Level)

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the trend in thermal stability of the Group 2 carbonates down the group.
parts.answer: increases (decomposition temperature increases)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain this trend.
parts.answer: Cation radius increases down the group, so charge density decreases; the cation polarises the carbonate ion (distorts its electron cloud) less; the C–O bonds are weakened less, so more energy is needed to decompose
parts.working: B1 ionic radius of M²⁺ increases / charge density decreases. B1 less polarisation of the CO₃²⁻ anion. B1 C–O bond less weakened, so higher temperature needed. Do not credit 'polarisation of the cation'.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Group 2 solubility & thermal stability trends (A Level)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an expression for the enthalpy change of solution of MgSO₄ in terms of its lattice energy and the enthalpy changes of hydration of its ions.
parts.answer: ΔHsol = ΔHhyd(Mg²⁺) + ΔHhyd(SO₄²⁻) − ΔHlatt(MgSO₄)
parts.working: B1 (lattice energy defined as exothermic formation of the lattice from gaseous ions).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the solubility of the Group 2 sulfates decreases down the group.
parts.answer: Lattice energy becomes only slightly less exothermic (dominated by the large sulfate ion); hydration enthalpy of the cation becomes much less exothermic as the cation gets larger; so ΔHsol becomes more endothermic and solubility decreases
parts.working: B1 lattice energy decreases only slightly because SO₄²⁻ is large. B1 hydration enthalpy decreases considerably as cation radius increases. B1 ΔHsol less exothermic / more endothermic, so less soluble.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Group 2 solubility & thermal stability trends (A Level)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why barium hydroxide is more soluble in water than magnesium hydroxide.
parts.answer: OH⁻ is small, so lattice energy depends strongly on cation size and decreases a lot down the group; hydration enthalpy of the cation decreases less; ΔHsol becomes more exothermic (less endothermic) for Ba(OH)₂
parts.working: B1 lattice energy falls more than hydration enthalpy down the group. B1 reason: small anion so inter-ionic distance changes greatly with cation radius. B1 ΔHsol more negative for Ba(OH)₂, so more soluble.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the trend for hydroxides is the opposite of the trend for sulfates.
parts.answer: The anions differ in size: with the small OH⁻ the lattice energy change dominates; with the large SO₄²⁻ the hydration enthalpy change dominates

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Group 2 solubility & thermal stability trends (A Level)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Use these data (kJ mol⁻¹) to calculate the enthalpy change of solution of MgSO₄ and of BaSO₄.
ΔHhyd: Mg²⁺ −1920; Ba²⁺ −1360; SO₄²⁻ −1160
lattice energy: MgSO₄ −2989; BaSO₄ −2546
parts.answer: MgSO₄ −91 kJ mol⁻¹; BaSO₄ +26 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why barium sulfate is used in 'barium meals' for X-ray imaging of the gut, while magnesium sulfate is used as a bath salt.
parts.answer: ΔHsol of BaSO₄ is endothermic (+26), which together with the much larger hydration-enthalpy loss for Ba²⁺ is consistent with BaSO₄ being very insoluble – so toxic Ba²⁺ ions are not absorbed from the gut; ΔHsol of MgSO₄ is exothermic (−91) and MgSO₄ is soluble, so it dissolves in bath water
parts.working: B1 BaSO₄: endothermic ΔHsol linked to very low solubility, so barium ions are not absorbed (safe). B1 MgSO₄: exothermic ΔHsol linked to high solubility.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the difference between the lattice energies of the two sulfates and the difference between the hydration enthalpies of Mg²⁺ and Ba²⁺. Use these to explain the trend.
parts.answer: lattice energies differ by 443 kJ mol⁻¹; hydration enthalpies by 560 kJ mol⁻¹
parts.working: B1 both differences. B1 hydration enthalpy falls by more (560) than lattice energy (443), so ΔHsol becomes more endothermic down the group.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Group 2 solubility & thermal stability trends (A Level)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Use these data (kJ mol⁻¹) to calculate the enthalpy change of hydration of Sr²⁺.
lattice energy of SrCl₂ = −2156
enthalpy change of solution of SrCl₂ = −52
enthalpy change of hydration of Cl⁻ = −364
parts.answer: −1480 kJ mol⁻¹
parts.working: M1 ΔHhyd(Sr²⁺) = ΔHsol + ΔHlatt − 2ΔHhyd(Cl⁻). A1 −52 − 2156 + 728 = −1480. (Factor of 2 for Cl⁻ needed.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict, with a reason, whether the enthalpy change of hydration of Ca²⁺ is more or less exothermic than your answer.
parts.answer: More exothermic; Ca²⁺ is smaller with a higher charge density, so it attracts water molecules more strongly
parts.working: B1 more exothermic. B1 smaller ion / higher charge density – stronger ion–dipole attraction.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Group 2 solubility & thermal stability trends (A Level)

parts.label: a
parts.text: The ionic radii are Mg²⁺ 0.072 nm and Ba²⁺ 0.135 nm. Use these data to explain why barium carbonate must be heated to a much higher temperature than magnesium carbonate before it decomposes.
parts.answer: Mg²⁺ is smaller with the same charge, so higher charge density; it polarises the carbonate ion more, weakening a C–O bond; MgCO₃ decomposes at a lower temperature, BaCO₃ needs a higher temperature
parts.working: B1 Mg²⁺ higher charge density. B1 greater polarisation / distortion of CO₃²⁻ electron cloud. B1 C–O bond weakened more, so MgCO₃ less stable.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Magnesium oxide has a higher lattice energy than barium oxide. Explain how this also favours the decomposition of MgCO₃.
parts.answer: The smaller Mg²⁺ forms a much more exothermic lattice with the small O²⁻ ion, so the products of decomposition are relatively more stable; ΔH of decomposition is less endothermic
parts.working: B1 MgO lattice energy much more exothermic than BaO. B1 makes decomposition less endothermic for MgCO₃.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Group 2 solubility & thermal stability trends (A Level)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Beryllium carbonate is very unstable and decomposes near room temperature. Suggest an explanation in terms of the Be²⁺ ion.
parts.answer: Be²⁺ is extremely small with very high charge density; it strongly polarises the carbonate ion
parts.working: B1 very small ion / very high charge density. B1 strong polarisation of CO₃²⁻ weakens C–O bonds.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict how the thermal stability of radium carbonate compares with that of barium carbonate. Explain.
parts.answer: More stable; Ra²⁺ is larger, lower charge density, polarises carbonate less
parts.working: B1 more stable / higher decomposition temperature. B1 reason.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Group 2 solubility & thermal stability trends (A Level)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use these standard enthalpy changes of formation (kJ mol⁻¹) to calculate ΔH for the decomposition of calcium carbonate: CaCO₃ −1207; CaO −635; CO₂ −394.
parts.answer: +178 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: ΔS for the decomposition is +161 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Calculate the minimum temperature at which the decomposition becomes feasible. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Values of ΔH for decomposition are: MgCO₃ +117, CaCO₃ +178, SrCO₃ +234, BaCO₃ +267 kJ mol⁻¹. The values of ΔS are similar. Explain how these data are consistent with the trend in thermal stability, and give the chemical reason for the trend.
parts.answer: ΔH becomes more endothermic down the group, so T = ΔH/ΔS increases – stability increases; larger cations with lower charge density polarise the carbonate ion less
parts.working: B1 increasing ΔH so higher decomposition temperature. B1 cation radius increases / charge density decreases. B1 less polarisation of anion.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Group 2 solubility & thermal stability trends (A Level)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Lattice energies (kJ mol⁻¹): MgO −3791; BaO −3054; MgSO₄ −2989; BaSO₄ −2546. Calculate the change in lattice energy from Mg to Ba for the oxides and for the sulfates.
parts.answer: oxides: 737 kJ mol⁻¹ less exothermic; sulfates: 443 kJ mol⁻¹ less exothermic

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the lattice energy changes much more for the oxides than for the sulfates.
parts.answer: Lattice energy depends on the sum of ionic radii; O²⁻ is small so changing the cation from Mg²⁺ to Ba²⁺ makes a large fractional change in the inter-ionic distance; SO₄²⁻ is large so the fractional change is small
parts.working: B1 lattice energy ∝ 1/(r⁺ + r⁻). B1 large anion means cation size has a smaller effect.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The radius of Ca²⁺ (0.100 nm) lies between those of Mg²⁺ (0.072 nm) and Ba²⁺ (0.135 nm). Predict, with a reason, how the lattice energy of CaSO₄ compares with those of MgSO₄ and BaSO₄, and state whether CaSO₄ is more or less soluble in water than MgSO₄.
parts.answer: Lattice energy of CaSO₄ lies between −2989 and −2546 kJ mol⁻¹ (less exothermic than MgSO₄, more exothermic than BaSO₄) because Ca²⁺ is intermediate in size; CaSO₄ is less soluble than MgSO₄
parts.working: B1 between the two values, with reason: larger cation → greater inter-ionic distance → weaker attraction. B1 less soluble than MgSO₄ (sulfate solubility decreases down the group).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Group 2 solubility & thermal stability trends (A Level)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Lithium nitrate decomposes in the same way as Group 2 nitrates, but sodium nitrate decomposes to sodium nitrite and oxygen. Write equations for the decomposition of lithium nitrate and of sodium nitrate.
parts.answer: 4LiNO₃ → 2Li₂O + 4NO₂ + O₂; 2NaNO₃ → 2NaNO₂ + O₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: Li⁺ has an ionic radius of 0.076 nm, similar to Mg²⁺ (0.072 nm). Na⁺ has a radius of 0.102 nm. Use the idea of charge density to explain why LiNO₃ behaves like Mg(NO₃)₂ and why NaNO₃ is more thermally stable.
parts.answer: Li⁺ is small, so its charge density is high enough to polarise the nitrate ion strongly, like Mg²⁺; Na⁺ is larger with the same +1 charge, so lower charge density; nitrate ion is polarised less, so NaNO₃ does not decompose to the oxide
parts.working: B1 Li⁺ small, high charge density (comparable effect to Mg²⁺). B1 polarises NO₃⁻, weakening N–O bonds. B1 Na⁺ lower charge density – less polarisation – more stable.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict whether magnesium nitrate or calcium nitrate would release nitrogen dioxide at a lower temperature, giving a reason.
parts.answer: magnesium nitrate; Mg²⁺ is smaller with higher charge density so it polarises the nitrate ion more

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A solution may contain either Ba²⁺ ions or Mg²⁺ ions. Which reagent added in small amounts gives a white precipitate with Ba²⁺(aq) but no precipitate with Mg²⁺(aq)?
A dilute sulfuric acid
B dilute hydrochloric acid
C aqueous sodium hydroxide
D aqueous ammonia
parts.answer: A dilute sulfuric acid
parts.working: BaSO₄ is insoluble but MgSO₄ is soluble. C is the main distractor: aqueous NaOH gives a white precipitate of Mg(OH)₂ with Mg²⁺, not with Ba²⁺ (barium hydroxide is fairly soluble).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the trends in solubility down Group 2 of (i) the hydroxides and (ii) the sulfates.
parts.answer: (i) hydroxides become more soluble; (ii) sulfates become less soluble

parts.label: b
parts.text: Magnesium hydroxide is used in some antacid tablets sold in Pakistani pharmacies. Write an equation for its reaction with stomach acid (hydrochloric acid).
parts.answer: Mg(OH)₂ + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + 2H₂O

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why magnesium hydroxide is preferred to calcium hydroxide or barium hydroxide as an antacid.
parts.answer: It is only sparingly soluble, so the solution is only weakly alkaline (and Mg²⁺ is not toxic, unlike Ba²⁺)
parts.working: B1 low solubility gives mild alkalinity / Ba compounds toxic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Aqueous sodium hydroxide is added drop by drop to separate solutions of magnesium chloride and barium chloride of the same concentration. Describe and explain what is seen in each case.
parts.answer: MgCl₂: white precipitate; BaCl₂: no precipitate (or only a very faint one); Mg(OH)₂ is sparingly soluble, Ba(OH)₂ is much more soluble
parts.working: B1 white ppt with Mg²⁺. B1 no (or faint) ppt with Ba²⁺. B1 solubility of hydroxides increases down the group.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an ionic equation, with state symbols, for the formation of the precipitate.
parts.answer: Mg²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Mg(OH)₂(s)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Dilute sulfuric acid is then added to a fresh sample of each solution. Describe what is seen.
parts.answer: white precipitate (BaSO₄) with barium chloride; no change with magnesium chloride

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Three solutions, P, Q and R, are calcium nitrate, magnesium nitrate and barium nitrate, but not in that order. Results:
P: aqueous NaOH – white precipitate, insoluble in excess; aqueous NH₃ – white precipitate; dilute H₂SO₄ – no change
Q: aqueous NaOH – no precipitate; aqueous NH₃ – no precipitate; dilute H₂SO₄ – dense white precipitate
R: aqueous NaOH – white precipitate, insoluble in excess; aqueous NH₃ – no precipitate; dilute H₂SO₄ – slight white precipitate
Identify P, Q and R.
parts.answer: P magnesium nitrate; Q barium nitrate; R calcium nitrate

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why R gives only a slight precipitate with dilute sulfuric acid while Q gives a dense one.
parts.answer: CaSO₄ is slightly soluble; BaSO₄ is much less soluble (sulfate solubility decreases down the group)
parts.working: B1 CaSO₄ sparingly soluble. B1 BaSO₄ insoluble / trend.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why aqueous ammonia gives a precipitate with P but not with R.
parts.answer: Aqueous ammonia gives only a low concentration of OH⁻; this is enough to exceed the solubility of Mg(OH)₂ but not of the more soluble Ca(OH)₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of calcium with cold water and describe two observations.
parts.answer: Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂; fizzing/bubbles; calcium sinks/disappears; cloudy white suspension forms
parts.working: B1 equation. B1 B1 any two observations: effervescence, metal disappears, milky solution / white solid, warmth.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Magnesium reacts only very slowly with cold water. Write an equation for this reaction.
parts.answer: Mg + 2H₂O → Mg(OH)₂ + H₂
parts.working: B1 (hydroxide, not oxide, with cold water).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of strontium with oxygen to form its oxide.
parts.answer: 2Sr + O₂ → 2SrO

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which equation correctly represents the reaction of magnesium with steam?
A Mg + 2H₂O → Mg(OH)₂ + H₂
B Mg + H₂O → MgO + H₂
C 2Mg + 2H₂O → 2MgO + 2H₂ + O₂
D Mg + H₂O → MgH₂ + O
parts.answer: B Mg + H₂O → MgO + H₂
parts.working: With steam, magnesium forms the oxide and hydrogen. A is the slow reaction with cold water, which forms the hydroxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 0.100 g of calcium reacts completely with water and the solution is made up to 250 cm³. Calculate the volume of hydrogen produced, in cm³ at room conditions. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 59.9 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of hydroxide ions in the solution.
parts.answer: 0.0200 mol dm⁻³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the volume of 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid needed to neutralise 25.0 cm³ of the solution.
parts.answer: 24.9 cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why does the reactivity of the Group 2 elements with water increase down the group?
A The first and second ionisation energies decrease.
B The metals become more electronegative.
C The nuclear charge decreases.
D The metallic radius decreases.
parts.answer: A The first and second ionisation energies decrease.
parts.working: Less energy is needed to remove the two outer electrons, so M²⁺ forms more easily. C is wrong: nuclear charge increases down the group, but shielding and distance outweigh it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the first ionisation energy decreases down Group 2.
parts.answer: Outer electron further from nucleus (more shells); more shielding by inner electrons; weaker attraction despite larger nuclear charge
parts.working: B1 increased atomic radius / distance. B1 increased shielding. B1 weaker attraction for the outer electron.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student heats equal amounts of calcium carbonate and barium carbonate with the same Bunsen flame and passes the gas into limewater. Predict which limewater turns milky first and state the trend shown.
parts.answer: calcium carbonate; thermal stability of carbonates increases down the group

parts.label: a
parts.text: Farmers in Sindh spread calcium hydroxide (slaked lime) on acidic soil. Write an equation for the reaction of calcium hydroxide with nitric acid in the soil.
parts.answer: Ca(OH)₂ + 2HNO₃ → Ca(NO₃)₂ + 2H₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: A field contains acid equivalent to 50.0 mol of H⁺ ions. Calculate the mass, in kg, of calcium hydroxide (Mr 74.1) needed to neutralise it. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calcium hydroxide is made by adding water to calcium oxide, which is made from limestone. Write equations for the two steps.
parts.answer: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂; CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the reagents and conditions for the two stages needed to convert nitrobenzene into phenylamine.
parts.answer: Stage 1: tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid, heat under reflux. Stage 2: add aqueous sodium hydroxide (excess)
parts.working: B1 Sn + conc HCl. B1 heat/reflux. B1 then NaOH(aq) to release the free amine from its salt.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Phenylamine is shaken with bromine water at room temperature. Describe what is seen and name the organic product.
parts.answer: orange/brown bromine water decolourised and a white precipitate forms; 2,4,6-tribromophenylamine
parts.working: B1 decolourises + white ppt. B1 name.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Phenylamine reacts with nitrous acid to form benzenediazonium chloride. State the reagents used to produce nitrous acid in the flask and the temperature needed.
parts.answer: sodium nitrite (NaNO₂) and dilute hydrochloric acid; below 10 °C (ice bath)
parts.working: B1 NaNO₂ + HCl. B1 temperature below 10 °C (accept 0–10 °C).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the formula of the benzenediazonium ion.
parts.answer: C₆H₅N₂⁺ (C₆H₅–N≡N⁺)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the temperature must be kept low, and write an equation for what happens if the solution is warmed.
parts.answer: Diazonium ion decomposes above about 10 °C; C₆H₅N₂⁺ + H₂O → C₆H₅OH + N₂ + H⁺
parts.working: B1 decomposes / unstable at higher temperature. B1 equation (phenol and nitrogen formed).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A solution of benzenediazonium chloride is added to a cold solution of phenol in aqueous sodium hydroxide. A yellow-orange precipitate forms. Give the structural formula of the product and name the type of reaction.
parts.answer: 4-hydroxyazobenzene: C₆H₅–N=N–C₆H₄–OH with the OH para (4-position) to the azo group; electrophilic substitution (coupling)
parts.working: B1 –N=N– linking two benzene rings. B1 OH in 4-position. B1 electrophilic substitution / coupling.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the product is coloured.
parts.answer: The –N=N– group links two benzene rings so there is an extended delocalised system; it absorbs light in the visible region
parts.working: B1 extended delocalisation / conjugation. B1 absorbs some visible wavelengths; the colour seen is the light not absorbed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one use of compounds of this type.
parts.answer: dyes (for fabric, e.g. cotton in Faisalabad mills) / food colouring / indicators

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reduction of nitrobenzene to phenylamine using [H] to represent the reducing agent.
parts.answer: C₆H₅NO₂ + 6[H] → C₆H₅NH₂ + 2H₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: 12.3 g of nitrobenzene gave 6.51 g of pure phenylamine. Calculate the percentage yield. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (Mr: C₆H₅NO₂ 123.0, C₆H₅NH₂ 93.0)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why phenylamine reacts with aqueous bromine at room temperature without a catalyst, whereas benzene does not react.
parts.answer: The lone pair on N is delocalised into the ring; this increases the electron density of the ring (especially at 2, 4, 6 positions); the ring is more easily attacked by electrophiles / Br₂ is polarised
parts.working: B1 lone pair on N overlaps with / delocalised into π system. B1 increased electron density in ring. B1 more susceptible to electrophilic attack, so no halogen carrier needed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction and calculate the maximum mass of organic product from 2.79 g of phenylamine. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (Mr: C₆H₅NH₂ 93.0, product 329.7)
parts.answer: C₆H₅NH₂ + 3Br₂ → C₆H₂Br₃NH₂ + 3HBr; 9.89 g

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline a four-step synthesis of the azo dye formed between benzene-derived diazonium ions and naphthalen-2-ol, starting from benzene. For each step give the reagents and conditions and the organic product.
parts.answer: 1 benzene → nitrobenzene: conc HNO₃ + conc H₂SO₄, below 55 °C. 2 nitrobenzene → phenylamine: Sn + conc HCl, reflux, then NaOH(aq). 3 phenylamine → benzenediazonium chloride: NaNO₂ + HCl, below 10 °C. 4 couple with naphthalen-2-ol in aqueous NaOH, below 10 °C → azo dye
parts.working: B1 for each correct reagent set (4) and B1 for correct temperatures in steps 1 and 3; B1 all intermediates named correctly. Max 6.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why naphthalen-2-ol is dissolved in aqueous sodium hydroxide before coupling.
parts.answer: To form the naphthoxide (phenoxide-type) ion, which is more strongly activated / soluble in water
parts.working: B1 the anion makes the ring more electron-rich and dissolves the reagent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 4-nitrophenylamine is diazotised and the product is coupled with phenol in alkaline solution. Give the structural formula and the molecular formula of the azo compound formed.
parts.answer: O₂N–C₆H₄–N=N–C₆H₄–OH (both groups at 4-positions); C₁₂H₉N₃O₃

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the Mr of the azo compound.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A dye manufacturer wants to make the compound HO–C₆H₄–N=N–C₆H₄–CH₃ (both substituents in 4-positions). Identify the amine and the coupling agent that should be used, and explain why the coupling agent must contain an OH or NH₂ group.
parts.answer: amine: 4-methylphenylamine (diazotised); coupling agent: phenol. The OH group activates the ring so the weakly electrophilic diazonium ion can substitute it
parts.working: B1 4-methylphenylamine. B1 phenol. B1 diazonium ion is a weak electrophile; it reacts only with activated rings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Glycine is H₂NCH₂COOH. Give the structure of the zwitterion of glycine.
parts.answer: H₃N⁺CH₂COO⁻

parts.label: b
parts.text: Glycine is a solid that melts (with decomposition) above 230 °C and dissolves well in water. Explain these properties.
parts.answer: Zwitterions are held by strong ionic attractions in the lattice; ions are strongly hydrated by water molecules
parts.working: B1 strong electrostatic attraction between zwitterions, so high melting point. B1 ion–dipole interactions with water / hydrogen bonding, so soluble.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Alanine is CH₃CH(NH₂)COOH. Give the structure of the main form of alanine present in (i) a solution at pH 1 and (ii) a solution at pH 13.
parts.answer: (i) CH₃CH(NH₃⁺)COOH; (ii) CH₃CH(NH₂)COO⁻

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define the term isoelectric point.
parts.answer: The pH at which the amino acid exists as the zwitterion with no overall charge (does not move in an electric field)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why alanine is optically active but glycine is not.
parts.answer: Alanine has a chiral carbon (four different groups: H, CH₃, NH₂, COOH); glycine has two H on its central carbon

parts.label: a
parts.text: Glycine and alanine can combine to form two different dipeptides. Give the structural formula of each.
parts.answer: H₂NCH₂CONHCH(CH₃)COOH (Gly-Ala) and H₂NCH(CH₃)CONHCH₂COOH (Ala-Gly)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the linkage formed and the type of reaction.
parts.answer: peptide (amide) link –CONH–; condensation

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the Mr of either dipeptide. (Mr: glycine 75.0, alanine 89.0, water 18.0)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A mixture of lysine (isoelectric point 9.7), glycine (isoelectric point 6.0) and aspartic acid (isoelectric point 2.8) is placed in the centre of a strip of paper soaked in a buffer at pH 6.0. A voltage is applied. Predict and explain the movement of each amino acid.
parts.answer: lysine is positively charged at pH 6.0 and moves to the cathode (negative electrode); glycine is at its isoelectric point – zwitterion – does not move; aspartic acid is negatively charged and moves to the anode
parts.working: B1 each, with reason based on pH relative to isoelectric point.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the spots can be made visible after electrophoresis.
parts.answer: spray with ninhydrin (or a locating agent) and warm

parts.label: a
parts.text: A tripeptide has the sequence Ala-Gly-Ser. State the reagents and conditions for hydrolysing it completely.
parts.answer: 6 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid, heat under reflux for several hours
parts.working: B1 HCl(aq) (accept NaOH(aq)). B1 heat/reflux for a prolonged time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Serine is HOCH₂CH(NH₂)COOH. Give the structures of the three species formed when the hydrolysis is carried out in excess acid.
parts.answer: CH₃CH(NH₃⁺)COOH; ⁺H₃NCH₂COOH; HOCH₂CH(NH₃⁺)COOH

parts.label: a
parts.text: Electrophoresis is carried out at pH 1.0 on a mixture of glycine, the dipeptide Gly-Gly and lysine (which has two NH₂ groups). State the charge carried by each species at pH 1.0.
parts.answer: glycine +1; Gly-Gly +1; lysine +2
parts.working: B1 glycine and Gly-Gly +1 (amino group protonated, COOH un-ionised at pH 1.0). B1 lysine +2 (both amino groups protonated).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the order in which the three species are found from furthest to nearest from the starting point, towards the cathode. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: lysine (furthest) > glycine > Gly-Gly (nearest)
parts.working: B1 order. B1 lysine has the largest charge (charge/mass ratio highest). B1 glycine and Gly-Gly have the same charge but glycine is smaller, so moves further.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A pentapeptide has the sequence Gly-Ala-Val-Ala-Gly. Calculate its Mr. (Mr: glycine 75.0, alanine 89.0, valine 117.0, water 18.0)
parts.working: M1 four peptide bonds so 4 H₂O lost. A1 2(75.0) + 2(89.0) + 117.0 − 72.0 = 373.0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of chiral centres in the pentapeptide and explain your answer.
parts.answer: 3; each alanine and the valine residue has a chiral carbon, glycine does not
parts.working: B1 3. B1 glycine's α-carbon carries two H atoms.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Partial hydrolysis gives a mixture of dipeptides. List all the different dipeptides that could form.
parts.answer: Gly-Ala, Ala-Val, Val-Ala, Ala-Gly
parts.working: B1 for three correct. B1 all four with no extras.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Place ammonia, ethylamine and phenylamine in order of increasing base strength.
parts.answer: phenylamine < ammonia < ethylamine

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain your order.
parts.answer: Ethyl group is electron-donating so the lone pair on N is more available to accept H⁺; in phenylamine the lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring, so it is less available
parts.working: B1 base strength depends on availability of N lone pair to accept a proton. B1 alkyl group pushes electron density onto N. B1 lone pair delocalised into ring in phenylamine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the reagent and conditions for making ethylamine from bromoethane.
parts.answer: excess concentrated ammonia in ethanol; heat in a sealed tube (under pressure)
parts.working: B1 NH₃ in ethanol. B1 heat in sealed tube / under pressure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂Br + 2NH₃ → CH₃CH₂NH₂ + NH₄Br

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why ammonia is used in excess.
parts.answer: To reduce further substitution – ethylamine can itself react with bromoethane to form secondary and tertiary amines

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the reagents and conditions for reducing propanenitrile, CH₃CH₂CN, to an amine and give the structure of the amine.
parts.answer: LiAlH₄ in dry ether (or H₂ with Ni catalyst / heat); CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂ (propylamine)
parts.working: B1 reagent and conditions. B1 product.

parts.label: b
parts.text: N-methylethanamide, CH₃CONHCH₃, is reduced by LiAlH₄. Give the structure of the product and state whether it is a primary, secondary or tertiary amine.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂NHCH₃; secondary amine

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation to show why an aqueous solution of ethylamine is alkaline.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂NH₂ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺ + OH⁻

parts.label: b
parts.text: Ethylamine reacts with hydrochloric acid. Write an equation and name the product.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂NH₂ + HCl → CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺Cl⁻; ethylammonium chloride

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the salt formed in (b) has no fishy smell, while ethylamine does. Then explain how ethylamine could be recovered from the salt.
parts.answer: The salt is ionic and non-volatile; warming with aqueous NaOH (strong base) releases the free amine
parts.working: B1 ionic, so not volatile. B1 add NaOH(aq) and warm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Propylamine, CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂, can be made from bromoethane in two steps. Give the reagents, conditions and intermediate.
parts.answer: Step 1: KCN in ethanol, heat under reflux → propanenitrile CH₃CH₂CN. Step 2: LiAlH₄ in dry ether (or H₂/Ni) → CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂
parts.working: B1 step 1 reagents/conditions. B1 intermediate propanenitrile. B1 step 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this route gives a purer amine product than heating 1-bromopropane with ammonia.
parts.answer: Nitrile reduction gives only the primary amine; with ammonia, the amine product is a nucleophile and reacts further with the halogenoalkane to give secondary/tertiary amines and quaternary salts
parts.working: B1 no further substitution in the nitrile route. B1 mixture of amines in the ammonia route.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When 1-bromopropane is heated with ammonia, a mixture of products forms. Give the structures of the primary, secondary and tertiary amines and the quaternary ammonium salt that can form.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂; (CH₃CH₂CH₂)₂NH; (CH₃CH₂CH₂)₃N; (CH₃CH₂CH₂)₄N⁺Br⁻

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the Mr of the quaternary ammonium salt.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the quaternary ammonium ion cannot act as a base.
parts.answer: The nitrogen has no lone pair (all four electron pairs are used in bonds to carbon)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of propanoyl chloride with ammonia to form propanamide.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂COCl + NH₃ → CH₃CH₂CONH₂ + HCl (or with 2NH₃ → … + NH₄Cl)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Ethanoyl chloride reacts with ethylamine. Give the structure and name of the organic product.
parts.answer: CH₃CONHCH₂CH₃; N-ethylethanamide

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the type of reaction in (b).
parts.answer: condensation (nucleophilic addition–elimination)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethanamide is heated under reflux with dilute hydrochloric acid. Give the products.
parts.answer: ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, and ammonium chloride, NH₄Cl

parts.label: b
parts.text: Ethanamide is heated with aqueous sodium hydroxide. Give the products and describe a test for the gas evolved.
parts.answer: sodium ethanoate, CH₃COONa, and ammonia; ammonia turns damp red litmus paper blue
parts.working: B1 sodium ethanoate. B1 ammonia. B1 damp red litmus turns blue.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why ethanamide, CH₃CONH₂, is a much weaker base than ethylamine, CH₃CH₂NH₂.
parts.answer: In ethanamide the lone pair on N is delocalised over the C=O group (the electronegative O withdraws electron density); the lone pair is much less available to accept a proton; in ethylamine the ethyl group donates electrons
parts.working: B1 lone pair delocalised with the C=O π system. B1 so less available to bond to H⁺. B1 ethyl group electron-donating in ethylamine.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why ethanamide is a solid at room temperature, whereas ethanoyl chloride is a liquid.
parts.answer: Ethanamide molecules form hydrogen bonds (N–H…O=C); ethanoyl chloride molecules only have permanent dipole and London forces
parts.working: B1 hydrogen bonding in amide. B1 weaker forces in acyl chloride.

parts.label: a
parts.text: N-methylpropanamide, CH₃CH₂CONHCH₃, is reduced by LiAlH₄ in dry ether. Give the structure of the product.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂CH₂NHCH₃

parts.label: b
parts.text: 4.35 g of N-methylpropanamide (Mr 87.0) gave 2.92 g of the amine (Mr 73.0). Calculate the percentage yield. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the amide could be made from an acyl chloride.
parts.answer: propanoyl chloride + methylamine

parts.label: a
parts.text: Paracetamol, HO–C₆H₄–NHCOCH₃ (substituents 1,4), is manufactured from 4-aminophenol. Name the two functional groups in paracetamol.
parts.answer: phenol (OH on ring) and amide (secondary amide –NHCO–)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Industry uses ethanoic anhydride: HO–C₆H₄–NH₂ + (CH₃CO)₂O → HO–C₆H₄–NHCOCH₃ + CH₃COOH. Calculate the atom economy of this reaction. (Mr: 4-aminophenol 109.0, ethanoic anhydride 102.0, paracetamol 151.0)
parts.working: M1 atom economy = Mr(desired product) ÷ ΣMr(reactants) × 100. A1 151.0 ÷ 211.0 × 100 = 71.6 %.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Paracetamol is heated with excess aqueous sodium hydroxide. Give the structures of the organic products.
parts.answer: ⁻O–C₆H₄–NH₂ (sodium 4-aminophenoxide) and CH₃COO⁻Na⁺
parts.working: B1 amide hydrolysed to ethanoate. B1 4-aminophenoxide (phenol deprotonated by excess NaOH).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Three isomers, J, K and L, have the formula C₃H₇NO and are all amides. Each is heated with aqueous NaOH.
J gives sodium propanoate and ammonia.
K gives sodium ethanoate and methylamine.
L gives sodium methanoate and dimethylamine, (CH₃)₂NH.
Give the structures of J, K and L.
parts.answer: J CH₃CH₂CONH₂; K CH₃CONHCH₃; L HCON(CH₃)₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: Classify J, K and L as primary, secondary or tertiary amides.
parts.answer: J primary; K secondary; L tertiary

parts.label: c
parts.text: Only one of the three can be made from an acyl chloride and ammonia. Identify it and write the equation.
parts.answer: J: CH₃CH₂COCl + NH₃ → CH₃CH₂CONH₂ + HCl

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which reagent and conditions convert bromoethane into propanenitrile?
A KCN in ethanol, heat under reflux
B HCN in water, room temperature
C KCN in water, room temperature
D NH₃ in ethanol, heat in a sealed tube
parts.answer: A KCN in ethanol, heat under reflux
parts.working: Cyanide ions substitute the bromine when KCN in ethanol is heated under reflux. D gives ethylamine, not a nitrile; B (HCN) is used for addition to carbonyl compounds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Propanal reacts with HCN in the presence of a small amount of KCN. Give the structure and name of the product.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CN; 2-hydroxybutanenitrile

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the mechanism of this reaction.
parts.answer: nucleophilic addition

parts.label: c
parts.text: The product of (a) is heated under reflux with dilute hydrochloric acid. Give the structure of the organic product.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂CH(OH)COOH (2-hydroxybutanoic acid)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
2-bromopropane is heated under reflux with KCN in ethanol. The organic product is then heated under reflux with dilute sulfuric acid. What is the final organic product?
A butanoic acid
B 2-methylpropanoic acid
C propanoic acid
D propan-2-ol
parts.answer: B 2-methylpropanoic acid
parts.working: CH₃CHBrCH₃ → (CH₃)₂CHCN (2-methylpropanenitrile) → (CH₃)₂CHCOOH, 2-methylpropanoic acid. A assumes a straight chain, but the CN group attaches to the middle carbon.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Lactic acid, CH₃CH(OH)COOH, can be made from ethanal in two steps. Give the reagents and conditions for each step and the intermediate.
parts.answer: 1 HCN with KCN catalyst (about 10–20 °C) → CH₃CH(OH)CN (2-hydroxypropanenitrile); 2 dilute HCl or H₂SO₄, heat under reflux → lactic acid
parts.working: B1 step 1. B1 intermediate. B1 step 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Lactic acid made this way is not optically active, although its molecules are chiral. Explain why.
parts.answer: The C=O group in ethanal is planar; CN⁻ attacks equally from either side; a racemic mixture (50:50) of the two enantiomers forms, so the rotations cancel
parts.working: B1 planar carbonyl group. B1 equal chance of attack from above and below. B1 racemic mixture – no net rotation of plane-polarised light.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethanoic acid can be made from ethene in two steps via ethanol. Give the reagents and conditions for each step.
parts.answer: Step 1: steam with H₃PO₄ catalyst, about 300 °C and 6–7 MPa (high pressure). Step 2: acidified potassium dichromate(VI) (K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄), heat under reflux
parts.working: B1 steam + acid catalyst (H₃PO₄). B1 high temperature and pressure. B1 K₂Cr₂O₇ + H⁺. B1 reflux (not distil).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the colour change seen in step 2.
parts.answer: orange to green

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which sequence of reagents converts bromoethane into ethanoic acid?
A NaOH(aq), heat; then K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄, heat under reflux
B NaOH in ethanol, heat; then K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄, distil
C KCN in ethanol, heat; then dilute HCl, heat under reflux
D NH₃ in ethanol, heat; then K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄, heat under reflux
parts.answer: A NaOH(aq), heat; then K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄, heat under reflux
parts.working: Aqueous NaOH substitutes OH to give ethanol, which is fully oxidised under reflux. B gives ethene (elimination). C gives propanoic acid, with one more carbon – the main distractor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 1-bromobutane is converted into pentanoic acid in two steps. Give the reagents and conditions for each step and the structure of the intermediate.
parts.answer: Step 1: KCN in ethanol, heat under reflux → CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CN (pentanenitrile). Step 2: dilute HCl (or H₂SO₄), heat under reflux
parts.working: B1 step 1. B1 intermediate. B1 step 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this route is useful to a chemist designing a synthesis.
parts.answer: It increases the length of the carbon chain by one carbon atom

parts.label: a
parts.text: Benzoic acid can be made from benzene in two steps via methylbenzene. Give the reagents and conditions for each step.
parts.answer: Step 1: CH₃Cl with AlCl₃ catalyst (anhydrous), warm. Step 2: hot alkaline KMnO₄, heat under reflux, then acidify with dilute H₂SO₄ (or HCl)
parts.working: B1 CH₃Cl. B1 AlCl₃ (anhydrous). B1 KMnO₄ hot, alkaline. B1 acidify afterwards.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of reaction in step 1.
parts.answer: electrophilic substitution (Friedel–Crafts alkylation)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Propene is converted into propanone in two steps. Give the structure of the intermediate and the reagents and conditions for each step.
parts.answer: Intermediate propan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₃. Step 1: steam with H₃PO₄ catalyst (high temperature and pressure). Step 2: K₂Cr₂O₇ / dilute H₂SO₄, heat
parts.working: B1 propan-2-ol (Markovnikov product). B1 step 1. B1 step 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why propan-2-ol, not propan-1-ol, is the main product of step 1.
parts.answer: The secondary carbocation intermediate is more stable than the primary one, because of the electron-donating effect of two alkyl groups
parts.working: B1 secondary carbocation more stable. B1 inductive effect of two alkyl groups.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline a three-step synthesis of 2-hydroxypropanoic acid, CH₃CH(OH)COOH, from ethanol. Give reagents, conditions and intermediates.
parts.answer: 1 ethanol → ethanal: K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄, warm and distil off the aldehyde as it forms. 2 ethanal → CH₃CH(OH)CN: HCN with KCN catalyst. 3 hydrolysis: dilute HCl, heat under reflux
parts.working: B1 oxidation reagent. B1 distil (to stop further oxidation). B1 HCN/KCN. B1 intermediate 2-hydroxypropanenitrile. B1 acid hydrolysis under reflux.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why ethanal must be distilled off as soon as it forms in step 1.
parts.answer: Otherwise it is oxidised further to ethanoic acid

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A three-step synthesis has yields of 80 %, 65 % and 90 % for the individual steps. What is the overall percentage yield?
A 46.8 %
B 53.0 %
C 65.0 %
D 78.3 %
parts.working: Overall yield = 0.80 × 0.65 × 0.90 × 100 = 46.8 %. D is the mean of the three yields, which is not how yields combine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student wants to make ethyl ethanoate using ethanol as the only organic starting material. Describe the two stages, giving reagents and conditions.
parts.answer: Stage 1: oxidise half the ethanol to ethanoic acid with excess K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄, heat under reflux. Stage 2: heat the ethanoic acid with the rest of the ethanol and a few drops of concentrated H₂SO₄ under reflux (then distil)
parts.working: B1 split the ethanol. B1 oxidation under reflux with excess oxidant. B1 esterification with ethanol. B1 conc H₂SO₄ catalyst, heat.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student starts with 9.20 g of ethanol, uses half for each stage, and the overall yield is 60.0 %. Calculate the mass of ethyl ethanoate (Mr 88.0) obtained. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: M1 n(ethanol) = 9.20 ÷ 46.0 = 0.200 mol; 0.100 mol of each reactant → 0.100 mol ester at 100 %. A1 0.100 × 88.0 × 0.600 = 5.28 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 1-phenylethanol, C₆H₅CH(OH)CH₃, can be made from benzene in two steps. Give the reagents and conditions for each step and the intermediate.
parts.answer: Step 1: CH₃COCl with anhydrous AlCl₃ → phenylethanone, C₆H₅COCH₃. Step 2: NaBH₄ (in water/methanol) or LiAlH₄ in dry ether
parts.working: B1 CH₃COCl. B1 AlCl₃. B1 intermediate C₆H₅COCH₃. B1 reducing agent.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of reaction in each step.
parts.answer: step 1 electrophilic substitution (Friedel–Crafts acylation); step 2 reduction (nucleophilic addition)

parts.label: a
parts.text: (Chloromethyl)benzene, C₆H₅CH₂Cl, is converted into 2-phenylethylamine, C₆H₅CH₂CH₂NH₂, in two steps. Give the reagents and conditions for each step and the intermediate.
parts.answer: Step 1: KCN in ethanol, heat under reflux → C₆H₅CH₂CN. Step 2: LiAlH₄ in dry ether (or H₂ / Ni)
parts.working: B1 step 1. B1 intermediate. B1 step 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why chlorobenzene, C₆H₅Cl, could not be used instead in step 1.
parts.answer: In chlorobenzene the C–Cl bond is strengthened because a lone pair on Cl overlaps with the ring π system; the C–Cl bond is not broken by nucleophiles under these conditions
parts.working: B1 lone pair of Cl delocalised into ring. B1 C–Cl bond stronger / partial double-bond character – no nucleophilic substitution.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
But-1-ene undergoes this sequence:
but-1-ene → (HBr) → A → (NaOH(aq), heat) → B → (K₂Cr₂O₇/H⁺, heat) → C → (HCN/KCN) → D
Give the structures of the major products A, B, C and D.
parts.answer: A CH₃CHBrCH₂CH₃; B CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃; C CH₃COCH₂CH₃; D CH₃C(OH)(CN)CH₂CH₃

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of reaction for each step: but-1-ene → A, A → B and C → D.
parts.answer: electrophilic addition; nucleophilic substitution; nucleophilic addition

parts.label: a
parts.text: N-phenylethanamide, C₆H₅NHCOCH₃, is made from benzene in three steps. Give the reagents and conditions for each step and the intermediates.
parts.answer: 1 conc HNO₃ + conc H₂SO₄, below 55 °C → nitrobenzene. 2 Sn + conc HCl, reflux, then NaOH(aq) → phenylamine. 3 ethanoyl chloride, room temperature → N-phenylethanamide
parts.working: B1 nitration reagents. B1 nitrobenzene. B1 reduction reagents. B1 phenylamine. B1 CH₃COCl.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 7.80 g of benzene gave 8.10 g of N-phenylethanamide (Mr 135.0). Calculate the overall percentage yield. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 4-aminobenzoic acid, H₂N–C₆H₄–COOH (1,4), is made from methylbenzene in three steps: nitration, oxidation and reduction. Give the reagents and conditions for each step.
parts.answer: Nitration: conc HNO₃ + conc H₂SO₄ (about 30 °C), separate the 4-isomer. Oxidation: hot alkaline KMnO₄ under reflux, then acidify. Reduction: Sn + conc HCl, reflux, then neutralise
parts.working: B1 nitration. B1 separating 4-nitromethylbenzene from the 2-isomer. B1 oxidation. B1 reduction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the oxidation must be carried out before the reduction.
parts.answer: If the NO₂ were reduced first, the NH₂ group would be oxidised / destroyed by KMnO₄
parts.working: B1 order. B1 amino group is oxidised by KMnO₄.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why nitration gives a mixture of products.
parts.answer: The CH₃ group directs substitution to the 2- and 4-positions

parts.label: a
parts.text: Propanoic acid is to be made from ethene in three steps (no other organic reagent may be used). Give the reagents, conditions and intermediates for each step.
parts.answer: 1 HBr(g), room temperature → bromoethane. 2 KCN in ethanol, heat under reflux → propanenitrile. 3 dilute HCl, heat under reflux → propanoic acid
parts.working: B1 HBr. B1 bromoethane. B1 KCN/ethanol/reflux. B1 propanenitrile. B1 acid hydrolysis under reflux.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the overall yield of a multi-step synthesis is often low.
parts.answer: Losses at each step (incomplete reactions, side reactions, losses in purification) multiply together

parts.label: a
parts.text: 2-hydroxy-2-phenylethanoic acid, C₆H₅CH(OH)COOH, is made from benzaldehyde, C₆H₅CHO, in two steps. Give the reagents and conditions.
parts.answer: Step 1: HCN with KCN catalyst → C₆H₅CH(OH)CN. Step 2: dilute HCl, heat under reflux
parts.working: B1 step 1. B1 intermediate. B1 step 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 10.6 g of benzaldehyde (Mr 106.0) gave 9.12 g of the acid (Mr 152.0). Calculate the percentage yield. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The acid is then heated with methanol and concentrated sulfuric acid. Give the structure of the product and state whether the product mixture would rotate plane-polarised light.
parts.answer: C₆H₅CH(OH)COOCH₃; no – the acid was made as a racemic mixture, and the chiral centre is unchanged by esterification
parts.working: B1 structure. B1 no rotation – racemic.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which reagent gives a positive result with propanal but not with propanone?
A Tollens' reagent
B 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine
C sodium carbonate solution
D sodium metal
parts.answer: A Tollens' reagent
parts.working: Aldehydes are oxidised by Tollens' reagent (silver mirror); ketones are not. B is the main distractor: 2,4-DNPH gives an orange precipitate with both aldehydes and ketones. Neither compound reacts with sodium carbonate or with sodium (no acidic or OH group).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a simple chemical test to distinguish ethanol from ethanoic acid. Give the result for each.
parts.answer: Add sodium carbonate solution (or solid): effervescence (CO₂) with ethanoic acid; no change with ethanol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe a chemical test to distinguish propan-2-ol from 2-methylpropan-2-ol. Give the result for each.
parts.answer: Warm with acidified potassium dichromate(VI): propan-2-ol turns it from orange to green; 2-methylpropan-2-ol (tertiary) – stays orange
parts.working: B1 reagent and warm. B1 orange → green for secondary. B1 no change for tertiary.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a test to distinguish hexane from hex-1-ene. Give the result for each.
parts.answer: Shake with bromine water: hex-1-ene decolourises it (orange → colourless); hexane – no change (stays orange)

parts.label: b
parts.text: 1-chlorobutane and 1-iodobutane are each warmed with aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol. Describe and explain the differences seen.
parts.answer: 1-iodobutane gives a yellow precipitate (AgI) quickly; 1-chlorobutane gives a white precipitate (AgCl) slowly; the C–I bond is weaker than C–Cl, so it is hydrolysed faster
parts.working: B1 colours. B1 iodo faster. B1 C–I bond weaker / lower bond energy.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which compound gives an orange precipitate with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine AND a yellow precipitate when warmed with alkaline aqueous iodine?
A butanal
B butanone
C ethanol
D pentan-3-one
parts.answer: B butanone
parts.working: Butanone is a carbonyl compound with a CH₃CO– group, so both tests are positive. C (ethanol) gives tri-iodomethane but does not react with 2,4-DNPH; D has no CH₃CO– group.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Four unlabelled bottles contain propan-1-ol, propanal, propanone and propanoic acid. Describe a sequence of test-tube tests that would identify each liquid, giving the observations expected.
parts.answer: 1 Na₂CO₃(aq): only propanoic acid fizzes (CO₂ turns limewater milky). 2 2,4-DNPH on the other three: orange precipitate with propanal and propanone, none with propan-1-ol. 3 Tollens' reagent (warm) on the two carbonyls: silver mirror with propanal, no change with propanone. (Alternatively Fehling's: red-brown precipitate with propanal.)
parts.working: B1 test for acid. B1 result. B1 2,4-DNPH. B1 result separating the alcohol. B1 Tollens'/Fehling's. B1 result. Accept acidified dichromate for alcohol and aldehyde if the logic is complete.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a test to distinguish phenol from ethanol. Give the result for each.
parts.answer: Add bromine water: phenol decolourises it and gives a white precipitate (2,4,6-tribromophenol); ethanol – no change
parts.working: B1 reagent. B1 results (white precipitate and decolourisation with phenol; no change with ethanol).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how you could distinguish ethanoyl chloride from chloroethane using aqueous silver nitrate. Explain the difference.
parts.answer: Ethanoyl chloride gives an immediate white precipitate (AgCl) at room temperature (with steamy fumes as it hydrolyses); chloroethane gives a white precipitate only slowly on warming; the carbonyl carbon in the acyl chloride is very electron-deficient (bonded to O and Cl) so it is attacked rapidly by water
parts.working: B1 immediate ppt for acyl chloride. B1 slow / needs warming for chloroalkane. B1 reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compound X, C₄H₈O, gives an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH, does not react with Tollens' reagent, and gives a yellow precipitate with alkaline aqueous iodine. Identify X and explain each result.
parts.answer: X is butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃. Orange ppt: carbonyl group. No Tollens' reaction: ketone, not aldehyde. Yellow ppt (CHI₃): CH₃CO– group present
parts.working: B1 butanone. B1 B1 B1 for each result explained.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the structures of two isomers of X that would give a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent, and state what the yellow precipitate in (a) is.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO (butanal) and (CH₃)₂CHCHO (2-methylpropanal); tri-iodomethane, CHI₃

parts.label: a
parts.text: Four colourless liquids are ethanoyl chloride, ethanamide solution, ethyl ethanoate and ethanoic acid. Suggest simple tests that would identify each one. Give the observation for each test.
parts.answer: Add a few drops to water: ethanoyl chloride reacts violently, giving steamy fumes of HCl. Add Na₂CO₃(aq) to the rest: ethanoic acid effervesces. Warm the other two with NaOH(aq): ethanamide gives ammonia, which turns damp red litmus blue; ethyl ethanoate gives no ammonia (sweet smell disappears as it hydrolyses)
parts.working: B1 B1 acyl chloride test + observation. B1 B1 acid test + observation. B1 B1 amide test + observation; ester identified by elimination.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol are three isomers of C₄H₁₀O. Describe how acidified potassium dichromate(VI), followed by a further test on the products, can distinguish all three.
parts.answer: Warm each with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ and distil: 2-methylpropan-2-ol – stays orange (tertiary). Butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol turn it green. Test the distillates with Tollens' reagent: butanal (from butan-1-ol) gives a silver mirror; butanone (from butan-2-ol) does not
parts.working: B1 tertiary not oxidised. B1 the other two turn green. B1 distil and test distillate with Tollens'/Fehling's. B1 correct results.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give a single test, using a different reagent, that gives a positive result with butan-2-ol only. State the observation.
parts.answer: warm with alkaline aqueous iodine; yellow precipitate (tri-iodomethane) – butan-2-ol has a CH₃CH(OH)– group

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compound Y contains 54.5 % carbon, 9.1 % hydrogen and 36.4 % oxygen by mass. Calculate its empirical formula.
parts.answer: C₂H₄O

parts.label: b
parts.text: The mass spectrum of Y has its molecular ion peak at m/e 88. Deduce the molecular formula.
parts.answer: C₄H₈O₂

parts.label: c
parts.text: Y effervesces with aqueous sodium carbonate. Its IR spectrum has a very broad absorption at 2500–3000 cm⁻¹ and a strong one at about 1710 cm⁻¹. Give the structures of the two possible compounds Y could be.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH (butanoic acid) or (CH₃)₂CHCOOH (2-methylpropanoic acid)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Alkene P, C₅H₁₀, is heated with hot, concentrated acidified KMnO₄. The products are propanone and ethanoic acid. Deduce the structure and name of P.
parts.answer: (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃; 2-methylbut-2-ene

parts.label: b
parts.text: P reacts with steam in the presence of H₃PO₄. The major product Q is not oxidised by acidified dichromate(VI). Give the structure of Q and explain why it is not oxidised.
parts.answer: (CH₃)₂C(OH)CH₂CH₃ (2-methylbutan-2-ol); tertiary alcohol – no H on the carbon bearing the OH

parts.label: c
parts.text: Does P show cis/trans isomerism? Explain.
parts.answer: No – one carbon of the C=C carries two identical CH₃ groups

parts.label: a
parts.text: Q, C₉H₁₀O₂, is a neutral, sweet-smelling liquid containing a benzene ring. When Q is heated under reflux with aqueous NaOH, it gives ethanol and R, C₇H₅O₂Na. Acidifying R gives a white solid S, C₇H₆O₂. Identify Q, R and S.
parts.answer: Q ethyl benzoate, C₆H₅COOCH₂CH₃; R sodium benzoate, C₆H₅COONa; S benzoic acid, C₆H₅COOH

parts.label: b
parts.text: Isomer T of Q is also an ester. Alkaline hydrolysis of T followed by acidification gives methanol and 4-methylbenzoic acid. Give the structure of T.
parts.answer: CH₃–C₆H₄–COOCH₃ (methyl 4-methylbenzoate)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Isomer U of Q is hydrolysed by NaOH(aq) to give sodium ethanoate and a compound that, on acidification, gives a white precipitate with bromine water. Suggest a structure for U and explain the bromine water result.
parts.answer: CH₃COO–C₆H₄–CH₃ (e.g. 4-methylphenyl ethanoate); hydrolysis forms a phenol (4-methylphenol), and phenols react with bromine water to give a white precipitate
parts.working: B1 ester of ethanoic acid with a methylphenol. B1 phenol + bromine water → white ppt.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 0.290 g of compound Z, which contains C, H and O only, is burned completely in oxygen, forming 0.660 g of CO₂ and 0.270 g of H₂O. Calculate the empirical formula of Z.
parts.answer: C₃H₆O

parts.label: b
parts.text: The Mr of Z is 58. Z gives an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH, does not react with Fehling's solution, and gives a yellow precipitate with alkaline aqueous iodine. Identify Z.
parts.answer: propanone, CH₃COCH₃
parts.working: B1 propanone. B1 reasoning: carbonyl, not aldehyde, CH₃CO– group.

parts.label: c
parts.text: An isomer of Z gives a red-brown precipitate with Fehling's solution. Give its structure.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂CHO (propanal)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compound V has the structure CH₃COCH₂CH(OH)CH₂CHO. Name the three functional groups present.
parts.answer: ketone (C=O within chain); secondary alcohol (hydroxyl); aldehyde (CHO)
parts.working: B1 each; 'carbonyl' alone scores for only one of ketone/aldehyde.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the structure of the organic product when V is heated under reflux with excess acidified potassium dichromate(VI).
parts.answer: CH₃COCH₂COCH₂COOH
parts.working: B1 secondary alcohol → ketone. B1 aldehyde → carboxylic acid (ketone unchanged).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the structure of the product when V reacts with excess NaBH₄.
parts.answer: CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH(OH)CH₂CH₂OH

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compound W, a drug intermediate, has the structure HO–C₆H₄–CH₂–CH(NH₂)–COOCH₃ (the OH is attached directly to the benzene ring). Name the three functional groups in W, other than the benzene ring.
parts.answer: phenol; primary amine; ester

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the structure of the organic product formed when W is heated with excess aqueous sodium hydroxide.
parts.answer: ⁻O–C₆H₄–CH₂–CH(NH₂)–COO⁻ (with Na⁺ ions) and methanol
parts.working: B1 ester hydrolysed to carboxylate (+ CH₃OH). B1 phenol deprotonated to phenoxide.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the structure of the organic product formed when W reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid at room temperature.
parts.answer: HO–C₆H₄–CH₂–CH(NH₃⁺)–COOCH₃ Cl⁻

stem: A student in a Lahore college lab mixes 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid with 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide in a polystyrene cup. Both solutions start at 24.3 °C. The highest temperature reached is 31.0 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy released, in J, in this experiment. Assume the density of the mixture is 1.00 g/cm³ and its specific heat capacity is 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the enthalpy change of neutralisation, in kJ/mol. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: −56.0 kJ/mol
parts.working: M1 n(H₂O) = 0.0500 × 1.00 = 0.0500 mol; A1 ΔH = −2.8006 ÷ 0.0500 = −56.0 kJ/mol (negative sign needed)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the experiment is carried out in an expanded polystyrene cup with a lid.
parts.answer: Polystyrene is a good insulator and the lid reduces heat loss to the surroundings.
parts.working: B1 reduces heat loss / good insulator

author: HomiLabs

stem: A spirit burner containing ethanol is used to heat 200 g of water in a copper can. The temperature of the water rises from 21.0 °C to 45.5 °C. The burner loses 1.12 g in mass. The specific heat capacity of water is 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy transferred to the water, in kJ.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the enthalpy change of combustion of ethanol, in kJ/mol, from these results. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (Mr of ethanol = 46.0)
parts.answer: −841 kJ/mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: The data-book value is −1367 kJ/mol. Give two reasons why the experimental value is less exothermic.
parts.answer: Heat lost to the surroundings (air, can); incomplete combustion of ethanol.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: heat loss to surroundings / heating the can and air; incomplete combustion (soot seen); evaporation of ethanol from the wick; conditions not standard (water formed as vapour)

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
25.0 cm³ of 2.00 mol/dm³ KOH(aq) is mixed with 25.0 cm³ of 2.00 mol/dm³ HNO₃(aq). The enthalpy change of neutralisation is −57.0 kJ/mol. Assume the mixture has a density of 1.00 g/cm³ and a specific heat capacity of 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹. What is the temperature rise?
A 6.8 °C
B 13.6 °C
C 27.3 °C
D 57.0 °C
parts.working: n(H₂O) = 0.0500 mol, q = 0.0500 × 57 000 = 2850 J; ΔT = 2850 ÷ (50.0 × 4.18) = 13.6 °C. A (6.8) uses 100 g as the mass; C uses 25 g of solution only.

stem: 40.0 cm³ of 1.50 mol/dm³ ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, is mixed with 60.0 cm³ of 1.20 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide. The temperature rises by 7.9 °C. Assume the solution has a density of 1.00 g/cm³ and a specific heat capacity of 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show by calculation which reagent is in excess.
parts.answer: NaOH is in excess (0.0720 mol NaOH v 0.0600 mol CH₃COOH).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the enthalpy change of neutralisation of ethanoic acid, in kJ/mol, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: −55.0 kJ/mol
parts.working: M1 q = 100 × 4.18 × 7.9 = 3302.2 J; M1 moles water = 0.0600 (limiting acid); A1 ΔH = −55.0 kJ/mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: The value for hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide is about −57 kJ/mol. Explain why the value for ethanoic acid is less exothermic.
parts.answer: Ethanoic acid is a weak acid, only partly ionised; some energy is absorbed to ionise (break O–H bonds in) the acid as it reacts.
parts.working: B1 weak acid / partially dissociated; B1 energy needed to complete dissociation (endothermic), reducing the overall energy released

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student places 50.0 cm³ of 0.500 mol/dm³ copper(II) sulfate solution in an insulated cup and records the temperature every minute. At 3.5 minutes an excess of zinc powder is added and the mixture is stirred.
Time / min: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8
Temperature / °C: 22.0, 22.0, 22.0, 22.0, 40.5, 44.0, 43.4, 42.8, 42.2
Assume the solution has density 1.00 g/cm³ and specific heat capacity 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The cooling after 5 minutes is linear. By extrapolating this cooling line back to 3.5 minutes, find the maximum temperature the mixture would have reached with no heat loss. Hence find ΔT.
parts.working: M1 cooling rate 0.6 °C per minute; temperature at 3.5 min = 44.0 + 0.6 × 1.5 = 44.9 °C; A1 ΔT = 44.9 − 22.0 = 22.9 °C

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the enthalpy change, in kJ/mol, for Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s). Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: −191 kJ/mol
parts.working: M1 q = 50.0 × 4.18 × 22.9 = 4786 J; M1 n(CuSO₄) = 0.0250 mol (limiting); A1 ΔH = −191 kJ/mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the zinc is used as a powder and in excess.
parts.answer: Powder reacts fast, so the reaction finishes before much heat is lost; excess ensures all the CuSO₄ reacts, so moles reacting are known.
parts.working: B1 powder: large surface area, fast reaction, less heat loss during reaction; B1 excess: all copper(II) ions react / CuSO₄ is limiting

author: HomiLabs

stem: On a trip to Murree, a camping stove burns propane, C₃H₈. The standard enthalpy change of combustion of propane is −2220 kJ/mol. The stove heats 1.50 kg of water from 8 °C to 100 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy needed to heat the water, in kJ.
parts.answer: 577 kJ

parts.label: b
parts.text: Only 45% of the energy released by burning propane reaches the water. Calculate the mass of propane, in g, burned. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (Mr of propane = 44.0)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why less than half of the energy reaches the water.
parts.answer: Heat escapes to the surrounding cold air / heats the pan / wind carries hot gases away.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
0.0100 mol of a liquid fuel is burned completely. The energy released raises the temperature of 100 g of water by 30.0 K. The specific heat capacity of water is 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ and there is no heat loss. What is the enthalpy change of combustion of the fuel?
A −12.5 kJ/mol
B −125 kJ/mol
C −1250 kJ/mol
D +1250 kJ/mol
parts.answer: C −1250 kJ/mol
parts.working: q = 100 × 4.18 × 30.0 = 12 540 J = 12.54 kJ; ΔH = −12.54 ÷ 0.0100 = −1254 kJ/mol ≈ −1250 kJ/mol. D has the wrong sign: combustion is exothermic. A forgets to divide by the moles.

stem: Standard enthalpy changes of combustion: carbon (graphite) −394 kJ/mol; carbon monoxide −283 kJ/mol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation, with state symbols, for the standard enthalpy change of formation of carbon monoxide.
parts.answer: C(s) + ½O₂(g) → CO(g)
parts.working: B1 correct equation with state symbols, 1 mol CO

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this enthalpy change cannot easily be measured directly.
parts.answer: Burning carbon in limited oxygen also forms some CO₂ (and leaves unburnt carbon), so pure CO is not formed.
parts.working: B1 CO₂ also forms / cannot stop at CO

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the data to calculate the standard enthalpy change of formation of CO, in kJ/mol.
parts.answer: −111 kJ/mol
parts.working: M1 cycle: ΔHf(CO) = ΔHc(C) − ΔHc(CO); A1 = −394 − (−283) = −111 kJ/mol

author: HomiLabs

stem: Standard enthalpy changes of combustion: C(graphite) −394 kJ/mol; H₂(g) −286 kJ/mol; C₂H₅OH(l) −1367 kJ/mol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Draw (describe) a Hess cycle linking the formation of ethanol from its elements with the combustion products.
parts.answer: Elements 2C(s) + 3H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → C₂H₅OH(l) (ΔHf); both elements and ethanol go down to 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l) with excess O₂.
parts.working: B1 top line correct formation equation; B1 arrows to 2CO₂ + 3H₂O labelled with ΔHc values (2 × C, 3 × H₂, 1 × ethanol)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the standard enthalpy change of formation of ethanol, in kJ/mol.
parts.answer: −279 kJ/mol

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Two experiments are done. In each, the solid is added to 50.0 g of water in an insulated cup (specific heat capacity 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹).
Experiment 1: 3.99 g of anhydrous CuSO₄ — temperature rises by 7.6 K.
Experiment 2: 6.24 g of CuSO₄·5H₂O — temperature falls by 1.1 K.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for dissolving each solid, in kJ/mol. (Mr: CuSO₄ = 159.6, CuSO₄·5H₂O = 249.6)
parts.answer: Anhydrous: −63.5 kJ/mol; hydrated: +9.20 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use a Hess cycle to calculate ΔH for CuSO₄(s) + 5H₂O(l) → CuSO₄·5H₂O(s), in kJ/mol, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: −72.7 kJ/mol
parts.working: M1 ΔH = ΔH(anhydrous) − ΔH(hydrated); A1 = −63.5 − (+9.2) = −72.7 kJ/mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this enthalpy change cannot be found by direct measurement.
parts.answer: Water cannot be added in exactly the right amount; the solid would dissolve/partly hydrate, so the reaction cannot be made to go to completion cleanly.
parts.working: B1 cannot control hydration / excess water dissolves solid / slow, incomplete reaction

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Iron is extracted in a blast furnace by the reaction Fe₂O₃(s) + 3CO(g) → 2Fe(s) + 3CO₂(g).
Standard enthalpy changes of formation / kJ/mol: Fe₂O₃(s) −824; CO(g) −111; CO₂(g) −394.
What is the standard enthalpy change of this reaction?
A −25 kJ/mol
B +25 kJ/mol
C +541 kJ/mol
D −2339 kJ/mol
parts.answer: A −25 kJ/mol
parts.working: ΔH = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants) = 3(−394) − [(−824) + 3(−111)] = −1182 + 1157 = −25 kJ/mol. B reverses the subtraction; C uses only one CO and one CO₂ (−394 + 824 + 111); D adds the reactant values instead of subtracting them.

stem:
A cement works near Dera Ghazi Khan needs the enthalpy change for making quicklime. Two reactions with hydrochloric acid are measured:
CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)   ΔH₁ = −15 kJ/mol
CaO(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l)   ΔH₂ = −193 kJ/mol

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔH for the thermal decomposition CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g), in kJ/mol.
parts.answer: +178 kJ/mol
parts.working: M1 ΔH = ΔH₁ − ΔH₂; A1 = −15 − (−193) = +178 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why ΔH for this decomposition is found indirectly rather than by heating calcium carbonate in a calorimeter.
parts.answer: The reaction needs a high temperature (about 800 °C or more), so it is impossible to measure the heat absorbed with a simple calorimeter; and it is hard to make decomposition complete.
parts.working: B1 high temperature needed / continuous heating; B1 cannot measure energy taken in / decomposition incomplete

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Standard enthalpy changes of combustion / kJ/mol: C(graphite) −394; H₂(g) −286; C₃H₈(g) −2219.
Standard enthalpy changes of formation / kJ/mol: C₂H₄(g) +52; CH₄(g) −75.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard enthalpy change of formation of propane, in kJ/mol.
parts.answer: −107 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Propane is cracked: C₃H₈(g) → C₂H₄(g) + CH₄(g). Using your answer to (a), calculate ΔH for this reaction, in kJ/mol.
parts.answer: +84 kJ/mol
parts.working: M1 ΔH = ΔHf(C₂H₄) + ΔHf(CH₄) − ΔHf(C₃H₈); A1 = 52 − 75 − (−107) = +84 kJ/mol (ecf from a)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why cracking needs a high temperature, using your answer to (b).
parts.answer: It is endothermic (and has a high activation energy, C–C bonds are strong), so heat must be supplied.
parts.working: B1 endothermic / energy needed to break bonds

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
S(s) + O₂(g) → SO₂(g)   ΔH = −297 kJ/mol
SO₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → SO₃(g)   ΔH = −98 kJ/mol
What is ΔH for S(s) + 1½O₂(g) → SO₃(g)?
A −199 kJ/mol
B −395 kJ/mol
C +199 kJ/mol
D −493 kJ/mol
parts.answer: B −395 kJ/mol
parts.working: By Hess's law the two steps add: −297 + (−98) = −395 kJ/mol. A subtracts the steps; D doubles the second step.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define standard enthalpy change of formation.
parts.answer: The enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states under standard conditions (298 K, 101 kPa).
parts.working: B1 one mole of compound formed from its elements; B1 in standard states under standard conditions

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an equation, with state symbols, for the standard enthalpy change of formation of ethanol, C₂H₅OH(l).
parts.answer: 2C(s) + 3H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → C₂H₅OH(l)
parts.working: B1 correct formula and balancing for 1 mol; B1 state symbols

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which equation represents both the standard enthalpy change of formation of a compound and the standard enthalpy change of combustion of an element?
A CO(g) + ½O₂(g) → CO₂(g)
B C(graphite) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g)
C H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(g)
D 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l)
parts.answer: B C(graphite) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g)
parts.working: Graphite is carbon in its standard state; one mole burns completely to form one mole of CO₂, which is also formation of CO₂ from its elements. C forms water as a gas, not its standard state (liquid). D forms two moles. A starts from a compound.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define standard enthalpy change of neutralisation.
parts.answer: The enthalpy change when an acid and an alkali react to form one mole of water under standard conditions.
parts.working: B1 one mole of water formed; B1 acid + alkali (base) under standard conditions

parts.label: b
parts.text: For H₂SO₄(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na₂SO₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l), ΔH = −114 kJ per mole of sulfuric acid. State the standard enthalpy change of neutralisation and explain your answer.
parts.answer: −57 kJ/mol, because two moles of water form per mole of H₂SO₄.
parts.working: B1 −57 kJ/mol; B1 2 mol water formed so divide by 2

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each equation, state whether its ΔH is a standard enthalpy change of formation, a standard enthalpy change of combustion, both, or neither. Give a reason in each case.
(i) 2Na(s) + Cl₂(g) → 2NaCl(s)
(ii) CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g)
(iii) C(graphite) + 2H₂(g) → CH₄(g)
(iv) CO(g) + ½O₂(g) → CO₂(g)
parts.answer: (i) neither: two moles of NaCl formed. (ii) neither: water should be liquid under standard conditions. (iii) formation only: one mole of CH₄ from elements in standard states. (iv) combustion of CO only: CO₂ is formed from a compound, not from elements.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct decision with reason

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the standard enthalpy change of formation of oxygen gas, O₂(g), is zero but that of ozone, O₃(g), is not.
parts.answer: O₂(g) is oxygen's standard state, so no change occurs in forming it; O₃ is a different form made from O₂ with an energy change.
parts.working: B1 O₂ is the element in its standard state; O₃ is not the standard state

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the standard conditions of temperature and pressure used for standard enthalpy changes.
parts.answer: 298 K (25 °C) and 101 kPa (1 atm).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define standard enthalpy change of combustion.
parts.answer: The enthalpy change when one mole of a substance is burned completely in oxygen under standard conditions.
parts.working: B1 one mole of substance; B1 complete combustion in excess oxygen, standard conditions

stem: The standard enthalpy change of combustion of propan-1-ol is −2021 kJ/mol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation, with state symbols, that represents the standard enthalpy change of combustion of propan-1-ol, C₃H₇OH(l).
parts.answer: C₃H₇OH(l) + 4½O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(l)
parts.working: B1 correctly balanced for 1 mol propan-1-ol; B1 state symbols with H₂O(l)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy released, in kJ, when 15.0 g of propan-1-ol burns completely. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (Mr of propan-1-ol = 60.0)
parts.answer: 505 kJ

author: HomiLabs

stem: Bond energies / kJ/mol: C=C 610; C–C 350; C–H 410; H–H 436. This reaction is used to harden vegetable oils in ghee factories.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the enthalpy change for C₂H₄(g) + H₂(g) → C₂H₆(g), in kJ/mol.
parts.answer: −124 kJ/mol
parts.working: M1 bonds broken: C=C + H–H = 610 + 436 = 1046 (4 C–H unchanged); M1 bonds made: C–C + 2 C–H = 350 + 820 = 1170; A1 ΔH = 1046 − 1170 = −124 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why a value found from bond energies may differ from the accurate value.
parts.answer: Bond energies are average values from many compounds.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Bond energies / kJ/mol: C–H 410; O=O 496; C=O (in CO₂) 805; O–H 460. Methane is the main gas in Pakistan's Sui gas supply.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the enthalpy change for CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g), in kJ/mol.
parts.answer: −818 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: The standard enthalpy change of combustion of methane is −890 kJ/mol. Give two reasons why your answer differs from this.
parts.answer: Bond energies are averages; the standard value forms liquid water, releasing extra energy when water vapour condenses.
parts.working: B1 average bond energies; B1 water as liquid in standard ΔHc (condensation exothermic)

author: HomiLabs

stem:
N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g)   ΔH = −92 kJ/mol
Bond energies / kJ/mol: N≡N 944; H–H 436.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the bond energy of the N–H bond, in kJ/mol, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 391 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the bond energy of N≡N to explain why the Haber process needs an iron catalyst.
parts.answer: N≡N is very strong (944 kJ/mol), giving a high activation energy; the catalyst gives an alternative route with lower Ea so the rate is acceptable.
parts.working: B1 strong triple bond / high Ea; B1 catalyst lowers Ea via alternative pathway

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Bond energies / kJ/mol: C–H 410; Cl–Cl 242; C–Cl 340; H–Cl 431.
What is the enthalpy change for CH₄(g) + Cl₂(g) → CH₃Cl(g) + HCl(g)?
A +119 kJ/mol
B −119 kJ/mol
C +312 kJ/mol
D −771 kJ/mol
parts.answer: B −119 kJ/mol
parts.working: Only one C–H and one Cl–Cl bond break: 410 + 242 = 652; one C–Cl and one H–Cl bond form: 340 + 431 = 771; ΔH = 652 − 771 = −119 kJ/mol. A has the sign reversed; C leaves out the H–Cl bond formed; D counts only the bonds made.

stem: For a reaction, the activation energy is +75 kJ/mol and ΔH = −40 kJ/mol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the reaction pathway diagram for this reaction. Say where the reactants and products are and how Ea and ΔH are shown.
parts.answer: Products lower than reactants; curve rises to a maximum (transition state) then falls; Ea is from reactants up to the peak; ΔH is the drop from reactants to products (downward arrow).
parts.working: B1 products below reactants (exothermic); B1 Ea arrow from reactant level to top of curve; B1 ΔH arrow from reactants down to products

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the activation energy of the reverse reaction, in kJ/mol.
parts.answer: 115 kJ/mol

author: HomiLabs

stem: An endothermic reaction has ΔH = +30 kJ/mol. Without a catalyst the forward activation energy is 120 kJ/mol; with a catalyst it is 70 kJ/mol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the activation energy of the reverse reaction with and without the catalyst, in kJ/mol.
parts.answer: Without catalyst: 90 kJ/mol; with catalyst: 40 kJ/mol.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the value of ΔH with the catalyst and explain.
parts.answer: +30 kJ/mol; the catalyst does not change the energies of reactants or products.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction, using the idea of a Boltzmann distribution.
parts.answer: It provides an alternative pathway with lower Ea, so a larger fraction of molecules have energy ≥ Ea; more successful collisions per second.
parts.working: B1 alternative route, lower Ea; B1 more particles with E ≥ Ea (greater area under the curve beyond Ea) so more effective collisions

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A two-step reaction is described by these energies, measured relative to the reactants (0 kJ/mol):
first transition state +85; intermediate +20; second transition state +60; products −45 (all in kJ/mol).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the overall enthalpy change of the reaction, and whether it is exothermic or endothermic.
parts.answer: −45 kJ/mol; exothermic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the rate-determining step and give a reason.
parts.answer: Step 1 (reactants → intermediate), because its activation energy (85 kJ/mol) is larger than that of step 2 (60 − 20 = 40 kJ/mol).
parts.working: B1 step 1; B1 compares Ea of each step: 85 v 40

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the activation energy for the overall reverse reaction (products → reactants), in kJ/mol.
parts.answer: 130 kJ/mol
parts.working: B1 from −45 up to highest transition state +85: 85 − (−45) = 130

parts.label: d
parts.text: State how the diagram shows that the intermediate could, in principle, be detected.
