parts.answer: It sits in an energy minimum (a dip) between the two peaks, so it has a finite lifetime.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A sports first-aid cold pack used at a cricket ground contains solid ammonium nitrate and a pouch of water. When the pouch is broken, the pack becomes cold.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether dissolving ammonium nitrate in water is exothermic or endothermic, and give the sign of ΔH.
parts.answer: Endothermic; ΔH is positive.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, in terms of bonds broken and formed, why some reactions are exothermic.
parts.answer: Breaking bonds absorbs energy and making bonds releases energy; if more energy is released forming new bonds than is absorbed breaking bonds, the reaction is exothermic.
parts.working: B1 bond breaking endothermic, bond making exothermic; B1 energy released > energy absorbed

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one everyday exothermic reaction.
parts.answer: Burning natural gas in a stove (or respiration, neutralisation, hand warmers).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Photosynthesis and respiration are reverse processes. Explain which is endothermic and which is exothermic.
parts.answer: Photosynthesis is endothermic: it absorbs light energy to make glucose; respiration is exothermic: it releases energy from glucose.
parts.working: B1 photosynthesis endothermic with reason; B1 respiration exothermic

parts.label: b
parts.text: Methane burning is very exothermic, yet a gas stove needs a spark to light. Explain why.
parts.answer: The reaction has an activation energy; the spark supplies energy so some molecules can overcome Ea; once started the energy released keeps the reaction going.
parts.working: B1 activation energy needed / bonds must break first; B1 heat released sustains reaction

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what happens to the temperature of the surroundings during an endothermic reaction.
parts.answer: It falls.

stem:
To find ΔHf of magnesium oxide, two reactions with excess dilute hydrochloric acid (100 cm³ each time) are carried out in an insulated cup. Assume the solution has density 1.00 g/cm³ and specific heat capacity 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Experiment 1: 0.240 g Mg ribbon, temperature rise 10.9 °C.
Experiment 2: 0.400 g MgO powder, temperature rise 3.5 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔH₁ for Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g) and ΔH₂ for MgO(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l), in kJ/mol, to 3 significant figures. (Ar: Mg = 24.3; Mr: MgO = 40.3)
parts.answer: ΔH₁ = −461 kJ/mol; ΔH₂ = −147 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use a Hess cycle and ΔHf(H₂O(l)) = −286 kJ/mol to calculate the standard enthalpy change of formation of MgO, in kJ/mol.
parts.answer: −600 kJ/mol
parts.working: M1 ΔHf(MgO) = ΔH₁ − ΔH₂ + ΔHf(H₂O); A1 = −461 − (−147) − 286 = −600 kJ/mol (ecf)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Each thermometer reading has an uncertainty of ±0.05 °C. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in ΔT for experiment 2.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one change that would reduce the percentage uncertainty in experiment 2 and explain why.
parts.answer: Use a larger mass of MgO (or less acid solution) so that ΔT is larger.
parts.working: B1 bigger ΔT gives smaller percentage uncertainty

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Halide ions: tests & reactions with H2SO4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is seen when aqueous silver nitrate is added to separate acidified solutions of potassium chloride, potassium bromide and potassium iodide.
parts.answer: Chloride: white precipitate; bromide: cream precipitate; iodide: yellow precipitate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how aqueous ammonia can be used to confirm the identity of each precipitate.
parts.answer: AgCl dissolves in dilute NH₃; AgBr dissolves only in concentrated NH₃; AgI is insoluble even in concentrated NH₃.
parts.working: B1 AgCl soluble in dilute; B1 AgBr soluble in conc only and AgI insoluble in both

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write an ionic equation, with state symbols, for the formation of the precipitate with bromide ions.
parts.answer: Ag⁺(aq) + Br⁻(aq) → AgBr(s)

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Halide ions: tests & reactions with H2SO4

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An acidified solution of a sodium halide gives a cream precipitate with aqueous silver nitrate. The precipitate does not dissolve in dilute aqueous ammonia but dissolves in concentrated aqueous ammonia. Which ion is present?
A F⁻
B Cl⁻
C Br⁻
D I⁻
parts.answer: C Br⁻
parts.working: Cream AgBr dissolves in concentrated but not dilute NH₃. Cl⁻ gives white AgCl, soluble in dilute NH₃; I⁻ gives yellow AgI, insoluble in both; AgF is soluble so F⁻ gives no precipitate.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Halide ions: tests & reactions with H2SO4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is seen when concentrated sulfuric acid is added to solid sodium chloride.
parts.answer: Steamy (misty) white fumes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: NaCl(s) + H₂SO₄(l) → NaHSO₄(s) + HCl(g)
parts.working: B1 (accept formation of Na₂SO₄ with 2NaCl if balanced)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why no further reaction takes place between the hydrogen chloride and the sulfuric acid.
parts.answer: Cl⁻/HCl is a weak reducing agent; it is not strong enough to reduce sulfuric acid (S in +6 state), so Cl₂ is not formed.
parts.working: B1 chloride/HCl weak reducing agent; B1 cannot reduce H₂SO₄ / S stays +6

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the type of reaction occurring in (b).
parts.answer: Acid–base reaction (proton transfer).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Halide ions: tests & reactions with H2SO4
stem: Concentrated sulfuric acid is added to solid potassium bromide. First, steamy fumes of hydrogen bromide form. Some of the hydrogen bromide then reacts further with the sulfuric acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the two gases (other than water vapour) formed in the redox step, and describe one observation.
parts.answer: Bromine and sulfur dioxide; orange/brown fumes (of bromine) seen.
parts.working: B1 Br₂ and SO₂; B1 orange-brown/red-brown fumes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction in which hydrogen bromide reduces sulfuric acid.
parts.answer: 2HBr + H₂SO₄ → Br₂ + SO₂ + 2H₂O

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the change in oxidation number of sulfur in (b).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Halide ions: tests & reactions with H2SO4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Concentrated sulfuric acid is added to solid sodium iodide. Name three sulfur-containing products that can form, giving the oxidation number of sulfur in each.
parts.working: 1 mark each, name with oxidation number

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction that forms hydrogen sulfide.
parts.answer: 8HI + H₂SO₄ → 4I₂ + H₂S + 4H₂O

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why iodide ions reduce sulfuric acid further than bromide ions do.
parts.answer: I⁻ is larger than Br⁻ so its outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded; it is lost more easily, so iodide is the stronger reducing agent.
parts.working: B1 larger ion / more shielding / weaker attraction to outer electrons; B1 loses electrons more easily, stronger reducing agent

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give one observation that shows iodine has been formed.
parts.answer: Purple fumes or a black/grey solid.
parts.working: B1 purple fumes / black (grey-black) solid (not a yellow solid, which is sulfur)

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Halide ions: tests & reactions with H2SO4

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Solid potassium bromide is warmed with concentrated sulfuric acid. Which set of products forms?
A HBr only
B HBr, Br₂ and SO₂
C HBr, Br₂ and H₂S
D Br₂ and S only
parts.answer: B HBr, Br₂ and SO₂
parts.working: Br⁻ reduces H₂SO₄ only to SO₂ (S +6 → +4), forming Br₂ as well as HBr. H₂S and S need the stronger reducing agent I⁻; HBr only is the chloride pattern.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Halide ions: tests & reactions with H2SO4
stem:
Three white solids P, Q and R are each sodium halides. They are tested in a school laboratory in Peshawar.
Test 1 (solution + dilute HNO₃ + AgNO₃(aq)): P yellow precipitate; Q white precipitate; R cream precipitate.
Test 2 (precipitate + dilute NH₃(aq)): P no change; Q dissolves; R no change.
Test 3 (solid + concentrated H₂SO₄): P purple fumes and smell of bad eggs; Q steamy fumes only; R steamy fumes and orange-brown fumes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anion in each of P, Q and R.
parts.answer: P: I⁻ (iodide); Q: Cl⁻ (chloride); R: Br⁻ (bromide).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the solutions are acidified with dilute nitric acid, and not dilute hydrochloric acid, before silver nitrate is added.
parts.answer: Nitric acid removes carbonate (or hydroxide) ions that would also give a precipitate with Ag⁺; HCl would add Cl⁻ ions, giving a white precipitate in every test.
parts.working: B1 removes CO₃²⁻/OH⁻ that interfere; B1 HCl adds chloride ions

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one safety precaution needed when testing with concentrated sulfuric acid.
parts.answer: Work in a fume cupboard (toxic fumes) and wear goggles/gloves.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Halide ions: tests & reactions with H2SO4
stem: 1.000 g of a mixture of sodium chloride and sodium bromide is dissolved in water and acidified. Excess aqueous silver nitrate is added. The dried precipitate of silver chloride and silver bromide has a mass of 2.000 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of sodium chloride in the mixture, to 3 significant figures. (Mr: NaCl = 58.5, NaBr = 102.9, AgCl = 143.4, AgBr = 187.8)

parts.label: b
parts.text: The precipitate is shaken with an excess of dilute aqueous ammonia and the solid left is filtered off and dried. Calculate the mass of solid left, in g, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 1.32 g (AgBr)
parts.working: M1 AgCl dissolves, AgBr remains; A1 mass AgBr = 1.8251 × 0.7207 = 1.315 g ≈ 1.32 g

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Halide ions: tests & reactions with H2SO4

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student tests tap water for chloride ions. State the reagents she should add, in order, and the result for chloride ions.
parts.answer: Dilute nitric acid, then aqueous silver nitrate; a white precipitate forms.
parts.working: B1 HNO₃ then AgNO₃; B1 white precipitate

parts.label: b
parts.text: The white precipitate darkens when left on a sunny window-sill. Suggest what is happening.
parts.answer: Silver chloride decomposes in light to silver (and chlorine).
parts.working: B1 light decomposes AgCl to Ag

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the complex ion formed when the precipitate dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia.
parts.answer: Diamminesilver(I) ion, [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Halide ions: tests & reactions with H2SO4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why hydrogen iodide cannot be prepared by adding concentrated sulfuric acid to sodium iodide.
parts.answer: The HI formed is a strong reducing agent and is oxidised by the sulfuric acid to iodine, so little HI is collected.
parts.working: B1 HI/I⁻ strong reducing agent; B1 oxidised to I₂ (H₂SO₄ reduced)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Concentrated phosphoric(V) acid, H₃PO₄, can be used instead. Suggest why this works.
parts.answer: Phosphoric acid is not an oxidising agent, so it does not oxidise HI.
parts.working: B1 not an oxidising agent / non-oxidising acid

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of sodium iodide with phosphoric(V) acid to form hydrogen iodide.
parts.answer: NaI + H₃PO₄ → NaH₂PO₄ + HI

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Halide ions: tests & reactions with H2SO4
stem: 0.050 mol of potassium bromide reacts with excess concentrated sulfuric acid. All the bromide is first converted to HBr. 40% of this HBr then reacts: 2HBr + H₂SO₄ → Br₂ + SO₂ + 2H₂O.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of bromine, in g, formed. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (Mr Br₂ = 159.8)
parts.working: M1 HBr oxidised = 0.40 × 0.050 = 0.020 mol, Br₂ = 0.010 mol; A1 1.60 g

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of sulfur dioxide, in cm³, formed at room temperature and pressure. (1 mol of gas occupies 24.0 dm³)
parts.answer: 240 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the remaining hydrogen bromide is not oxidised.
parts.answer: It escapes as a gas before it can react / the acid becomes diluted by the water formed.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Halide ions: tests & reactions with H2SO4
stem: A student collects seawater at Clifton beach, Karachi, and tests it with dilute nitric acid and aqueous silver nitrate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State why a halide test on seawater gives a white precipitate even though seawater contains small amounts of bromide.
parts.answer: Chloride ions are in large excess, so white AgCl dominates and hides the cream AgBr.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the equation for the dissolving of silver chloride in aqueous ammonia.
parts.answer: AgCl(s) + 2NH₃(aq) → [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why adding ammonia allows the bromide to be detected.
parts.answer: AgCl dissolves in dilute ammonia, leaving the cream AgBr as a small amount of solid.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Halogen trends (volatility, bond strength, oxidising power)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the colour and physical state at room temperature of chlorine, bromine and iodine.
parts.answer: Chlorine: pale yellow-green gas; bromine: red-brown liquid; iodine: grey-black solid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the trend in volatility down the group.
parts.answer: Volatility decreases because molecules have more electrons, so instantaneous dipole–induced dipole (London) forces are stronger and need more energy to overcome.
parts.working: B1 more electrons / larger molecules; B1 stronger id–id forces, more energy to separate molecules

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Halogen trends (volatility, bond strength, oxidising power)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A hot glass rod is placed into separate gas jars of HCl, HBr and HI. In which jar do violet fumes appear most readily?
A HCl
B HBr
C HI
D none of them
parts.answer: C HI
parts.working: The H–I bond is the weakest (longest), so HI decomposes most easily to H₂ and violet iodine vapour. HCl has the strongest bond and does not decompose at this temperature.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Halogen trends (volatility, bond strength, oxidising power)
stem: Bond energies / kJ/mol: H–Cl 431; H–Br 366; H–I 299; Cl–Cl 242; Br–Br 193; I–I 151.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain the trend in the H–X bond energies.
parts.answer: Bond energy decreases from H–Cl to H–I because the halogen atom is larger, so the bond is longer and the shared electrons are further from the halogen nucleus (weaker attraction).
parts.working: B1 decreases; B1 larger atom / longer bond / weaker attraction of bonding pair

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use these values to explain the trend in thermal stability of the hydrogen halides.
parts.answer: Thermal stability decreases from HCl to HI because less energy is needed to break the weaker bond.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the Cl–Cl bond is stronger than the I–I bond.
parts.answer: Cl atoms are smaller; the bonding pair is closer to both nuclei, so it is attracted more strongly.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Halogen trends (volatility, bond strength, oxidising power)

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the trend in oxidising power of the halogens from chlorine to iodine.
parts.answer: It decreases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain this trend in terms of atomic structure.
parts.answer: Atomic radius increases down the group and there is more shielding by inner shells; the attraction of the nucleus for an incoming electron is weaker, so the atom gains an electron less readily.
parts.working: B1 larger atom / more shells; B1 more shielding; B1 weaker attraction for electron to be gained, so weaker oxidising agent

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the trend in electronegativity down the group.
parts.answer: It decreases.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Halogen trends (volatility, bond strength, oxidising power)
stem: Boiling points: Cl₂ −34 °C; Br₂ 59 °C; I₂ 184 °C. Astatine, At, is below iodine in Group 17.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the state of astatine at room temperature and explain your prediction using the data.
parts.answer: Solid; its boiling point should be well above that of iodine because At₂ has even more electrons and stronger London forces.
parts.working: B1 solid (black); B1 stronger id–id forces, b.p. higher than 184 °C

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict how astatine would react with hydrogen and how stable hydrogen astatide, HAt, would be to heat. Explain.
parts.answer: Very slow, incomplete (reversible) reaction even on heating; HAt very unstable, decomposing easily, because the H–At bond is very weak (large atom, long bond).
parts.working: B1 slow/reversible reaction; B1 HAt decomposes easily, weak bond

parts.label: c
parts.text: Would astatine displace iodine from potassium iodide solution? Explain.
parts.answer: No; astatine is a weaker oxidising agent than iodine.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Halogen trends (volatility, bond strength, oxidising power)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which property increases from chlorine to iodine?
A first ionisation energy
B electronegativity
C strength of instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces
D oxidising power
parts.answer: C strength of instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces
parts.working: Iodine molecules have the most electrons, so their London forces are strongest. Ionisation energy, electronegativity and oxidising power all decrease down the group.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Halogen trends (volatility, bond strength, oxidising power)
stem:
Chlorine and hydrogen explode in sunlight. Bromine and hydrogen react only on heating with a catalyst. Iodine and hydrogen react slowly and reversibly when heated.
Bond energies / kJ/mol: H–H 436; Cl–Cl 242; Br–Br 193; I–I 151; H–Cl 431; H–Br 366; H–I 299.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the bond energies to calculate ΔH for H₂(g) + X₂(g) → 2HX(g) for X = Cl, Br and I. Assume all species are gases.
parts.answer: Cl: −184 kJ/mol; Br: −103 kJ/mol; I: −11 kJ/mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answers to explain the observations.
parts.answer: Reactions become much less exothermic down the group (the H–X bond formed gets weaker faster than X–X); the reaction with iodine releases little energy, so it is slow and reversible, while chlorine's large release makes it explosive.
parts.working: B1 less exothermic down group; B1 links to reactivity: iodine reaction barely favourable / reversible

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of chlorine with water.
parts.answer: Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of chlorine in each chlorine-containing species in your equation.
parts.answer: Cl₂ 0; HCl −1; HClO +1
parts.working: B1 HCl −1 and Cl₂ 0; B1 HClO +1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answer to (b) to explain why this is a disproportionation reaction.
parts.answer: Chlorine is simultaneously oxidised (0 → +1) and reduced (0 → −1).
parts.working: B1 same element both oxidised and reduced

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of chlorine with cold dilute aqueous sodium hydroxide.
parts.answer: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of chlorine with hot concentrated aqueous sodium hydroxide.
parts.answer: 3Cl₂ + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO₃ + 3H₂O
parts.working: B1 products NaCl and NaClO₃; B1 balanced

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the chlorine-containing product of (b) in which chlorine has a positive oxidation number, and give that oxidation number.
parts.answer: Sodium chlorate(V), +5.

stem: A factory near Kala Shah Kaku makes household bleach from chlorine and sodium hydroxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of sodium chlorate(I), NaClO, in kg, that could be made from 10.0 kg of chlorine with cold dilute NaOH. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (Mr: Cl₂ = 71.0, NaClO = 74.5)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume, in dm³, of 2.00 mol/dm³ NaOH needed for (a). Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 141 dm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: If the NaOH were hot and concentrated, what mass of sodium chlorate(V), NaClO₃, in kg, would form from the same mass of chlorine? (Mr NaClO₃ = 106.5)

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Chlorine is bubbled into hot concentrated aqueous potassium hydroxide. What are the oxidation numbers of chlorine in the two chlorine-containing products?
A −1 and +1
B −1 and +5
C +1 and +5
D −1 and +7
parts.answer: B −1 and +5
parts.working: Hot concentrated alkali gives KCl (−1) and KClO₃ (+5). A (−1 and +1) is the result with cold dilute alkali.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the two ionic half-equations for chlorine in hot alkali, one forming Cl⁻ and one forming ClO₃⁻.
parts.answer: Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻; Cl₂ + 12OH⁻ → 2ClO₃⁻ + 6H₂O + 10e⁻
parts.working: B1 reduction; B1 oxidation half-equation balanced

parts.label: b
parts.text: Combine them to give the overall ionic equation.
parts.answer: 3Cl₂ + 6OH⁻ → 5Cl⁻ + ClO₃⁻ + 3H₂O

parts.label: c
parts.text: A solution of chlorate(I) ions, ClO⁻, is warmed. Write an ionic equation for the disproportionation that occurs and state the oxidation number changes.
parts.answer: 3ClO⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + ClO₃⁻; Cl +1 → −1 (reduced) and +1 → +5 (oxidised).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why household bleach should be stored in a cool place.
parts.answer: Warming makes the chlorate(I) disproportionate, so the bleach loses its active ingredient.

stem: Chlorine water is added to three tubes containing aqueous potassium bromide (A), potassium iodide (B) and potassium chloride (C). A little cyclohexane is added to each tube and the tubes are shaken.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the colour of the aqueous layer and of the cyclohexane layer in tubes A and B after shaking.
parts.answer: A: aqueous orange/yellow, cyclohexane orange; B: aqueous brown, cyclohexane purple/violet.
parts.working: B1 tube A; B1 tube B

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write ionic equations for the reactions in tubes A and B.
parts.answer: A: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂; B: Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what is seen in tube C and explain.
parts.answer: No change (colourless/pale); chlorine cannot oxidise chloride, and no reaction occurs.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which mixture produces a reaction?
A iodine solution + potassium bromide solution
B bromine water + potassium chloride solution
C bromine water + potassium iodide solution
D iodine solution + potassium chloride solution
parts.answer: C bromine water + potassium iodide solution
parts.working: Bromine is a stronger oxidising agent than iodine, so it oxidises I⁻ to I₂. In A, B and D the halogen is weaker than the halide's own element, so there is no reaction.

stem: 25.0 cm³ of a chlorine water sample is added to an excess of aqueous potassium iodide. The iodine formed is titrated with 0.100 mol/dm³ sodium thiosulfate; 18.40 cm³ is needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an ionic equation for the reaction of chlorine with iodide ions.
parts.answer: Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: The equation for the titration is I₂ + 2S₂O₃²⁻ → 2I⁻ + S₄O₆²⁻. Calculate the concentration of chlorine in the sample in g/dm³. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 2.61 g/dm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name a suitable indicator and give the colour change at the end-point.
parts.answer: Starch, added near the end-point; blue-black to colourless.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why chlorine is added to drinking water.
parts.answer: To kill bacteria (and other microorganisms) that cause disease such as cholera and typhoid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the species formed when chlorine reacts with water that acts as the main disinfectant.
parts.answer: Chloric(I) acid, HClO (and ClO⁻ ions).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one risk of using chlorine in water treatment.
parts.answer: Chlorine is toxic; it can react with organic matter to form harmful chlorinated compounds.

stem: A water treatment plant serving part of Lahore treats 2.4 × 10⁷ dm³ of water per day, adding chlorine at 1.5 mg per dm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of chlorine, in kg, used each day.
parts.answer: 36 kg

parts.label: b
parts.text: Chlorine arrives in cylinders each containing 68 kg. How many full cylinders are needed for one week?
parts.answer: 4 cylinders

parts.label: c
parts.text: The chlorine reacts with water: Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO. Explain why this is described as a disproportionation reaction.
parts.answer: Chlorine (0) is both oxidised to +1 in HClO and reduced to −1 in HCl.
parts.working: B1 oxidation numbers 0 → +1 and 0 → −1; B1 same element oxidised and reduced

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of chlorine in each of: Cl₂O₇, ClO₂, NaClO₄, HClO, Cl₂O.
parts.answer: Cl₂O₇ +7; ClO₂ +4; NaClO₄ +7; HClO +1; Cl₂O +1
parts.working: 3 marks all five correct; 2 marks four; 1 mark three

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name NaClO₃ and NaClO using oxidation numbers.
parts.answer: Sodium chlorate(V) and sodium chlorate(I).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Chlorine dioxide, ClO₂, is used to bleach paper pulp. It can be made by reducing sodium chlorate(V) with sulfur dioxide in acid: 2ClO₃⁻ + SO₂ → 2ClO₂ + SO₄²⁻. Show, using oxidation numbers, that this is a redox reaction.
parts.answer: Cl goes from +5 to +4 (reduced); S goes from +4 to +6 (oxidised).
parts.working: B1 Cl change; B1 S change

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of phenol with aqueous sodium hydroxide.
parts.answer: C₆H₅OH + NaOH → C₆H₅O⁻Na⁺ + H₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: Place ethanol, phenol and water in order of increasing acidity.
parts.answer: ethanol < water < phenol

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why phenol is more acidic than ethanol.
parts.answer: In the phenoxide ion the negative charge on oxygen is delocalised into the benzene ring (a p-orbital lone pair overlaps with the π system), stabilising the anion; in ethoxide the ethyl group donates electrons, intensifying the charge on O; so phenol ionises more.
parts.working: B1 phenoxide charge delocalised into ring; B1 ethoxide charge concentrated / alkyl group electron-donating; B1 more stable anion means equilibrium further to the right / more H⁺ released

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is seen when bromine water is added to aqueous phenol at room temperature.
parts.answer: Orange/brown bromine water is decolourised and a white precipitate forms.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction, naming the organic product.
parts.answer: C₆H₅OH + 3Br₂ → C₆H₂Br₃OH + 3HBr; 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the conditions needed for benzene to react with bromine.
parts.answer: Liquid bromine (not bromine water) with a halogen carrier catalyst such as FeBr₃ / AlBr₃ / iron, at room temperature.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Phenol reacts with dilute nitric acid at room temperature. Name the two main organic products.
parts.answer: 2-nitrophenol and 4-nitrophenol.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Benzene needs a mixture of concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids at about 55 °C to be nitrated. Explain why phenol reacts under much milder conditions.
parts.answer: A lone pair on the oxygen of the OH group is delocalised into the ring; this increases the electron density of the ring (especially at the 2, 4 and 6 positions); the ring is attacked more easily by electrophiles.
parts.working: B1 O lone pair (p-orbital) overlaps / delocalised into π system; B1 higher electron density in ring; B1 more susceptible to electrophilic attack (ring activated)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of phenol with sodium metal.
parts.answer: 2C₆H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₆H₅ONa + H₂

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which reagent reacts with phenol but not with ethanol?
A sodium metal
B aqueous sodium hydroxide
C acidified potassium dichromate(VI)
D aqueous sodium carbonate, forming CO₂
parts.answer: B aqueous sodium hydroxide
parts.working: Phenol is acidic enough to react with NaOH(aq) to form sodium phenoxide; ethanol is not. Both react with sodium metal. Phenol is too weak an acid to release CO₂ from carbonate. Dichromate oxidises ethanol, not phenol.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which list shows the compounds in order of increasing acidity?
A phenol, ethanol, water, ethanoic acid
B ethanol, water, phenol, ethanoic acid
C water, ethanol, ethanoic acid, phenol
D ethanol, phenol, water, ethanoic acid
parts.answer: B ethanol, water, phenol, ethanoic acid
parts.working: Ethanol is the weakest acid (alkyl group donates electrons); water next; phenol is stronger because phenoxide is stabilised by delocalisation; ethanoic acid is strongest (carboxylate charge spread over two O atoms). D puts phenol below water.

stem: 4.70 g of phenol is dissolved in water and an excess of bromine water is added. The yield of 2,4,6-tribromophenol is 85%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of 2,4,6-tribromophenol, in g, obtained. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (Mr: phenol = 94.0; 2,4,6-tribromophenol = 330.7)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the minimum mass of bromine, Br₂, in g, needed to react with all of the phenol. (Mr Br₂ = 159.8)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a simple test to show that the product contains no unreacted phenol.
parts.answer: Its melting point is sharp and matches the data-book value (or it gives a single spot on a chromatogram).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Phenol is dissolved in aqueous sodium hydroxide and cooled below 10 °C. A cold solution of benzenediazonium chloride is added. Describe what is seen and name the type of compound formed.
parts.answer: An orange/yellow precipitate (dye) forms; it is an azo compound.
parts.working: B1 orange/yellow precipitate; B1 azo compound/dye

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the structural formula of the product, showing where the coupling occurs on the phenol ring.
parts.answer: HO–C₆H₄–N=N–C₆H₅ with the N=N joined at the 4-position (para) to the OH group.
parts.working: B1 –N=N– link between two rings; B1 para to OH

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the reaction is carried out in alkaline solution.
parts.answer: Phenol forms the phenoxide ion, which has a more electron-rich ring and couples more readily (and dissolves).

stem:
X, Y and Z are isomers with formula C₇H₈O. Each contains a benzene ring.
X reacts with aqueous NaOH and with bromine water at room temperature forming C₇H₅Br₃O.
Y does not react with aqueous NaOH but reacts with sodium, giving hydrogen.
Z does not react with aqueous NaOH or with sodium.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify X, Y and Z, giving their structures and names.
parts.answer: X: 3-methylphenol (CH₃C₆H₄OH, OH and CH₃ at 1,3); Y: phenylmethanol, C₆H₅CH₂OH; Z: methoxybenzene, C₆H₅OCH₃.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why X gives a tribromo product but 4-methylphenol would give only a dibromo product.
parts.answer: Bromine substitutes at the 2, 4 and 6 positions relative to OH; in 3-methylphenol all three positions are free; in 4-methylphenol the 4-position is taken by CH₃, so only 2 and 6 can be substituted.
parts.working: B1 2,4,6 directing by OH; B1 4-position blocked in 4-methylphenol

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of Y with sodium.
parts.answer: 2C₆H₅CH₂OH + 2Na → 2C₆H₅CH₂ONa + H₂

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the reagents and conditions for converting phenylamine into benzenediazonium chloride.
parts.answer: Sodium nitrite (NaNO₂) and dilute HCl (nitrous acid made in situ), below 10 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how benzenediazonium chloride is then converted into phenol and write the equation.
parts.answer: Warm the solution with water (above 10 °C): C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + H₂O → C₆H₅OH + N₂ + HCl
parts.working: B1 warm in water; B1 equation

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the first step must be kept below 10 °C.
parts.answer: The diazonium salt is unstable and decomposes (to phenol and N₂) at higher temperatures.

stem: Phenol, used in some antiseptics, has Ka = 1.3 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol/dm³ at 298 K.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the pH of 0.100 mol/dm³ phenol. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the pH of 0.100 mol/dm³ ethanoic acid (Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ mol/dm³), to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why ethanoic acid is a stronger acid than phenol.
parts.answer: In the ethanoate ion the negative charge is delocalised over two electronegative oxygen atoms; in phenoxide it is spread into the ring of carbon atoms (less electronegative), so it is less stabilised.
parts.working: B1 carboxylate delocalised over two O atoms; B1 phenoxide charge partly on C atoms, less stable anion

author: HomiLabs

stem: Propan-1-ol is warmed with acidified potassium dichromate(VI).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the colour change of the dichromate reagent.
parts.answer: Orange to green.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the product formed when propan-1-ol is heated under reflux with excess acidified dichromate, and write an equation using [O].
parts.answer: Propanoic acid; CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + 2[O] → CH₃CH₂COOH + H₂O

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the product formed if the oxidation is carried out with the alcohol in excess and the product distilled off immediately. Explain why distilling gives this product.
parts.answer: Propanal; it has a lower boiling point (no hydrogen bonding between molecules), so it distils out before it can be oxidised further.
parts.working: B1 propanal; B1 removed from reaction mixture as formed / low b.p.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which alcohol is NOT oxidised when heated under reflux with acidified potassium dichromate(VI)?
A butan-1-ol
B butan-2-ol
C 2-methylpropan-1-ol
D 2-methylpropan-2-ol
parts.answer: D 2-methylpropan-2-ol
parts.working: 2-Methylpropan-2-ol is tertiary: the carbon carrying OH has no H atom, so it is not oxidised. Butan-2-ol is secondary (forms butanone); the others are primary.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the four structural isomers of C₄H₉OH that are alcohols and classify each as primary, secondary or tertiary.
parts.answer: Butan-1-ol (primary); butan-2-ol (secondary); 2-methylpropan-1-ol (primary); 2-methylpropan-2-ol (tertiary).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the organic product formed when butan-2-ol is heated with acidified potassium dichromate(VI).
parts.answer: Butanone.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the product of (b) cannot be oxidised further by this reagent.
parts.answer: Ketones are not oxidised; further oxidation would need a C–C bond to break.

stem:
A student heats propan-1-ol and drips in acidified sodium dichromate(VI) from a dropping funnel. The flask is fitted with a still-head, thermometer and condenser set for distillation. The receiving flask stands in ice.
Boiling points: propanal 49 °C; propan-1-ol 97 °C; propanoic acid 141 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The student wants to collect propanal. State the temperature range on the thermometer at the still-head at which she should collect the distillate.
parts.answer: About 46–52 °C (around 49 °C).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the receiving flask is placed in ice.
parts.answer: Propanal is volatile (low b.p.), so cooling reduces loss by evaporation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a test, with the result, to show that the distillate contains an aldehyde.
parts.answer: Warm with Tollens' reagent: silver mirror forms (or warm with Fehling's solution: brick-red precipitate).
parts.working: B1 reagent with warming; B1 correct positive result

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the dichromate solution is added slowly from a dropping funnel to the warm alcohol.
parts.answer: The alcohol stays in excess, so the aldehyde is not oxidised further (and the exothermic reaction is controlled).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Older roadside breath-testing devices used the oxidation of ethanol by acidified dichromate(VI).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the oxidation of ethanol, C₂H₅OH, to ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, in acidic solution.
parts.answer: C₂H₅OH + H₂O → CH₃COOH + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻

parts.label: b
parts.text: The half-equation for dichromate is Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O. Construct the overall ionic equation.
parts.answer: 2Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 16H⁺ + 3C₂H₅OH → 4Cr³⁺ + 11H₂O + 3CH₃COOH
parts.working: M1 balances electrons (×2 and ×3); A1 cancels H⁺ and H₂O correctly

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the volume, in cm³, of 0.0200 mol/dm³ K₂Cr₂O₇ needed to oxidise 0.115 g of ethanol to ethanoic acid. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (Mr ethanol = 46.0)
parts.answer: 83.3 cm³

author: HomiLabs

stem: 6.00 g of propan-2-ol is heated with excess acidified potassium dichromate(VI). 4.35 g of propanone is collected.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the oxidation of propan-2-ol, using [O].
parts.answer: CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ + [O] → CH₃COCH₃ + H₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage yield of propanone. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (Mr: propan-2-ol = 60.0, propanone = 58.0)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the yield is below 100%.
parts.answer: Some propanone evaporates (volatile) / lost on transfer / incomplete reaction.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Alcohol A has molecular formula C₅H₁₂O.
• A is oxidised by hot acidified dichromate(VI) to a ketone.
• A has a chiral carbon atom.
• Dehydration of A gives three different alkenes (counting stereoisomers).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify A, explaining each piece of evidence.
parts.answer: A is pentan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₂CH₃: secondary (oxidised to ketone, pentan-2-one); chiral C2 carries H, OH, CH₃ and C₃H₇; dehydration gives pent-1-ene plus cis- and trans-pent-2-ene (three alkenes).
parts.working: B1 secondary alcohol from ketone; B1 chiral centre; B1 three alkenes explained (including cis/trans); B1 correct identity

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why 3-methylbutan-2-ol, which is also chiral and secondary, does not fit the evidence.
parts.answer: Its dehydration gives only two alkenes (3-methylbut-1-ene and 2-methylbut-2-ene), neither with cis/trans isomers.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Each alcohol is warmed with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) and the product is distilled off immediately. Which alcohol gives a distillate that forms a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent?
A butan-2-ol
B 2-methylpropan-2-ol
C propan-1-ol
D propan-2-ol
parts.answer: C propan-1-ol
parts.working: Primary propan-1-ol gives propanal, an aldehyde, which reduces Tollens' reagent. A and D are secondary and give ketones (no silver mirror); B is tertiary and is not oxidised.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two different reagents that convert ethanol into chloroethane.
parts.answer: Any two of: PCl₅ (room temperature); SOCl₂; PCl₃ with heat; HCl (with ZnCl₂ catalyst).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of ethanol with phosphorus(V) chloride.
parts.answer: C₂H₅OH + PCl₅ → C₂H₅Cl + POCl₃ + HCl

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what is seen in (b) that makes this a test for an –OH group.
parts.answer: Steamy white fumes of HCl.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give reagents and conditions for the dehydration of ethanol.
parts.answer: Pass vapour over heated aluminium oxide (about 350 °C) or heat with excess concentrated H₂SO₄/H₃PO₄ (about 170 °C).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: C₂H₅OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a test for the organic product, with the result.
parts.answer: Add bromine water; orange decolourised.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Butan-2-ol is heated with concentrated phosphoric acid. How many different alkenes, including stereoisomers, can form?
A 1
B 2
C 3
D 4
parts.answer: C 3
parts.working: But-1-ene forms, and but-2-ene, which has cis and trans isomers: three alkenes in total. B forgets the stereoisomers of but-2-ene.

stem: 9.20 g of ethanol is heated with potassium bromide and concentrated sulfuric acid. 14.2 g of pure bromoethane is obtained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write equations for the formation of HBr and for its reaction with ethanol.
parts.answer: KBr + H₂SO₄ → KHSO₄ + HBr; C₂H₅OH + HBr → C₂H₅Br + H₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage yield. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (Mr: ethanol = 46.0, bromoethane = 108.9)

parts.label: c
parts.text: The crude bromoethane is orange-brown. Suggest the cause of the colour.
parts.answer: Some HBr is oxidised by concentrated sulfuric acid to bromine.

author: HomiLabs

stem: W has formula C₃H₈O₂. 0.380 g of W reacts with excess PCl₅ and gives 240 cm³ of HCl gas at room temperature and pressure (1 mol of gas occupies 24.0 dm³).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that W contains two –OH groups. (Mr of W = 76.0)
parts.answer: n(W) = 0.380 ÷ 76.0 = 0.00500 mol; n(HCl) = 0.240 ÷ 24.0 = 0.0100 mol; ratio 1 : 2, so two OH groups (each OH gives one HCl).
parts.working: M1 both mole values; A1 ratio and conclusion

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of hydrogen, in cm³ at r.t.p., formed when the same mass of W reacts with excess sodium.
parts.answer: 120 cm³
parts.working: B1 2 OH → 1 H₂ per W: 0.00500 mol H₂ × 24 000 = 120 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the structures of the two possible diols. Describe a chemical test that would distinguish them, giving the result for each.
parts.answer: Propane-1,2-diol CH₃CH(OH)CH₂OH and propane-1,3-diol HOCH₂CH₂CH₂OH; warm with alkaline aqueous iodine: propane-1,2-diol gives a yellow precipitate (CHI₃) because it contains CH₃CH(OH)–; propane-1,3-diol gives no precipitate.
parts.working: B1 each structure; B1 test with both results

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of propan-1-ol with thionyl chloride, SOCl₂.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + SOCl₂ → CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl + SO₂ + HCl

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of SOCl₂ over PCl₅ for this conversion.
parts.answer: Both by-products (SO₂ and HCl) are gases, so the chloroalkane is easy to separate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the type of reaction occurring.
parts.answer: Substitution (nucleophilic substitution of OH by Cl).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the reaction must be carried out in a fume cupboard.
parts.answer: SO₂ and HCl are toxic/corrosive gases.

stem: 2-Methylbutan-2-ol is heated with concentrated phosphoric acid and the products are distilled.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the two alkenes formed from 2-methylbutan-2-ol and explain why neither shows cis/trans isomerism.
parts.answer: 2-methylbut-1-ene and 2-methylbut-2-ene; in each, one carbon of the C=C carries two identical groups (two H or two CH₃).

parts.label: b
parts.text: In a second experiment, 10.0 g of cyclohexanol (Mr 100.0) is dehydrated and 5.74 g of cyclohexene (Mr 82.0) is collected. Calculate the percentage yield to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The crude cyclohexene is shaken with sodium carbonate solution and then dried with anhydrous calcium chloride. State the purpose of each step.
parts.answer: Sodium carbonate neutralises/removes acid impurity; CaCl₂ removes water.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two observations when a small piece of sodium is added to ethanol.
parts.answer: Bubbles (effervescence) of gas; sodium sinks/dissolves slowly (less vigorously than with water).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: bubbles; sodium disappears slowly; solution warms; colourless solution forms

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction and name the organic product.
parts.answer: 2C₂H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₂H₅ONa + H₂; sodium ethoxide.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the reaction is less vigorous than that of sodium with water.
parts.answer: Ethanol is a weaker acid than water: the ethyl group donates electrons, making the O–H bond less polar.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ethanol and ethanoic acid are warmed with a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid. Write an equation for the reaction, name the organic product and state the role of the acid.
parts.answer: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O; ethyl ethanoate; catalyst.
parts.working: B1 equation; B1 name; B1 catalyst

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one use of the organic product.
parts.answer: Solvent (nail-varnish remover, glues) or flavouring.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write an equation for the complete combustion of ethanol.
parts.answer: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which alcohol gives a yellow precipitate when warmed with alkaline aqueous iodine?
A methanol
B propan-1-ol
C propan-2-ol
D 2-methylpropan-2-ol
parts.answer: C propan-2-ol
parts.working: Propan-2-ol contains the CH₃CH(OH)– group, which is oxidised and gives tri-iodomethane (CHI₃), a yellow precipitate. Methanol and propan-1-ol lack this group; 2-methylpropan-2-ol has no H on the carbinol carbon.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of hydrogen, in dm³ at r.t.p., formed when 0.92 g of ethanol reacts with excess sodium. (1 mol of gas occupies 24.0 dm³)

parts.label: b
parts.text: 1.48 g of an unknown alcohol, ROH, gives 240 cm³ of hydrogen with excess sodium. Calculate the Mr of the alcohol and deduce its molecular formula.
parts.answer: Mr = 74; C₄H₉OH

parts.label: c
parts.text: The alcohol gives a yellow precipitate with alkaline aqueous iodine. Identify it.
parts.answer: Butan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃.
parts.working: B1 (only C₄ alcohol with CH₃CH(OH)– group)

stem: Ethanol for hand sanitisers in Pakistan is made mainly by fermenting molasses from sugar mills, but elsewhere it is also made from ethene.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the conditions for the industrial hydration of ethene to make ethanol.
parts.answer: Steam, phosphoric acid catalyst, about 300 °C and 6–7 MPa (60–70 atm).
parts.working: B1 steam and H₃PO₄ catalyst; B1 temperature and pressure

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write equations for the hydration of ethene and for the fermentation of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆.
parts.answer: C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH; C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the atom economy of fermentation, to 3 significant figures. (Mr: glucose = 180.0, ethanol = 46.0)

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name a laboratory reagent that reduces ethanal to ethanol.
parts.answer: Sodium tetrahydridoborate, NaBH₄ (or LiAlH₄ in dry ether).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is seen when aqueous ammonia is added dropwise, until in excess, to aqueous copper(II) sulfate.
parts.answer: A pale blue precipitate forms first; it dissolves in excess ammonia to give a deep (dark) blue solution.
parts.working: B1 pale blue precipitate; B1 dissolves to deep blue solution

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an equation for the formation of the precipitate from [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺.
parts.answer: [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Cu(OH)₂(H₂O)₄ + 2H₂O (accept Cu²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Cu(OH)₂)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write an equation for the ligand exchange that forms the deep blue complex from [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺.
parts.answer: [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 4NH₃ → [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ + 4H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Concentrated hydrochloric acid is added to aqueous copper(II) sulfate. Give the formula of the complex formed and its colour.
parts.answer: [CuCl₄]²⁻; yellow (yellow-green solution as some aqua complex remains).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the shape and coordination number of the complex in (a) and of [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺.
parts.answer: [CuCl₄]²⁻: tetrahedral, 4; [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺: octahedral, 6.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the coordination number changes.
parts.answer: Chloride ions are larger than water molecules, so fewer fit around the Cu²⁺ ion.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State what is seen when the solution from (a) is diluted with plenty of water, and explain.
parts.answer: It turns blue again; the equilibrium shifts back to [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ as water is in large excess.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term stability constant, Kstab, of a complex ion.
parts.answer: The equilibrium constant for the formation of the complex ion in a solvent from its constituent ions or molecules (the aqueous metal ion and the ligands).
parts.working: B1 equilibrium constant; B1 for formation of complex from metal ion and ligands (in water)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the expression for Kstab of [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ formed from [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺, and give its units.
parts.answer: Kstab = [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂²⁺] / ([Cu(H₂O)₆²⁺][NH₃]⁴); units dm¹² mol⁻⁴.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the concentration of water does not appear in the expression.
parts.answer: Water is the solvent, in large excess, so its concentration is effectively constant.

stem: lg Kstab values: [CuCl₄]²⁻ 5.6; [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ 13.1; [Cu(EDTA)]²⁻ 18.8.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict what happens when excess aqueous ammonia is added to a solution of [CuCl₄]²⁻. Explain using the data.
parts.answer: The solution turns deep blue: [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ forms, because its Kstab is much larger, so NH₃ replaces Cl⁻.
parts.working: B1 deep blue / ammine complex forms; B1 larger Kstab, more stable

parts.label: b
parts.text: EDTA⁴⁻ solution is added to the product of (a). Write an equation for the reaction and explain why it happens.
parts.answer: [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ + EDTA⁴⁻ → [Cu(EDTA)]²⁻ + 4NH₃ + 2H₂O; [Cu(EDTA)]²⁻ has the largest Kstab, so it is the most stable complex.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why lg Kstab values are often quoted rather than Kstab.
parts.answer: Kstab values are very large and vary over many powers of ten, so logarithms are easier to compare.

author: HomiLabs

stem: lg Kstab: [Ni(NH₃)₆]²⁺ 8.6; [Ni(en)₃]²⁺ 18.3. Both N–Ni bonds are similar in strength.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the exchange of all the NH₃ ligands in [Ni(NH₃)₆]²⁺ by 1,2-diaminoethane, en.
parts.answer: [Ni(NH₃)₆]²⁺ + 3en → [Ni(en)₃]²⁺ + 6NH₃

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the equilibrium constant for this exchange. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: ΔH for the exchange is close to zero. Explain, in terms of entropy, why the reaction is very favourable.
parts.answer: Four particles on the left become seven on the right, so the disorder (entropy) increases greatly; ΔS is positive so ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is negative.
parts.working: B1 4 → 7 particles, entropy increases; B1 ΔG negative / feasible because ΔH ≈ 0

author: HomiLabs

stem: Kstab of [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ is 1.7 × 10⁷ dm⁶ mol⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the expression for Kstab of [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺.
parts.answer: Kstab = [Ag(NH₃)₂⁺] / ([Ag⁺][NH₃]²)

parts.label: b
parts.text: In a solution, the equilibrium concentration of free ammonia is 0.50 mol/dm³. Calculate the ratio [Ag(NH₃)₂⁺] : [Ag⁺]. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence calculate the fraction of the silver present as free Ag⁺(aq) ions. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Use your answer to explain why silver chloride dissolves in aqueous ammonia.
parts.answer: Free [Ag⁺] becomes so small that [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] falls below the solubility product, so more AgCl dissolves.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Concentrated hydrochloric acid is added to a pink solution containing [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺. Which row describes the new complex?
A [CoCl₄]²⁻, blue, tetrahedral
B [CoCl₆]⁴⁻, blue, octahedral
C [CoCl₄]²⁻, pink, square planar
D [Co(H₂O)₄Cl₂], green, octahedral
parts.answer: A [CoCl₄]²⁻, blue, tetrahedral
parts.working: Four large Cl⁻ ligands replace six H₂O, giving blue tetrahedral [CoCl₄]²⁻. B wrongly keeps six ligands; Cl⁻ ions are too large to fit six around Co²⁺.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Aqueous potassium thiocyanate is added to aqueous iron(III) chloride. Write an equation for the formation of the blood-red complex [Fe(SCN)(H₂O)₅]²⁺ from [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺.
parts.answer: [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ + SCN⁻ ⇌ [Fe(SCN)(H₂O)₅]²⁺ + H₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: When aqueous sodium fluoride is added to the blood-red solution, the colour fades to almost colourless as [FeF(H₂O)₅]²⁺ forms. What does this show about the stability constants of the two complexes? Explain.
parts.answer: Kstab of [FeF(H₂O)₅]²⁺ is larger than that of [Fe(SCN)(H₂O)₅]²⁺; F⁻ competes for Fe³⁺ and the equilibrium favours the more stable complex.
parts.working: B1 Kstab(F complex) larger; B1 competing equilibria / ligand exchange to more stable complex

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the Kstab expression for [Fe(SCN)(H₂O)₅]²⁺ and give its units.
parts.answer: Kstab = [Fe(SCN)(H₂O)₅²⁺] / ([Fe(H₂O)₆³⁺][SCN⁻]); dm³ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Carbon monoxide is dangerous because it binds to the Fe²⁺ ion in haemoglobin. Which statement explains this?
A CO forms a weaker bond to Fe²⁺ than O₂, so O₂ cannot bind
B The complex with CO has a larger stability constant than the complex with O₂, so the exchange is effectively irreversible
C CO oxidises Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺, which cannot carry oxygen
D CO is a bidentate ligand that replaces two water molecules
parts.answer: B The complex with CO has a larger stability constant than the complex with O₂, so the exchange is effectively irreversible
parts.working: CO replaces O₂ in a ligand exchange; its complex is much more stable (larger Kstab), so O₂ cannot displace it and oxygen transport stops. CO is monodentate and does not oxidise the iron.

stem: Equal volumes of solutions are mixed to give initial concentrations [Fe³⁺] = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol/dm³ and [SCN⁻] = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol/dm³. Using a colorimeter, the equilibrium concentration of [Fe(SCN)(H₂O)₅]²⁺ is found to be 1.20 × 10⁻³ mol/dm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the equilibrium concentrations of Fe³⁺(aq) and SCN⁻(aq).
parts.answer: Both 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol/dm³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Kstab for [Fe(SCN)(H₂O)₅]²⁺, giving its units. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 1.88 × 10³ dm³ mol⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the colorimeter was used to find the concentration of the complex.
parts.answer: A calibration graph of absorbance against known concentrations of the complex is made (using a complementary filter, blue-green); the absorbance of the equilibrium mixture is read and the concentration taken from the graph.
parts.working: B1 calibration with standard solutions; B1 read concentration from absorbance (suitable filter)

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Complex ions: ligands, shapes & coordination number

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the terms ligand and complex ion.
parts.answer: Ligand: a species with a lone pair of electrons that forms a dative (coordinate) bond to a central metal atom/ion. Complex ion: a central metal ion surrounded by ligands joined by dative bonds, with an overall charge.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define coordination number and give the coordination number of the metal in [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ and in [CuCl₄]²⁻.
parts.answer: The number of dative bonds formed to the central metal ion; 6 and 4.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Complex ions: ligands, shapes & coordination number

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What are the shape and the coordination number of the complex ion [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺?
A linear, 2
B bent, 2
C tetrahedral, 4
D linear, 4
parts.answer: A linear, 2
parts.working: Two NH₃ ligands each form one dative bond, so the coordination number is 2, and the two bonds point in opposite directions (180°). Bent shapes arise from lone pairs on a central atom, not here.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Complex ions: ligands, shapes & coordination number

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of the metal in each complex: (i) [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ (ii) [Cr(H₂O)₄Cl₂]⁺ (iii) [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]²⁺ (iv) [Cu(EDTA)]²⁻ (EDTA⁴⁻).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the coordination number in (ii) and (iv).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Complex ions: ligands, shapes & coordination number

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term bidentate ligand, using ethanedioate, C₂O₄²⁻, as an example.
parts.answer: A ligand that forms two dative bonds to the metal ion; ethanedioate donates a lone pair from each of two O⁻ atoms.
parts.working: B1 two dative bonds; B1 two O atoms with lone pairs

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the overall charge, coordination number and shape of the complex formed by Fe³⁺ with three ethanedioate ions.
parts.answer: [Fe(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻: charge 3−, coordination number 6, octahedral.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name another bidentate ligand.
parts.answer: 1,2-diaminoethane (en), H₂NCH₂CH₂NH₂.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Complex ions: ligands, shapes & coordination number
stem: Chromium(III) chloride hexahydrate, CrCl₃·6H₂O, exists in forms with different colours. A solution containing 0.0100 mol of the pale green form is treated with excess aqueous silver nitrate at once; 2.87 g of silver chloride (Mr 143.4) is precipitated. Chromium has coordination number 6 in all forms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of chloride ions precipitated per mole of complex.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Deduce the formula of the complex ion and the full formula of the compound, explaining your reasoning.
parts.answer: [Cr(H₂O)₅Cl]²⁺; [Cr(H₂O)₅Cl]Cl₂·H₂O. Only free Cl⁻ ions (not ligands) precipitate, so two Cl⁻ are outside and one is a ligand; coordination number 6 is completed by five H₂O.
parts.working: B1 complex ion; B1 full formula with reasoning

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the type of bond between the chloride ligand and the chromium ion.
parts.answer: Dative covalent (coordinate) bond.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Complex ions: ligands, shapes & coordination number

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the shape and the bond angles in each of: [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂], [CoCl₄]²⁻ and [Ni(H₂O)₆]²⁺.
parts.answer: Square planar, 90°; tetrahedral, 109.5°; octahedral, 90°.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why most aqua complexes of first-row transition metal ions are octahedral.
parts.answer: Water molecules are small, so six can fit around the ion.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Complex ions: ligands, shapes & coordination number
stem: 25.0 cm³ of a solution of Ni²⁺ ions is titrated with 0.0500 mol/dm³ EDTA⁴⁻. 18.60 cm³ is needed. The ions react in a 1 : 1 ratio.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the coordination number of nickel in [Ni(EDTA)]²⁻ and explain how one EDTA⁴⁻ ion achieves this.
parts.answer: 6; EDTA⁴⁻ is hexadentate, forming dative bonds from two N atoms and four O⁻ atoms.
parts.working: B1 6; B1 six donor atoms (2 N, 4 O)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of Ni²⁺ in the solution, in mol/dm³, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 0.0372 mol/dm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: The solution was made by dissolving a nickel alloy sample in acid and making it up to 250 cm³. Calculate the mass of nickel in the sample, to 3 significant figures. (Ar Ni = 58.7)

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Complex ions: ligands, shapes & coordination number

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which of these can act as a ligand? NH₃, CH₄, Cl⁻, NH₄⁺, H₂O, CO
parts.answer: NH₃, Cl⁻, H₂O and CO.
parts.working: 2 marks all four and no others; 1 mark for three correct

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why NH₄⁺ cannot act as a ligand.
parts.answer: The lone pair on nitrogen is used to bond to H⁺, so it has no lone pair to donate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the type of bond a ligand forms with a metal ion and the feature of the ligand that makes it possible.
parts.answer: Dative (coordinate) bond, using a lone pair of electrons.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Complex ions: ligands, shapes & coordination number

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the coordination number of cobalt in [Co(en)₂Cl₂]⁺, where en is H₂NCH₂CH₂NH₂?
A 3
B 4
C 6
D 8
parts.answer: C 6
parts.working: Each en is bidentate (2 bonds), so 2 × 2 + 2 Cl⁻ = 6. B counts each en as one bond.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the two stereoisomers of square planar [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂].
parts.answer: Cis: the two Cl ligands are next to each other (90° apart); trans: the two Cl ligands are opposite each other (180° apart).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the type of stereoisomerism shown.
parts.answer: Geometric (cis/trans) isomerism.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The cis isomer, cisplatin, is an anticancer drug. Explain how it acts.
parts.answer: Its two Cl ligands are replaced by nitrogen atoms of guanine bases on DNA; this binds adjacent bases, distorts the DNA and stops the cancer cell dividing.
parts.working: B1 ligand exchange: binds to N on DNA bases; B1 prevents DNA replication / cell division

parts.label: a
parts.text: Octahedral [Ni(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ has two geometric isomers. Describe the arrangement of the water ligands in each.
parts.answer: Cis: two water ligands adjacent (90°); trans: two water ligands opposite (180°).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why [Ni(NH₃)₅(H₂O)]²⁺ has no geometric isomers.
parts.answer: With only one water ligand, every position is equivalent; all arrangements are identical.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether either isomer in (a) is optically active and explain.
parts.answer: No; each has a plane of symmetry, so its mirror image is superimposable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why [Ni(en)₃]²⁺ shows optical isomerism.
parts.answer: The three bidentate ligands make a propeller shape with no plane of symmetry; the complex and its mirror image are non-superimposable.
parts.working: B1 no plane/centre of symmetry; B1 non-superimposable mirror images

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the total number of stereoisomers of [Co(en)₂Cl₂]⁺. Explain.
parts.answer: Three: the trans isomer (Cl ligands opposite) has a plane of symmetry and is not chiral; the cis isomer is chiral, giving a pair of optical isomers.
parts.working: B1 three; B1 trans optically inactive; B1 cis exists as two enantiomers

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the two optical isomers could be distinguished.
parts.answer: They rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which complex ion shows optical isomerism?
A [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺
B trans-[Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]⁺
C [Cr(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻
D [CuCl₄]²⁻
parts.answer: C [Cr(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻
parts.working: Three bidentate ethanedioate ligands give a chiral octahedral complex. The trans complex has a plane of symmetry; tetrahedral [CuCl₄]²⁻ with four identical ligands is not chiral.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two different compounds of formula [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] exist. Explain how this shows that the complex is square planar and not tetrahedral.
parts.answer: A tetrahedral MA₂B₂ complex has all positions adjacent, so only one arrangement exists; two isomers are possible only for square planar (cis and trans).
parts.working: B1 tetrahedral: one form only; B1 square planar gives cis and trans

parts.label: b
parts.text: One isomer has a dipole moment and the other does not. Identify which, and explain.
parts.answer: Cis is polar: the Pt–Cl bond dipoles do not cancel; trans is non-polar: the bond dipoles are opposite and cancel.
parts.working: B1 cis polar; B1 dipoles cancel in trans

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest which isomer is more soluble in water, and why.
parts.answer: Cis, because it is polar and interacts more strongly with polar water molecules.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each complex, state whether it shows geometric isomerism, optical isomerism, or neither. Give a reason in each case.
(i) tetrahedral [Zn(NH₃)₂Cl₂]
(ii) octahedral [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]²⁺
(iii) octahedral [Fe(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻
(iv) octahedral [Cr(H₂O)₄Cl₂]⁺
parts.answer: (i) neither: in a tetrahedron all positions are adjacent. (ii) neither: only one Cl, all positions equivalent. (iii) optical: three bidentate ligands, non-superimposable mirror images. (iv) geometric: Cl ligands can be cis (90°) or trans (180°).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ is coloured.
parts.answer: Ligands split the d orbitals into two energy levels; an electron absorbs visible light and moves to a higher d orbital (energy ΔE = hf); the light not absorbed (complementary colour, blue) is transmitted/seen.
parts.working: B1 d orbitals split by ligands; B1 electron promoted absorbing visible light of energy ΔE; B1 remaining colour transmitted

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why [Zn(H₂O)₆]²⁺ and [Sc(H₂O)₆]³⁺ are colourless.
parts.answer: Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰ (full: no space to promote an electron); Sc³⁺ is 3d⁰ (no d electrons to promote).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the d orbitals that are raised in energy in an octahedral complex and explain why.
parts.answer: dx²−y² and dz²; their lobes point along the axes directly at the ligands; electrons in them are repelled more by the ligand lone pairs.
parts.working: B1 names; B1 lobes along axes / towards ligands; B1 greater repulsion

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the splitting in a tetrahedral complex differs from that in an octahedral complex.
parts.answer: Reversed: dxy, dxz, dyz are higher and dx²−y², dz² lower; the energy gap is smaller.
parts.working: B1 reversed pattern (three up, two down); B1 smaller ΔE

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Excess ammonia is added to aqueous [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺, forming deep blue [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺. Which statement is correct?
A The d-orbital splitting decreases, so light of longer wavelength is absorbed
B The d-orbital splitting increases, so light of shorter wavelength is absorbed
C The d orbitals are no longer split
D The oxidation state of copper changes from +2 to +1
parts.answer: B The d-orbital splitting increases, so light of shorter wavelength is absorbed
parts.working: NH₃ splits the d orbitals more than H₂O, so ΔE is larger and higher-energy (shorter-wavelength) light is absorbed, deepening the blue. A reverses the trend; the oxidation state stays +2.

stem: The complex [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ has one absorption peak in the visible region, at 500 nm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy gap ΔE between the split d orbitals, in J per ion, to 3 significant figures. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert your answer to kJ/mol, to 3 significant figures. (L = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
parts.answer: 239 kJ/mol

parts.label: c
parts.text: Light of 500 nm is green-blue. Suggest the colour of the solution.
parts.answer: Purple/violet (red-purple).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the ion is coloured although titanium has only one d electron in this ion.
parts.answer: The single 3d electron can be promoted from a lower to a higher d orbital, absorbing light.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ is pink but [CoCl₄]²⁻ is blue. Give two reasons why the colours differ.
parts.answer: Different ligands (H₂O v Cl⁻) and different coordination number/shape (octahedral v tetrahedral) change the size of ΔE, so a different wavelength is absorbed.
parts.working: B1 ligand; B1 coordination number/geometry; (both linked to ΔE)

parts.label: b
parts.text: [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ is pale blue but [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ is deep blue, although both contain Cu²⁺ in an octahedral complex. Explain why their colours differ.
parts.answer: NH₃ ligands split the d orbitals by a different (larger) amount than H₂O, so ΔE is different and light of a different wavelength (frequency) is absorbed; the transmitted colour changes.
parts.working: B1 different ligands give different ΔE; B1 different wavelength absorbed, so different complementary colour seen

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one other factor that affects the colour of a transition element complex.
parts.answer: Oxidation state of the metal (or identity of the metal).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term standard electrode potential.
parts.answer: The potential (e.m.f.) of a half-cell measured relative to the standard hydrogen electrode, under standard conditions (298 K, 101 kPa, 1.00 mol dm⁻³ solutions).
parts.working: M1 e.m.f./potential of half-cell compared with (connected to) the standard hydrogen electrode. M1 standard conditions stated: 298 K, 1 atm/101 kPa, all ion concentrations 1.00 mol dm⁻³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student in a college laboratory in Peshawar sets up a standard hydrogen electrode. State three conditions or materials that must be used so that it is truly 'standard'.
parts.answer: H⁺(aq) of concentration 1.00 mol dm⁻³ (e.g. 1.00 mol dm⁻³ HCl); H₂ gas at 101 kPa (1 atm); temperature 298 K; platinum electrode (platinised Pt).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: [H⁺] = 1.00 mol dm⁻³; H₂ pressure 101 kPa; 298 K; electrode made of platinum (coated with platinum black). Max 3.

stem:
A cell is made from a Zn²⁺(aq)/Zn half-cell and an Ag⁺(aq)/Ag half-cell under standard conditions.
E°: Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇌ Zn −0.76 V; Ag⁺ + e⁻ ⇌ Ag +0.80 V

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard cell potential, E°cell.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which electrode is the negative electrode and give the direction of electron flow in the external circuit.
parts.answer: The zinc electrode is negative; electrons flow from zinc to silver through the wire.
parts.working: B1 zinc is negative (more negative E°). B1 electrons from Zn to Ag in the external circuit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the equation for the overall cell reaction.
parts.answer: Zn + 2Ag⁺ → Zn²⁺ + 2Ag
parts.working: B1 balanced, correct species (2 Ag⁺ per Zn).

parts.label: d
parts.text: The salt bridge is made from filter paper soaked in saturated potassium nitrate, not potassium chloride. Explain the purpose of the salt bridge and why KCl is not suitable here.
parts.answer: It completes the circuit by allowing ions to move between the half-cells (keeps each solution neutral); Cl⁻ would precipitate Ag⁺ as AgCl, lowering [Ag⁺] and changing the potential.
parts.working: B1 allows movement of ions / completes circuit without mixing solutions. B1 KCl gives AgCl precipitate with Ag⁺(aq).

author: HomiLabs

stem: E°: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ ⇌ Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O +1.52 V; Cl₂ + 2e⁻ ⇌ 2Cl⁻ +1.36 V

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data to calculate E°cell for the reaction between acidified MnO₄⁻ and Cl⁻ ions.
parts.answer: +0.16 V; the reaction is feasible
parts.working: M1 E°cell = 1.52 − 1.36. A1 +0.16 V (positive, so feasible).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why dilute hydrochloric acid is not used to acidify potassium manganate(VII) in a titration with iron(II) ions.
parts.answer: MnO₄⁻ would oxidise some Cl⁻ to Cl₂, so extra MnO₄⁻ is used and the titre is too large (toxic chlorine is also released).
parts.working: B1 Cl⁻ is oxidised by MnO₄⁻ (E°cell positive). B1 titre larger than it should be / results inaccurate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why dilute sulfuric acid is suitable.
parts.answer: SO₄²⁻ ions are not oxidised by MnO₄⁻ (sulfur is already in its highest oxidation state, +6).

author: HomiLabs

stem: E°: Cl₂/Cl⁻ +1.36 V; Br₂/Br⁻ +1.07 V; Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ +0.77 V; I₂/I⁻ +0.54 V

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the strongest oxidising agent in the list.
parts.answer: Cl₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use E°cell values to decide which of the halide ions Cl⁻, Br⁻ and I⁻ will be oxidised by Fe³⁺(aq) under standard conditions.
parts.working: M1 a correct E°cell calculation. A1 I⁻ +0.23 V feasible. A1 Br⁻ and Cl⁻ give negative E°cell, so no reaction.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the ionic equation for the reaction that occurs.
parts.answer: 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂

author: HomiLabs

stem: E°: Fe³⁺ + e⁻ ⇌ Fe²⁺ +0.77 V; Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇌ Cu +0.34 V

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the Fe³⁺(aq)/Fe²⁺(aq) half-cell is set up under standard conditions.
parts.answer: A platinum electrode dipping into a solution containing both Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ ions, each at 1.00 mol dm⁻³, at 298 K.
parts.working: B1 platinum (inert) electrode. B1 solution with Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ both 1.00 mol dm⁻³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate E°cell for the cell formed with the Cu²⁺/Cu half-cell.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Iron(III) chloride solution is used to remove unwanted copper when printed circuit boards are made. Write the equation for this reaction.
parts.answer: 2Fe³⁺ + Cu → 2Fe²⁺ + Cu²⁺

parts.label: d
parts.text: Predict and explain the effect on the cell e.m.f. of increasing the concentration of Cu²⁺(aq) in the copper half-cell.
parts.answer: E for the Cu²⁺/Cu half-cell becomes more positive (equilibrium Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇌ Cu moves right), so Ecell becomes smaller (less positive).
parts.working: M1 electrode potential of Cu²⁺/Cu becomes more positive. A1 Ecell decreases.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A solution of yellow VO₂⁺ ions in acid is reduced in steps.
E°: VO₂⁺ + 2H⁺ + e⁻ ⇌ VO²⁺ + H₂O +1.00 V; VO²⁺ + 2H⁺ + e⁻ ⇌ V³⁺ + H₂O +0.34 V; V³⁺ + e⁻ ⇌ V²⁺ −0.26 V; Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇌ Zn −0.76 V; Sn²⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇌ Sn −0.14 V

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, using E°cell values, why zinc reduces VO₂⁺ all the way to V²⁺.
parts.answer: E°cell for each step with Zn is positive: VO₂⁺→VO²⁺ +1.76 V, VO²⁺→V³⁺ +1.10 V, V³⁺→V²⁺ +0.50 V, so every step is feasible.
parts.working: M1 calculation of at least the last step: −0.26 − (−0.76) = +0.50 V. A1 all steps positive so V²⁺ (oxidation state +2) is formed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Tin metal is added instead of zinc. Deduce the final oxidation state of vanadium. Show your working.
parts.answer: +3 (V³⁺). Step E°cell values with Sn: +1.14 V, +0.48 V, −0.12 V; the last step is not feasible.
parts.working: M1 E°cell for VO₂⁺→VO²⁺ = +1.14 V and VO²⁺→V³⁺ = +0.48 V. M1 V³⁺→V²⁺ = −0.12 V (not feasible). A1 stops at V³⁺, oxidation state +3.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the equation for the reduction of VO²⁺ to V³⁺ by tin.
parts.answer: 2VO²⁺ + 4H⁺ + Sn → 2V³⁺ + Sn²⁺ + 2H₂O

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell with an alkaline electrolyte is being trialled in a bus in Islamabad.
E°: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ ⇌ 4OH⁻ +0.40 V; 2H₂O + 2e⁻ ⇌ H₂ + 2OH⁻ −0.83 V

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the reaction at each electrode when the cell produces electricity.
parts.answer: Negative electrode: H₂ + 2OH⁻ → 2H₂O + 2e⁻. Positive electrode: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻.
parts.working: B1 each correct half-equation in the correct direction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate E°cell.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the overall equation for the cell reaction.
parts.answer: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give one advantage of using fuel cells in city buses rather than diesel engines.
parts.answer: The only product is water, so no CO₂/CO/NOx/particulates are released at the point of use (or higher efficiency).

author: HomiLabs

stem: E°: H₂O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇌ 2H₂O +1.77 V; O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇌ H₂O₂ +0.68 V

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data to show that hydrogen peroxide can disproportionate under standard conditions. Calculate E°cell.
parts.answer: H₂O₂ acts as both oxidising agent (+1.77 V couple) and reducing agent (+0.68 V couple): E°cell = 1.77 − 0.68 = +1.09 V, positive so feasible.
parts.working: M1 identifies both couples involving H₂O₂. A1 +1.09 V.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the equation for the disproportionation.
parts.answer: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂

parts.label: c
parts.text: A bottle of 6% hydrogen peroxide from a pharmacy can be kept for months. Explain why this does not contradict your answer to (a).
parts.answer: E° shows only that the reaction is energetically feasible; it says nothing about rate. The activation energy is high, so the reaction is very slow without a catalyst (e.g. MnO₂).
parts.working: B1 E° values give no information on rate/kinetics. B1 high activation energy / reaction very slow at room temperature.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A metal M forms M²⁺ ions. A cell is made from an M²⁺/M half-cell and a standard Cu²⁺/Cu half-cell. The voltmeter reads 0.74 V and M is the negative electrode. E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V.
The cell is then allowed to deliver a steady current of 0.150 A for 2.00 hours. Electrode M loses 0.629 g. F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate E° for the M²⁺/M half-cell.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of copper deposited on the copper electrode. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the loss in mass of electrode M to calculate the relative atomic mass of M and suggest its identity.
parts.answer: Ar = 112; M is cadmium (Cd)

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student measures the e.m.f. of cells made by connecting a metal/metal-ion half-cell (1.00 mol dm⁻³) to a standard Cu²⁺/Cu half-cell (E° = +0.34 V) using a salt bridge and a high-resistance voltmeter. In each cell the copper is the positive electrode.
Metal | Ecell / V
lead | 0.47
nickel | 0.59
iron | 0.77
zinc | 1.10

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a high-resistance voltmeter is used.
parts.answer: So that (almost) no current flows; the reading is then the maximum e.m.f. and the concentrations do not change.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the electrode potential of each metal half-cell.
parts.working: M1 E(metal) = +0.34 − Ecell (metal is negative). A1 all four correct.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The data-book value for Fe²⁺/Fe is −0.44 V. Suggest two reasons why the student's value is different.
parts.answer: Any two: temperature not 298 K; [Fe²⁺] not exactly 1.00 mol dm⁻³ (e.g. some Fe²⁺ oxidised to Fe³⁺ by air); oxide layer on the iron surface; Cu²⁺ concentration not exactly 1.00 mol dm⁻³.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid reasons linked to non-standard conditions or surface.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the order of reducing power of the four metals, strongest first.
parts.answer: Zn > Fe > Ni > Pb
parts.working: B1 most negative E° = strongest reducing agent.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data to show that Cu⁺ ions disproportionate in aqueous solution. Write the equation and calculate E°cell.
parts.answer: 2Cu⁺ → Cu + Cu²⁺; E°cell = 0.52 − 0.15 = +0.37 V, positive so feasible.
parts.working: B1 equation. M1 Cu⁺ is reduced (Cu⁺/Cu, +0.52) and oxidised (Cu²⁺/Cu⁺, +0.15). A1 +0.37 V.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest what is seen when solid copper(I) sulfate is added to water.
parts.answer: A blue solution forms (Cu²⁺(aq)) and a brown/pink solid (copper metal) appears.
parts.working: B1 blue solution. B1 brown/pink-brown solid.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Electrode potentials cannot simply be added, but ΔG values can. Use ΔG° = −nFE° for the two half-reactions to calculate E° for Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇌ Cu. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Sodium tetrathionate, Na₂S₄O₆, is formed in iodine–thiosulfate titrations. What is the average oxidation number of sulfur in the S₄O₆²⁻ ion?
A +2
B +2.5
C +4
D +5
parts.working: 4x + 6(−2) = −2, so 4x = 10 and x = +2.5. Option A (+2) is the value in S₂O₃²⁻, not S₄O₆²⁻.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In which reaction does nitrogen undergo disproportionation?
A 3NO₂ + H₂O → 2HNO₃ + NO
B N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃
C NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl
D 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O
parts.answer: A 3NO₂ + H₂O → 2HNO₃ + NO
parts.working: In A nitrogen goes from +4 to both +5 (HNO₃) and +2 (NO): the same element is oxidised and reduced. B and D are ordinary redox (different elements); C involves no change in oxidation number.

stem:
Chlorine is used to treat drinking water in many towns, including Faisalabad. With water it reacts as follows:
Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HOCl

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of chlorine in each chlorine-containing species in the equation.
parts.answer: Cl₂ 0; HCl −1; HOCl +1
parts.working: B1 two correct, B1 all three.

parts.label: b
