parts.text: Use your answers to explain why this is a disproportionation reaction.
parts.answer: Chlorine is both reduced (0 → −1) and oxidised (0 → +1) in the same reaction.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Chlorine reacts with cold dilute sodium hydroxide. Write the equation and state the oxidation number of chlorine in the chlorine-containing product that is used as household bleach.
parts.answer: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O; +1 in NaClO

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the oxidation number of chlorine in the product NaClO₃ formed with hot concentrated NaOH.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of chromium in Cr₂O₇²⁻ and in CrO₄²⁻.
parts.answer: +6 in both

parts.label: b
parts.text: When acid is added to yellow CrO₄²⁻(aq) it turns orange: 2CrO₄²⁻ + 2H⁺ ⇌ Cr₂O₇²⁻ + H₂O. State, with a reason, whether this is a redox reaction.
parts.answer: Not redox: no oxidation number changes (Cr stays +6).

parts.label: c
parts.text: For the reaction Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 3SO₂ + 2H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 3SO₄²⁻ + H₂O, identify the oxidising agent and give the change in oxidation number of sulfur.
parts.answer: Oxidising agent: Cr₂O₇²⁻ (Cr +6 → +3); sulfur +4 → +6.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Show that the total increase in oxidation number equals the total decrease in this equation.
parts.answer: Decrease: 2 Cr × 3 = 6; increase: 3 S × 2 = 6.

stem:
Small amounts of chlorine can be made in the laboratory by the reaction:
2KMnO₄ + 16HCl → 2KCl + 2MnCl₂ + 5Cl₂ + 8H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the element that is oxidised and the element that is reduced, giving the oxidation numbers.
parts.answer: Chlorine is oxidised (−1 in HCl → 0 in Cl₂); manganese is reduced (+7 in KMnO₄ → +2 in MnCl₂).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the HCl molecules in the equation that act as a reducing agent.
parts.working: M1 10 of the 16 Cl atoms end up in Cl₂ (5 Cl₂). A1 10/16 × 100 = 62.5 %; the other 6 HCl act as an acid.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the volume of chlorine, measured at room conditions, produced from 3.16 g of KMnO₄ with excess acid. (Mr KMnO₄ = 158.0; molar gas volume 24.0 dm³)
parts.answer: 1.20 dm³

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the relationship between the Faraday constant F, the Avogadro constant L and the charge on an electron e, and use it to calculate F to 3 significant figures. (L = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
parts.answer: F = L × e = 9.63 × 10⁴ C mol⁻¹
parts.working: B1 F = Le. B1 9.63 × 10⁴ C mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: A jeweller in Hyderabad silver-plates a spoon using a current of 0.500 A for 30.0 minutes. Calculate the mass of silver deposited. (F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹, Ar Ag = 107.9)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the anode should be made of and write the half-equation at the anode.
parts.answer: Silver (pure silver); Ag → Ag⁺ + e⁻

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the product at each electrode when concentrated aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed with inert electrodes.
parts.answer: Cathode: hydrogen; anode: chlorine.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the product at each electrode when dilute aqueous sodium sulfate is electrolysed with inert electrodes, and explain the cathode product.
parts.answer: Cathode H₂, anode O₂; H⁺/H₂O is reduced in preference to Na⁺ because its E° is much less negative (Na⁺/Na −2.71 V).
parts.working: B1 both products. B1 explanation using E°.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Dilute sulfuric acid is electrolysed with a current of 2.00 A for 25.0 minutes. Calculate the volumes of hydrogen and of oxygen produced at room conditions, in cm³, to 3 significant figures. (F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹; molar gas volume 24.0 dm³)
parts.answer: H₂ 373 cm³; O₂ 187 cm³
parts.working: M1 Q = 3000 C, mol e⁻ = 0.03109. M1 H₂: ÷2; O₂: ÷4 (4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ / 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻). A1 373 cm³ and 187 cm³

stem:
A student electrolyses copper(II) sulfate solution using copper electrodes and a constant current of 0.400 A for 40.0 minutes.
mass of cathode before / g 25.416; after / g 25.734
mass of anode before / g 24.980; after / g 24.649

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the charge passed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the cathode results to calculate a value for the Avogadro constant, to 3 significant figures. (Ar Cu = 63.5, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
parts.answer: 5.99 × 10²³ mol⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: The anode lost 0.331 g, more than the cathode gained. Suggest why, and state which electrode gives the more reliable value.
parts.answer: Some copper (or impurities) falls off the anode without being deposited; the cathode gain is more reliable.
parts.working: B1 copper flakes off/impurities lost from anode. B1 cathode.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Each mass was read on a balance accurate to ±0.001 g. Calculate the percentage error in the cathode mass gain.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A chromium-plating bath in a Sialkot factory contains a chromium salt. A current of 1.50 A is passed for 2.00 hours and 1.94 g of chromium is deposited. (Ar Cr = 52.0, F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of electrons passed and the number of moles of chromium deposited, and hence deduce the charge on the chromium ion.
parts.answer: mol e⁻ = 0.1119; mol Cr = 0.0373; ratio 3.00 : 1 so the ion is Cr³⁺

parts.label: b
parts.text: A bicycle part of surface area 150 cm² needs a chromium layer 0.020 mm thick. Calculate the time needed with the same current, in minutes, to 3 significant figures. (density of Cr = 7.19 g cm⁻³)
parts.answer: 133 min

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Copper reacts with dilute nitric acid to give nitrogen monoxide.
aCu + bNO₃⁻ + cH⁺ → dCu²⁺ + eNO + fH₂O
What is the value of c when the equation is balanced with the smallest whole numbers?
A 2
B 4
C 6
D 8
parts.answer: D 8
parts.working: 3Cu + 2NO₃⁻ + 8H⁺ → 3Cu²⁺ + 2NO + 4H₂O: Cu loses 2e⁻ each (×3 = 6), N gains 3e⁻ each (×2 = 6); charge 8 − 2 = 6 = 3 × 2. Option B (4) is the number of water molecules, not of H⁺ ions.

stem: Older roadside breath-testing devices use acidified potassium dichromate(VI), which is reduced by ethanol in the breath.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the reduction of acidified dichromate(VI) to chromium(III) ions.
parts.answer: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the oxidation of ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, to ethanal, CH₃CHO.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂OH → CH₃CHO + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻

parts.label: c
parts.text: Combine your half-equations to give the overall ionic equation.
parts.answer: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 3CH₃CH₂OH + 8H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 3CH₃CHO + 7H₂O
parts.working: M1 ethanol half-equation × 3 to match 6e⁻. A1 H⁺ cancelled to 8, correct H₂O.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the colour change seen.
parts.answer: Orange to green

author: HomiLabs

stem: A dilute solution of potassium manganate(VII) is used to detect sulfur dioxide in gases leaving a factory chimney. MnO₄⁻ is reduced to Mn²⁺ and SO₂ is oxidised to SO₄²⁻.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Deduce the change in oxidation number of manganese and of sulfur.
parts.answer: Mn +7 → +2 (decrease of 5); S +4 → +6 (increase of 2)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answers to construct the balanced ionic equation. Water and H⁺ may be included as needed.
parts.answer: 2MnO₄⁻ + 5SO₂ + 2H₂O → 2Mn²⁺ + 5SO₄²⁻ + 4H⁺
parts.working: M1 ratio MnO₄⁻ : SO₂ = 2 : 5. M1 balance O with H₂O. A1 balance H with H⁺ and check charge (−2 each side).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the colour change in the potassium manganate(VII) solution.
parts.answer: Purple to colourless

author: HomiLabs

stem: Iodised table salt sold in Pakistan contains potassium iodate, KIO₃. A 20.0 g sample of salt is dissolved in water, excess KI and dilute acid are added, and the iodine formed is titrated with 0.00200 mol dm⁻³ sodium thiosulfate. The titre is 12.40 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Construct the equation for the reaction of IO₃⁻ with I⁻ in acid, using the half-equations IO₃⁻ + 6H⁺ + 5e⁻ → ½I₂ + 3H₂O and I⁻ → ½I₂ + e⁻.
parts.answer: IO₃⁻ + 5I⁻ + 6H⁺ → 3I₂ + 3H₂O
parts.working: M1 I⁻ half-equation × 5. A1 combined and simplified.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Deduce the number of moles of S₂O₃²⁻ that react with the iodine formed from 1 mol of IO₃⁻. (I₂ + 2S₂O₃²⁻ → 2I⁻ + S₄O₆²⁻)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of potassium iodate, KIO₃, in mg per kg of salt. (Mr KIO₃ = 214.0)
parts.answer: 44.2 mg kg⁻¹

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the electrode potential of a Cu²⁺/Cu half-cell in which [Cu²⁺] = 0.0100 mol dm⁻³ at 298 K. Use E = E° + (0.059/z) log[Cu²⁺]. (E° = +0.34 V)

parts.label: b
parts.text: This half-cell is connected to a standard Zn²⁺/Zn half-cell (E° = −0.76 V). Calculate the cell e.m.f.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the e.m.f. would change if the zinc half-cell solution were diluted, and explain.
parts.answer: E(Zn²⁺/Zn) becomes more negative (equilibrium Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇌ Zn shifts left), so the cell e.m.f. increases.
parts.working: M1 E for zinc electrode more negative. A1 Ecell increases.

stem:
A half-cell contains a platinum electrode in a solution with [Fe³⁺] = 0.050 mol dm⁻³ and [Fe²⁺] = 0.50 mol dm⁻³ at 298 K.
E = E° + 0.059 log([Fe³⁺]/[Fe²⁺]); E°(Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) = +0.77 V

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the electrode potential of the half-cell.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Deduce whether this half-cell can still oxidise I⁻ ions under standard conditions for the iodine half-cell (E° = +0.54 V). Calculate Ecell.
parts.answer: Yes; Ecell = 0.17 V (positive)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the electrode potential of this half-cell does not change if both [Fe³⁺] and [Fe²⁺] are halved.
parts.answer: E depends only on the ratio [Fe³⁺]/[Fe²⁺], which is unchanged.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A concentration cell is made from two silver electrodes. One dips into 1.00 mol dm⁻³ AgNO₃(aq). The other dips into a saturated solution of a sparingly soluble salt AgZ (which dissolves to give equal amounts of Ag⁺ and Z⁻). The cell e.m.f. at 298 K is 0.207 V.
E = E° + 0.059 log[Ag⁺]; E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain which electrode is positive.
parts.answer: The electrode in 1.00 mol dm⁻³ Ag⁺: its potential is more positive because [Ag⁺] is higher.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate [Ag⁺] in the saturated solution. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 3.10 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the solubility product, Ksp, of AgZ, including units.
parts.answer: 9.6 × 10⁻⁸ mol² dm⁻⁶

author: HomiLabs

stem: The Daniell cell, Zn | Zn²⁺ || Cu²⁺ | Cu, has E°cell = +1.10 V. F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔG° for the reaction Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, in kJ mol⁻¹, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: −212 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the sign of ΔG° tells you about the reaction.
parts.answer: Negative, so the reaction is feasible (spontaneous) under standard conditions.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A seawater-activated emergency battery uses magnesium and silver chloride. A simplified version is modelled as a Mg²⁺/Mg half-cell (E° = −2.38 V) and an Ag⁺/Ag half-cell (E° = +0.80 V). F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate E°cell.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate ΔG° for Mg + 2Ag⁺ → Mg²⁺ + 2Ag, in kJ mol⁻¹, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: −614 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: The equation is rewritten as ½Mg + Ag⁺ → ½Mg²⁺ + Ag. State the new values of E°cell and ΔG°, and explain the difference.
parts.answer: E°cell still +3.18 V; ΔG° = −307 kJ mol⁻¹. E° is an intensive property (independent of amount) but ΔG° depends on the number of moles of electrons, n = 1.
parts.working: B1 E° unchanged and ΔG° halved. B1 explanation using n.

author: HomiLabs

stem: For H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l): ΔH° = −286 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS° = −163 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. In a fuel cell this reaction involves 2 mol of electrons per mole of water. F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ΔG° at 298 K.
parts.answer: −237.4 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate E°cell for the fuel cell at 298 K, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Fuel cells of this type run at about 353 K. Assuming ΔH and ΔS do not change, calculate the cell e.m.f. at 353 K and comment on the result.
parts.answer: ΔG = −228.5 kJ mol⁻¹; E = 1.18 V; the e.m.f. is lower because ΔS is negative, so ΔG becomes less negative as T rises.
parts.working: M1 ΔG = −286 + 353 × 0.163 = −228.5. A1 E = 1.18 V. B1 comment linked to negative ΔS / −TΔS term.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which pollutant is removed from car exhaust gases by reduction in a catalytic converter?
A carbon monoxide
B unburned hydrocarbons
C nitrogen monoxide
D carbon dioxide
parts.answer: C nitrogen monoxide
parts.working: NO is reduced to N₂ (e.g. 2NO + 2CO → N₂ + 2CO₂). CO and hydrocarbons (A, B) are oxidised, not reduced; CO₂ (D) is not removed at all.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In sunlit air, nitrogen monoxide from vehicle exhausts is converted into nitrogen dioxide. Which row correctly gives the change in oxidation number of nitrogen and the colour of nitrogen dioxide?
A +2 → +4; brown
B +2 → +4; colourless
C +4 → +2; brown
D +1 → +2; brown
parts.answer: A +2 → +4; brown
parts.working: In NO nitrogen is +2; in NO₂ it is +4 (2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂, an oxidation). NO₂ is a brown gas. B has the correct oxidation numbers but NO is the colourless gas, not NO₂; C reverses the change.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about photochemical smog is correct?
A Peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN) forms when oxides of nitrogen react with unburned hydrocarbons.
B Nitrogen monoxide is produced inside the catalytic converter.
C Photochemical smog forms mainly at night when the air is cold.
D PAN is a primary pollutant released directly from car exhausts.
parts.answer: A Peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN) forms when oxides of nitrogen react with unburned hydrocarbons.
parts.working: PAN is a secondary pollutant made in the air from NO/NO₂ and hydrocarbons, so D is wrong. The converter removes NO (B wrong); the reactions need sunlight (C wrong).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a catalytic converter: 2NO + 2CO → N₂ + 2CO₂
What are the changes in oxidation number of nitrogen and of carbon?
A N: +2 → 0; C: +2 → +4
B N: +4 → 0; C: +2 → +4
C N: +2 → 0; C: +4 → +2
D N: −3 → 0; C: +2 → +4
parts.working: In NO nitrogen is +2 and in N₂ it is 0 (reduced); carbon in CO is +2 and in CO₂ it is +4 (oxidised). B uses the value for NO₂; C reverses the carbon change.

stem: Traffic on the main roads of Lahore releases oxides of nitrogen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why nitrogen monoxide, NO, is formed inside a car engine although nitrogen and oxygen do not react in the air at room temperature.
parts.answer: The very high temperature in the engine (spark/combustion) provides enough energy to break the strong N≡N triple bond (overcome the high activation energy): N₂ + O₂ → 2NO.
parts.working: B1 high temperature in engine. B1 enough energy to break N≡N / overcome high Ea (equation accepted).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an equation for the reaction of NO in the air to form NO₂.
parts.answer: 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one natural source of oxides of nitrogen.
parts.answer: Lightning (or volcanic activity / bacterial action in soil).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction between carbon monoxide and nitrogen monoxide in a catalytic converter.
parts.answer: 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: Unburned octane, C₈H₁₈, can also be removed by reaction with NO, forming CO₂, H₂O and N₂. Write a balanced equation.
parts.answer: 2C₈H₁₈ + 50NO → 16CO₂ + 18H₂O + 25N₂
parts.working: M1 correct products. A1 balanced (or C₈H₁₈ + 25NO → 8CO₂ + 9H₂O + 12½N₂).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name one metal used as the catalyst.
parts.answer: Platinum (or rhodium / palladium)

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the catalyst is spread as a thin layer on a ceramic honeycomb.
parts.answer: Gives a very large surface area for the gases to be adsorbed, using little expensive metal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write two equations to show how NO₂ catalyses the oxidation of SO₂ in the atmosphere.
parts.answer: SO₂ + NO₂ → SO₃ + NO; NO + ½O₂ → NO₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how your equations show that NO₂ acts as a catalyst.
parts.answer: NO₂ is used in the first step but re-formed in the second, so it is not used up overall (overall SO₂ + ½O₂ → SO₃).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of nitrogen in NO₂ and in NO.
parts.answer: +4 in NO₂; +2 in NO

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why this reaction makes the problem of acid rain worse.
parts.answer: SO₃ formed dissolves in rainwater to give sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄.

stem: A rickshaw engine without a catalytic converter releases 1.50 m³ of exhaust gas (measured at room conditions) for each kilometre travelled. The exhaust contains 0.12 % of NO by volume.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of NO, in dm³, released per kilometre.
parts.answer: 1.80 dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of NO released per kilometre. (molar gas volume 24.0 dm³ at room conditions; Mr NO = 30.0)

parts.label: c
parts.text: If a catalytic converter were fitted, state the volume of CO needed to remove all of this NO and the volume of N₂ formed, both at room conditions.
parts.answer: CO 1.80 dm³; N₂ 0.90 dm³
parts.working: 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂: CO : NO = 1 : 1 and N₂ : NO = 1 : 2.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN) is a component of photochemical smog. It causes eye irritation and damages plants.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the two types of pollutant from vehicle exhausts that react together in sunlight to form PAN.
parts.answer: Oxides of nitrogen (NO/NO₂) and unburned hydrocarbons

parts.label: b
parts.text: PAN has the molecular formula C₂H₃NO₅. Calculate its relative molecular mass.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why levels of photochemical smog in a large city such as Karachi are usually highest on sunny afternoons rather than early in the morning.
parts.answer: Morning traffic first releases NOx and hydrocarbons; the reactions that form PAN need sunlight (UV) and time, so secondary pollutants build up later in the day.
parts.working: B1 sunlight needed for the reactions. B1 time for primary pollutants from rush-hour traffic to react / build up.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g)   ΔH = +180 kJ mol⁻¹
At 2000 K, Kc = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use Le Chatelier's principle to explain why more NO is present at the high temperatures inside an engine.
parts.answer: The forward reaction is endothermic, so increasing the temperature shifts the position of equilibrium to the right, increasing the yield of NO.
parts.working: M1 forward reaction endothermic. A1 equilibrium moves right at high T.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why changing the pressure has no effect on the position of this equilibrium.
parts.answer: There are equal numbers of moles of gas on each side (2 and 2).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the expression for Kc and calculate the equilibrium concentration of NO at 2000 K when [N₂] = 4.8 × 10⁻³ and [O₂] = 1.2 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: Kc = [NO]² ÷ ([N₂][O₂]); [NO] = 4.8 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe, in terms of adsorption, how the metal catalyst in a catalytic converter speeds up the reaction between CO and NO.
parts.answer: Gas molecules are adsorbed onto the metal surface (weak bonds form to active sites); bonds within the molecules are weakened and the molecules are held close together in a favourable orientation, lowering Ea; the products (CO₂, N₂) are desorbed, freeing the sites.
parts.working: B1 adsorption onto surface/active sites. B1 bonds weakened / molecules held close, so lower activation energy. B1 desorption of products.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Some 'lean-burn' engines run with a large excess of air. Suggest why a normal catalytic converter removes NO less effectively from these engines.
parts.answer: The excess O₂ oxidises CO and hydrocarbons on the catalyst, so little CO/hydrocarbon is left to reduce the NO to N₂.
parts.working: B1 O₂ reacts with CO/hydrocarbons. B1 so not enough reducing agent for NO.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why leaded petrol must not be used in cars with catalytic converters.
parts.answer: Lead is adsorbed strongly onto the active sites and poisons the catalyst.

stem:
An air-quality station beside a busy road in Lahore recorded these concentrations (in µg m⁻³):
time | NO | NO₂
06:00 | 20 | 15
09:00 | 110 | 40
12:00 | 40 | 85

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why the NO concentration rises sharply between 06:00 and 09:00.
parts.answer: Morning rush-hour traffic: engines produce NO from N₂ and O₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why NO₂ reaches its highest concentration later in the day than NO does. Include an equation.
parts.answer: NO is gradually oxidised by oxygen in the air: 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂.
parts.working: B1 equation. B1 NO converted to NO₂ over time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the NO concentration falls between 09:00 and 12:00.
parts.answer: Less traffic after rush hour, and NO is being converted into NO₂ (and dispersed).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Exhaust gas from a car engine was analysed before and after its catalytic converter (percentages by volume):
gas | before | after
CO | 1.20 | 0.10
NO | 0.080 | 0.012

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of CO and of NO removed by the converter. Give each answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the converter removes much less pollution in the first few minutes after a cold start.
parts.answer: The catalyst is cold, so the reactions are slow until it reaches its working temperature.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the percentage of CO₂ in the exhaust is higher after the converter.
parts.answer: CO and hydrocarbons are oxidised to CO₂.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What are the shape and bond angle of the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺?
A trigonal pyramidal, 107°
B tetrahedral, 109.5°
C trigonal planar, 120°
D square planar, 90°
parts.answer: B tetrahedral, 109.5°
parts.working: NH₄⁺ has four bonding pairs and no lone pair, so it is tetrahedral. A describes NH₃, which has one lone pair.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which mixture gives off ammonia when warmed?
A ammonium chloride and aqueous sodium hydroxide
B ammonium chloride and dilute hydrochloric acid
C sodium nitrate and dilute sulfuric acid
D ammonium sulfate and aqueous barium chloride
parts.answer: A ammonium chloride and aqueous sodium hydroxide
parts.working: OH⁻ removes H⁺ from NH₄⁺: NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O. In D the only reaction is precipitation of BaSO₄; no base is present to release NH₃.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In which reaction does the nitrogen-containing reactant act as a Brønsted–Lowry acid?
A NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl
B NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O
C NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻
D N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃
parts.answer: B NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O
parts.working: NH₄⁺ donates a proton to OH⁻. In A and C ammonia accepts a proton (base); D is not an acid–base reaction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the bonding in the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, and explain how it forms from NH₃ and H⁺.
parts.answer: Four covalent N–H bonds; the fourth is a dative (coordinate) bond formed when the lone pair on N is donated to H⁺. All four bonds are then identical.
parts.working: B1 dative/coordinate bond. B1 lone pair on N donated to H⁺.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the H–N–H bond angle in NH₃ and in NH₄⁺, and explain the difference.
parts.answer: NH₃ 107°, NH₄⁺ 109.5°. NH₃ has a lone pair, which repels more strongly than bonding pairs, pushing the N–H bonds closer; NH₄⁺ has four bonding pairs only.
parts.working: B1 both angles. B1 lone pair–bond pair repulsion greater than bond pair–bond pair.

stem: A farmer near Multan buys a bag of white fertiliser that is labelled as an ammonium salt.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a test to show that a fertiliser sample contains ammonium ions. Give the reagent, condition and positive result.
parts.answer: Add aqueous sodium hydroxide and warm; a gas is given off that turns damp red litmus paper blue (ammonia).
parts.working: B1 NaOH(aq). B1 warm. B1 damp red litmus turns blue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the ionic equation for the reaction in the test.
parts.answer: NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O

author: HomiLabs

stem: 2.00 g of a fertiliser containing ammonium sulfate is boiled with 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ NaOH (an excess) until no more ammonia is given off. The remaining NaOH needs 41.20 cm³ of 0.500 mol dm⁻³ HCl for neutralisation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction of ammonium sulfate with sodium hydroxide.
parts.answer: (NH₄)₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2NH₃ + 2H₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in moles, of NaOH that reacted with the ammonium ions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of ammonium sulfate in the fertiliser. (Mr (NH₄)₂SO₄ = 132.1)

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in the fertiliser.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Household glass cleaners often contain dilute aqueous ammonia, which has a pH of about 11.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction of ammonia with water and identify the two conjugate acid–base pairs.
parts.answer: NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻. Pairs: NH₄⁺/NH₃ and H₂O/OH⁻.
parts.working: B1 equation with ⇌. B1 NH₄⁺/NH₃. B1 H₂O/OH⁻.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why ammonia is described as a weak base.
parts.answer: It is only partially protonated (the equilibrium lies well to the left), so few OH⁻ ions form.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write an equation for the formation of the fertiliser ammonium sulfate from ammonia.
parts.answer: 2NH₃ + H₂SO₄ → (NH₄)₂SO₄

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Ammonia is made at a fertiliser plant near Daharki by the Haber process:
N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)   ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹
In one equilibrium mixture at a total pressure of 20.0 MPa the mole fractions are N₂ 0.20, H₂ 0.60 and NH₃ 0.20.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the expression for Kp and calculate its value, with units, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: Kp = p(NH₃)² ÷ (p(N₂) × p(H₂)³) = 2.31 × 10⁻³ MPa⁻²
parts.working: M1 partial pressures: N₂ 4.0, H₂ 12.0, NH₃ 4.0 MPa. M1 Kp = 4.0² ÷ (4.0 × 12.0³). A1 2.31 × 10⁻³ MPa⁻²

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the plant runs at about 450 °C even though a lower temperature gives a higher equilibrium yield.
parts.answer: The forward reaction is exothermic so a low temperature favours yield, but the rate would be too slow; 450 °C is a compromise giving acceptable yield at a fast enough rate (with an iron catalyst).
parts.working: B1 lower T gives higher yield (exothermic). B1 rate too slow at low T; compromise.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃ (Mr 80.0), ammonium sulfate, (NH₄)₂SO₄ (Mr 132.1), and urea, CO(NH₂)₂ (Mr 60.0). Give each to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: NH₄NO₃ 35.0 %; (NH₄)₂SO₄ 21.2 %; urea 46.7 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: A farmer spreads slaked lime, Ca(OH)₂, on acidic soil at the same time as ammonium sulfate. Explain, with an equation, why some of the nitrogen is wasted.
parts.answer: (NH₄)₂SO₄ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaSO₄ + 2NH₃ + 2H₂O; the base displaces ammonia gas, which escapes into the air.
parts.working: B1 equation. B1 NH₃ gas lost to the air.

stem: A student heats a mixture of 1.07 g of ammonium chloride with excess calcium hydroxide and collects the ammonia in a gas syringe. 432 cm³ of ammonia is collected at room conditions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: 2NH₄Cl + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCl₂ + 2NH₃ + 2H₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum volume of ammonia, in cm³ at room conditions. (Mr NH₄Cl = 53.5; molar gas volume 24.0 dm³)
parts.answer: 480 cm³
parts.working: M1 mol NH₄Cl = 0.0200 = mol NH₃. A1 × 24 000 = 480 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage yield.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the gas is collected in a dry syringe rather than over water, and suggest one reason for the yield being below 100 %.
parts.answer: Ammonia is very soluble in water; yield low because the reaction was incomplete / some NH₃ escaped before the syringe was connected / NH₃ dissolved in condensed water in the tube.
parts.working: B1 very soluble in water. B1 any valid reason.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The Thar coalfield in Sindh supplies power stations that burn lignite.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how sulfur dioxide is released when coal is burned in a power station.
parts.answer: Coal contains sulfur compounds, which burn to form SO₂ (S + O₂ → SO₂).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write two equations to show how SO₂ is converted into sulfuric acid in the atmosphere.
parts.answer: SO₂ + ½O₂ → SO₃; SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄
parts.working: B1 each (accept SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃ then oxidation).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two harmful effects of acid rain.
parts.answer: Any two: kills fish/aquatic life in lakes; damages trees/leaches nutrients from soil; corrodes limestone/marble buildings and metal structures; releases toxic Al³⁺ into water.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A coal sample contains 1.8 % sulfur by mass. Assume all the sulfur is converted to SO₂ on burning. (Ar S = 32.1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in moles, of sulfur in 1.00 tonne (1.00 × 10⁶ g) of coal.
parts.answer: 561 mol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of SO₂, in m³ at room conditions, formed when 1.00 tonne of coal burns. (molar gas volume 24.0 dm³)

parts.label: c
parts.text: The SO₂ is removed by powdered calcium carbonate: CaCO₃ + SO₂ → CaSO₃ + CO₂. Calculate the mass of CaCO₃, in kg, needed per tonne of coal. (Mr CaCO₃ = 100.1)
parts.working: M1 mol CaCO₃ = mol SO₂ = 560.7. A1 × 100.1 = 56131 g = 56.1 kg

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one disadvantage of this method of removing SO₂.
parts.answer: It releases CO₂ (a greenhouse gas) / limestone must be quarried / large amounts of solid waste.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction of sulfuric acid in rain with marble, CaCO₃.
parts.answer: CaCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + H₂O + CO₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: During one year, 5000 dm³ of rain containing 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ of H₂SO₄ falls on a marble monument. Calculate the maximum mass of marble that can be dissolved. (Mr CaCO₃ = 100.1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one natural source of sulfur dioxide.
parts.answer: Volcanoes

stem: To monitor sulfur dioxide near a brick kiln, 50.0 m³ of air is bubbled through excess hydrogen peroxide solution, which converts all the SO₂ to sulfuric acid. The solution needs 18.60 cm³ of 0.0100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH for neutralisation. (Mr SO₂ = 64.1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction of SO₂ with H₂O₂ and give the change in oxidation number of sulfur.
parts.answer: SO₂ + H₂O₂ → H₂SO₄; S +4 → +6

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of SO₂ in the air sample, in µg, to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: M1 mol NaOH = 1.86 × 10⁻⁴. M1 mol H₂SO₄ = mol SO₂ = 9.30 × 10⁻⁵. A1 × 64.1 = 0.00596 g = 5960 µg

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the SO₂ concentration in µg m⁻³ and state whether it is above a guideline limit of 40 µg m⁻³ (24-hour average).
parts.answer: 119 µg m⁻³; above the limit

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why nitrogen gas is very unreactive.
parts.answer: The N≡N triple bond is very strong (high bond energy), and the molecule is non-polar, so it does not attract electrophiles or nucleophiles.
parts.working: B1 strong triple bond / high bond energy. B1 non-polar molecule.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one use of nitrogen that depends on its lack of reactivity.
parts.answer: Filling packets of food (e.g. crisps) to prevent oxidation / an inert atmosphere for welding or storing chemicals.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The bond energy of O=O is 496 kJ mol⁻¹ and that of N≡N is 944 kJ mol⁻¹. Oxygen is far more reactive than nitrogen. Use the bond energies to explain this difference.
parts.answer: Much less energy is needed to break O=O than N≡N, so reactions of O₂ have lower activation energies.

stem: Bond energies / kJ mol⁻¹: N≡N 944; H–H 436; N–H 388

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the bond energies to calculate the enthalpy change for N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃.
parts.answer: −76 kJ mol⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: The reaction is exothermic, yet nitrogen and hydrogen do not react at room temperature. Explain this and state how industry overcomes it.
parts.answer: The activation energy is very high because the N≡N bond must be broken first; an iron catalyst (and a raised temperature) is used to give a reasonable rate.
parts.working: B1 high activation energy (N≡N). B1 iron catalyst / high temperature.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Ammonium nitrate fertiliser is made in Pakistan from ammonia, part of which is oxidised to nitric acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the formation of ammonium nitrate from ammonia and nitric acid.
parts.answer: NH₃ + HNO₃ → NH₄NO₃

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of each nitrogen atom in ammonium nitrate.
parts.answer: −3 in NH₄⁺; +5 in NO₃⁻

parts.label: c
parts.text: In the factory, half of the ammonia is first converted into nitric acid, which then reacts with the rest of the ammonia. Calculate the maximum mass of ammonium nitrate, in tonnes, made from 1.00 tonne of ammonia. (Mr NH₃ = 17.0; Mr NH₄NO₃ = 80.0)
parts.answer: 2.35 tonnes
parts.working: M1 mol NH₃ = 1.00 × 10⁶ ÷ 17.0 = 58824. M1 2 mol NH₃ give 1 mol NH₄NO₃: 29412 mol. A1 × 80.0 = 2.35 × 10⁶ g = 2.35 tonnes

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which compound gives an orange precipitate with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine but no change when warmed with Tollens' reagent?
A propanal
B propanone
C propan-1-ol
D propanoic acid
parts.answer: B propanone
parts.working: Propanone is a ketone: it has C=O (positive 2,4-DNPH) but cannot be oxidised by Tollens'. Propanal (A) gives both a precipitate and a silver mirror.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A compound with molecular formula C₄H₈O gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent. How many structural isomers fit this information?
A 1
B 2
C 3
D 4
parts.answer: B 2
parts.working: Only aldehydes give a silver mirror: butanal, CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO, and 2-methylpropanal, (CH₃)₂CHCHO. Butanone is also C₄H₈O but is a ketone, so 3 (C) is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Compound Y, C₅H₁₀O, gives an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH and does not react with Tollens' reagent. Reduction of Y with NaBH₄ gives an alcohol with no chiral centre. What is Y?
A pentan-2-one
B pentan-3-one
C 3-methylbutan-2-one
D pentanal
parts.answer: B pentan-3-one
parts.working: Y is a ketone (D is an aldehyde). Pentan-3-one gives pentan-3-ol, CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₂CH₃, whose C-3 carries two identical ethyl groups, so it is not chiral. A and C give pentan-2-ol and 3-methylbutan-2-ol, which are both chiral.

stem: A technician at a school in Rawalpindi finds two unlabelled bottles; one contains propanal and the other propanone.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how Tollens' reagent can be used to distinguish between propanal and propanone. Give the condition and the observation with each compound.
parts.answer: Warm each with Tollens' reagent (in a water bath). Propanal: silver mirror (grey/black precipitate). Propanone: no change (stays colourless).
parts.working: B1 warm. B1 propanal silver mirror. B1 propanone no change.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an equation, using [O], for the oxidation of propanal.
parts.answer: CH₃CH₂CHO + [O] → CH₃CH₂COOH

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Four liquids W, X, Y and Z are ethanol, ethanal, propanone and ethanoic acid (in some order). A student carried out four tests:
test | W | X | Y | Z
2,4-DNPH | no change | orange ppt | orange ppt | no change
Fehling's, warm | stays blue | red-brown ppt | stays blue | stays blue
Na₂CO₃(aq) | no change | no change | no change | effervescence
acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, warm | orange to green | orange to green | stays orange | stays orange

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify W, X, Y and Z.
parts.answer: W ethanol; X ethanal; Y propanone; Z ethanoic acid

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why X, but not Y, turns acidified dichromate green.
parts.answer: X is an aldehyde and is oxidised (to ethanoic acid); Y is a ketone and is not oxidised.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the gas given off when Z reacts with sodium carbonate and give a test for it.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide: turns limewater milky.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Unknown carbonyl compound G gives an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH. After recrystallisation the precipitate melts at 124 °C. G also gives a red-brown precipitate with warm Fehling's solution.
Melting points of 2,4-DNPH derivatives from a data book:
compound | melting point / °C
propanal | 156
propanone | 126
butanal | 123
butanone | 117

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of reaction between a carbonyl compound and 2,4-DNPH.
parts.answer: Condensation (addition–elimination)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the orange solid is recrystallised before its melting point is measured.
parts.answer: To purify it; impurities lower the melting point (and widen its range).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify G, giving your reasoning.
parts.answer: G is butanal. 124 °C is close to the values for both butanal (123 °C) and propanone (126 °C), but the positive Fehling's test shows that G is an aldehyde, not a ketone.
parts.working: M1 melting point matches butanal or propanone. M1 Fehling's positive shows aldehyde. A1 butanal.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Fehling's solution is a deep blue alkaline solution containing a complex of copper.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the metal ion in Fehling's solution that acts as the oxidising agent, and give the formula of the red-brown precipitate.
parts.answer: Copper(II), Cu²⁺; copper(I) oxide, Cu₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the change in oxidation number of copper.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Glucose has an aldehyde group but sucrose has neither an aldehyde nor a ketone group. Predict what is seen when each is warmed with Fehling's solution.
parts.answer: Glucose: blue solution gives a red-brown precipitate. Sucrose: remains a blue solution.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how Tollens' reagent is prepared from aqueous silver nitrate.
parts.answer: Add a few drops of aqueous sodium hydroxide to give a brown precipitate (Ag₂O), then add dilute aqueous ammonia dropwise until the precipitate just dissolves.
parts.working: B1 NaOH gives brown ppt. B1 aqueous ammonia until it dissolves.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the tubes are warmed in a beaker of hot water rather than over a Bunsen flame.
parts.answer: Carbonyl compounds are volatile and flammable; a water bath also gives gentle, even heating.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the formula of the silver complex ion in Tollens' reagent, and the change in oxidation number of silver in a positive test.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the reagent is made fresh and any left over is washed away at once.
parts.answer: On standing it can form explosive silver compounds.

stem: R and S are isomers with molecular formula C₄H₈O. Both give an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH. R gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent and has a branched carbon chain. S does not react with Tollens' reagent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify R and give its displayed or structural formula.
parts.answer: 2-methylpropanal, (CH₃)₂CHCHO
parts.working: M1 aldehyde (Tollens' positive). A1 branched chain → 2-methylpropanal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify S.
parts.answer: Butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the structural formula of the organic product formed when R reacts with Tollens' reagent and the mixture is then acidified.
parts.answer: (CH₃)₂CHCOOH, 2-methylpropanoic acid

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give the structural formula of the product when S is reduced by NaBH₄, and state whether it is chiral.
parts.answer: CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃, butan-2-ol; yes, C-2 is chiral

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Each mole of aldehyde reduces two moles of Ag⁺. Calculate the maximum mass of silver formed from 0.580 g of propanal with excess Tollens' reagent. (Mr propanal = 58.0, Ar Ag = 107.9)

parts.label: b
parts.text: A 1.00 g mixture of propanal and propanone gives 1.62 g of silver with excess Tollens' reagent. Calculate the percentage by mass of propanal in the mixture.
parts.working: M1 mol Ag = 1.62 ÷ 107.9 = 0.01501. M1 mol propanal = ÷ 2 = 0.00751; mass = 0.4354 g. A1 43.5 % (propanone does not react)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What type of reaction occurs when ethanal reacts with HCN in the presence of KCN?
A electrophilic addition
B nucleophilic addition
C nucleophilic substitution
D condensation
parts.answer: B nucleophilic addition
parts.working: CN⁻ (a nucleophile) attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon and the C=O π bond breaks; nothing is replaced. A is the typical reaction of alkenes, not carbonyls.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the name of the organic product when propanone reacts with HCN?
A 2-hydroxybutanenitrile
B 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile
C 2-methylpropanenitrile
D 3-hydroxybutanenitrile
parts.answer: B 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile
parts.working: (CH₃)₂C(OH)CN: the CN joins the former carbonyl carbon, giving a 4-carbon nitrile with OH and CH₃ on C-2. A is the product from propanal.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which carbonyl compound reacts with HCN to give a product with no chiral centre?
A ethanal
B propanone
C butanone
D benzaldehyde
parts.answer: B propanone
parts.working: (CH₃)₂C(OH)CN has two identical CH₃ groups on the central carbon. The products from A, C and D each have four different groups on that carbon (they form racemic mixtures).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the reagents and conditions for the reaction of propanal with HCN.
parts.answer: HCN with a small amount of KCN (or NaCN), at 10–20 °C

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the mechanism of this reaction. In your answer, say where each curly arrow starts and ends, and give the intermediate.
parts.answer: Step 1: a curly arrow from the lone pair on the carbon of CN⁻ to the δ+ carbonyl carbon; a second arrow from the C=O π bond to the oxygen, forming the anion CH₃CH₂CH(O⁻)CN. Step 2: an arrow from a lone pair on O⁻ to the H of HCN, and an arrow from the H–C bond of HCN to its C, giving CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CN and regenerating CN⁻.
parts.working: B1 arrow from CN⁻ lone pair (on C) to carbonyl C. B1 arrow from C=O bond to O (dipole on C=O shown). B1 correct intermediate with negative charge on O. B1 O⁻ takes H⁺ from HCN (or H₂O), regenerating CN⁻.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the product.
parts.answer: 2-hydroxybutanenitrile

stem: Lactic acid is used in the food industry. One laboratory route to it starts from ethanal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the structural formula of the product when ethanal reacts with HCN.
parts.answer: CH₃CH(OH)CN

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the reagent and condition to convert this product into lactic acid, CH₃CH(OH)COOH.
parts.answer: Heat under reflux with dilute hydrochloric (or sulfuric) acid

parts.label: c
parts.text: Lactic acid made in this way is optically inactive, although it has a chiral centre. Explain why.
parts.answer: The carbonyl group (and the C atom attacked) is planar; CN⁻ can attack from either side with equal probability; so equal amounts of both enantiomers form (a racemic mixture), whose effects on plane-polarised light cancel.
parts.working: B1 planar C=O. B1 attack equally from above and below. B1 racemic mixture / 50:50 enantiomers cancel.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: HCN is a weak acid. Explain why a little KCN is added to the reaction mixture.
parts.answer: HCN is only slightly dissociated, so there are very few CN⁻ ions; KCN provides CN⁻ ions, which are the nucleophile needed to start the reaction.
parts.working: B1 HCN gives few CN⁻. B1 CN⁻ is the nucleophile.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the carbon atom of the carbonyl group is attacked by nucleophiles.
parts.answer: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so the C=O bond is polar and the carbon is δ+.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why alkenes do not undergo nucleophilic addition.
parts.answer: The C=C bond is non-polar and electron-rich, so it repels nucleophiles and attracts electrophiles instead.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give one safety precaution needed for this reaction.
parts.answer: Work in a fume cupboard because HCN is extremely toxic (or avoid acidifying KCN in the open laboratory).

stem:
2-Hydroxy-2-methylpropanoic acid, (CH₃)₂C(OH)COOH, can be made from propan-2-ol in three steps:
propan-2-ol → (step 1) → ketone → (step 2) → hydroxynitrile → (step 3) → product

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the reagents and conditions for each of the three steps and the structural formula of each intermediate.
parts.answer: Step 1: K₂Cr₂O₇ / dilute H₂SO₄, heat (reflux) → propanone, CH₃COCH₃. Step 2: HCN with KCN, 10–20 °C → (CH₃)₂C(OH)CN. Step 3: heat under reflux with dilute HCl(aq) → (CH₃)₂C(OH)COOH.
parts.working: B1 step 1 reagents. B1 propanone. B1 HCN/KCN and nitrile intermediate. B1 acid hydrolysis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The yields of the three steps are 80 %, 70 % and 90 %. Calculate the mass of 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanoic acid (Mr 104.0) made from 6.00 g of propan-2-ol (Mr 60.0).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each compound, give the structural formula of the product with HCN and state whether that product has a chiral centre: methanal, ethanal, pentan-3-one, butanone.
parts.answer: methanal → HOCH₂CN, not chiral; ethanal → CH₃CH(OH)CN, chiral; pentan-3-one → (CH₃CH₂)₂C(OH)CN, not chiral; butanone → CH₃CH₂C(CH₃)(OH)CN, chiral.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct product with correct chirality statement.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of carbon atoms in the product from pentan-3-one and explain why this reaction is useful in synthesis.
parts.answer: 6 carbon atoms; the reaction lengthens the carbon chain by one carbon atom.
parts.working: B1 6. B1 increases chain length by one C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction of ethanal with HCN.
parts.answer: CH₃CHO + HCN → CH₃CH(OH)CN

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the Mr of the product and the percentage by mass of nitrogen in it.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the functional groups present in the product.
parts.answer: Hydroxy (alcohol) and nitrile

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the type of reaction.
parts.answer: Nucleophilic addition

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which compound gives a pale yellow precipitate when warmed with alkaline aqueous iodine?
A propan-2-ol
B propan-1-ol
C pentan-3-one
D methanol
parts.answer: A propan-2-ol
parts.working: Propan-2-ol has the CH₃CH(OH)– group, which is oxidised to CH₃CO– and then forms CHI₃. Pentan-3-one (C) is a ketone but has no CH₃CO– group.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the reagents and conditions for the tri-iodomethane (iodoform) test and the observation for a positive result.
parts.answer: Iodine and aqueous sodium hydroxide (alkaline I₂), warm; pale yellow precipitate (of CHI₃) with an antiseptic smell.
parts.working: B1 reagents and warm. B1 pale yellow precipitate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the two structural features that give a positive result.
parts.answer: CH₃CO– (methyl carbonyl) or CH₃CH(OH)– (secondary alcohol with an adjacent methyl group)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which of these give a positive result: ethanol, propanal, butanone, pentan-3-one, ethanal, methanol.
parts.answer: Positive: ethanol, butanone, ethanal. Negative: propanal, pentan-3-one, methanol.
parts.working: 3 marks for all six correctly classified; 2 marks for four or five; 1 mark for two or three.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete and balance the equation: CH₃COCH₃ + 3I₂ + 4NaOH → CHI₃ + ____ + 3NaI + 3H₂O
parts.answer: CH₃COONa (sodium ethanoate)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum mass of CHI₃ formed from 0.290 g of propanone. (Mr propanone 58.0, Mr CHI₃ 393.7)

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student obtains 75.0 % of this mass after filtering and drying. Calculate the mass obtained and suggest one reason for the loss.
parts.answer: 1.48 g; e.g. some solid left on the filter paper/in the tube, or the reaction was incomplete.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a chemical test that distinguishes pentan-2-one from pentan-3-one. Give the result with each.
parts.answer: Warm with alkaline aqueous iodine: pentan-2-one gives a pale yellow precipitate; pentan-3-one gives no precipitate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the formulae of the two organic products formed in the positive test.
parts.answer: CHI₃ and CH₃CH₂CH₂COONa (sodium butanoate)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Tollens' reagent cannot be used to distinguish these two compounds.
parts.answer: Both are ketones, so neither is oxidised; both give no change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: There are four structural isomers of C₄H₁₀O that are alcohols. Identify the only one that gives a positive tri-iodomethane test and explain why.
parts.answer: Butan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃: it has the CH₃CH(OH)– group, which alkaline iodine oxidises to CH₃CO–.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the structural formula of the organic intermediate and the two final organic products.
parts.answer: Intermediate butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃; products CHI₃ and CH₃CH₂COONa (sodium propanoate)

stem: T is an unbranched alcohol, C₅H₁₂O, with a chiral centre. T gives a pale yellow precipitate with alkaline aqueous iodine. Oxidation of T with acidified dichromate gives U, which gives an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH but no change with Fehling's solution. The alkaline iodine reaction of T gives CHI₃ and the sodium salt V of a carboxylic acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify T, U and V, giving their structural formulae.
parts.answer: T pentan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₂CH₃; U pentan-2-one, CH₃COCH₂CH₂CH₃; V CH₃CH₂CH₂COONa (sodium butanoate)
parts.working: B1 each. T must be unbranched, chiral and have CH₃CH(OH)–.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the information shows that U is a ketone and that T is a secondary alcohol.
parts.answer: U gives an orange ppt with 2,4-DNPH (carbonyl) but does not reduce Fehling's (not an aldehyde); oxidation of an alcohol to a ketone shows T is secondary.
parts.working: B1 U ketone reasoning. B1 T secondary.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Pentan-3-ol is also an unbranched secondary alcohol. Give two pieces of evidence from the data that rule it out.
parts.answer: Pentan-3-ol has no chiral centre, and it does not give a positive tri-iodomethane test.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The tri-iodomethane reaction can be used in synthesis to convert a methyl ketone into a carboxylic acid with one fewer carbon atom. Phenylethanone, C₆H₅COCH₃, is warmed with alkaline iodine, the CHI₃ is filtered off and the filtrate is acidified to give benzoic acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the formula of the organic product formed in the alkaline iodine reaction before acidification.
parts.answer: C₆H₅COONa (sodium benzoate)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the theoretical mass of benzoic acid, C₆H₅COOH (Mr 122.0), from 3.00 g of phenylethanone (Mr 120.0), and the percentage yield if 2.20 g is obtained.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the benzoic acid can be purified.
parts.answer: Recrystallisation from (the minimum volume of) hot water

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student tested four liquids P, Q, R and S, which are ethanal, propanone, propanal and propan-1-ol (in some order). For the iodine test, aqueous iodine was added to each sample, then aqueous NaOH dropwise until the brown colour just disappeared, and the tube was warmed in a 60 °C water bath.
test | P | Q | R | S
2,4-DNPH | orange ppt | orange ppt | orange ppt | no change
Fehling's, warm | red-brown ppt | stays blue | red-brown ppt | stays blue
alkaline iodine, warm | yellow ppt | yellow ppt | no change | no change

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify P, Q, R and S.
parts.answer: P ethanal; Q propanone; R propanal; S propan-1-ol

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the structural feature shown by a positive result in the alkaline iodine test.
parts.answer: A CH₃CO– group (or a CH₃CH(OH)– group, which is oxidised to CH₃CO–)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which single test in the table distinguishes P from Q.
parts.answer: Fehling's solution (P, an aldehyde, gives a red-brown ppt; Q does not)

author: HomiLabs

stem: A 3.00 g sample of a solvent is a mixture of propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol. It is warmed with excess alkaline iodine. The dry tri-iodomethane formed has a mass of 5.91 g. Assume 1 mol of CHI₃ forms from each mole of the reacting alcohol.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why only one of the two alcohols reacts.
parts.answer: Only propan-2-ol has the CH₃CH(OH)– group; propan-1-ol does not.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of propan-2-ol in the mixture. (Mr propan-2-ol 60.0; Mr CHI₃ 393.7)

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the reagents for oxidising primary and secondary alcohols.
parts.answer: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) (K₂Cr₂O₇ with dilute H₂SO₄)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Propanal is made from propan-1-ol. Explain why the product is distilled off as it forms, rather than heated under reflux.
parts.answer: Propanal has a low boiling point and is removed immediately, so it is not oxidised further to propanoic acid, which would happen under reflux.
parts.working: B1 distil immediately. B1 prevents further oxidation to carboxylic acid.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the organic product when propan-2-ol is heated under reflux with the same reagent, and explain why it is not oxidised further.
parts.answer: Propanone; it is a ketone and has no H atom on the carbonyl carbon, so it is not oxidised further.
parts.working: B1 propanone. B1 no H on C=O carbon / ketones resist oxidation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the shape around the carbonyl carbon atom and the approximate bond angle.
parts.answer: Trigonal planar; 120°

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an equation, using [H], for the reduction of butanone by NaBH₄ and name the product.
parts.answer: CH₃COCH₂CH₃ + 2[H] → CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃; butan-2-ol

parts.label: c
parts.text: But-3-en-2-one, CH₂=CHCOCH₃, is reduced with NaBH₄. Give the structural formula of the product and explain why the C=C bond is not affected.
parts.answer: CH₂=CHCH(OH)CH₃ (but-3-en-2-ol). NaBH₄ provides H⁻, a nucleophile, which attacks the δ+ carbon of the polar C=O; the non-polar C=C does not attract nucleophiles.
parts.working: B1 product. B1 H⁻ nucleophile / C=C non-polar.

stem: 25.0 cm³ of an acidified solution of iron(II) sulfate is titrated with 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ potassium manganate(VII). The mean titre is 22.40 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the ionic equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the colour change at the end-point and explain why no indicator is needed.
parts.answer: From pale green/colourless to the first permanent pale pink; MnO₄⁻ is intensely purple and is decolourised until Fe²⁺ is used up, so it acts as its own indicator.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of Fe²⁺ in the solution.
parts.answer: 0.0896 mol dm⁻³

author: HomiLabs

stem:
One iron tablet (containing iron(II) sulfate) is crushed and dissolved in dilute sulfuric acid and the solution is made up to 250 cm³. 25.0 cm³ portions are titrated with 0.00200 mol dm⁻³ KMnO₄; the mean titre is 11.70 cm³.
MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of iron, in mg, in one tablet. (Ar Fe = 55.8)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the tablet is dissolved in dilute sulfuric acid rather than in water or hydrochloric acid.
parts.answer: H⁺ ions are needed for the reduction of MnO₄⁻ (and acid slows air oxidation of Fe²⁺); HCl is not used because Cl⁻ would be oxidised by MnO₄⁻, giving a larger titre.
parts.working: B1 H⁺ required. B1 Cl⁻ oxidised.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A 0.200 g sample of iron ore from a mine in Chiniot is dissolved in acid and all the iron is reduced to Fe²⁺. The solution needs 24.30 cm³ of 0.0167 mol dm⁻³ K₂Cr₂O₇ for complete oxidation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the ionic equation for the reaction between dichromate(VI) and iron(II) ions in acid.
parts.answer: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 6Fe²⁺ + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6Fe³⁺ + 7H₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of iron in the ore. (Ar Fe = 55.8)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the colour change of the dichromate ion as it reacts.
parts.answer: Orange to green

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A student standardises a KMnO₄ solution. 25.0 cm³ of 0.0500 mol dm⁻³ sodium ethanedioate, Na₂C₂O₄, is acidified with dilute H₂SO₄ and warmed to 60 °C, then titrated with KMnO₄ from a burette.
2MnO₄⁻ + 5C₂O₄²⁻ + 16H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 10CO₂ + 8H₂O
titration | rough | 1 | 2 | 3
final reading / cm³ | 23.80 | 23.15 | 23.60 | 23.25
initial reading / cm³ | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.20 | 0.00
titre / cm³ | 23.80 | 23.15 | 23.40 | 23.25

parts.label: a
parts.text: Select the concordant titres and calculate the mean titre.
parts.answer: Runs 1 and 3 (23.15 and 23.25); mean 23.20 cm³
parts.working: B1 runs 1 and 3 (within 0.10 cm³). B1 23.20 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of the KMnO₄ solution, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 0.0216 mol dm⁻³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the flask is warmed, and why the first few drops of KMnO₄ take a long time to lose their colour but later drops decolourise quickly.
parts.answer: The reaction is very slow at room temperature (high activation energy, two negative ions must collide). Mn²⁺ produced catalyses the reaction (autocatalysis), so it speeds up once some Mn²⁺ has formed.
parts.working: B1 slow at room temperature. B1 Mn²⁺ product acts as catalyst / autocatalysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: 10.0 cm³ of a hair bleach containing hydrogen peroxide is diluted to 250 cm³. 25.0 cm³ of the diluted solution is acidified and titrated with 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ KMnO₄; 21.80 cm³ is needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the reaction, using the half-equation H₂O₂ → O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻.
parts.answer: 2MnO₄⁻ + 5H₂O₂ + 6H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 5O₂ + 8H₂O

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of H₂O₂ in the original hair bleach in mol dm⁻³.
parts.answer: 1.09 mol dm⁻³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Convert your answer into g dm⁻³. (Mr H₂O₂ = 34.0)
parts.answer: 37.1 g dm⁻³

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Spinach leaves contain ethanedioic (oxalic) acid. An extract from 25.0 g of spinach is made up to 100 cm³. 25.0 cm³ of this is acidified, warmed to 60 °C and titrated with 0.0100 mol dm⁻³ KMnO₄; the titre is 14.80 cm³.
2MnO₄⁻ + 5C₂O₄²⁻ + 16H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 10CO₂ + 8H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of carbon in C₂O₄²⁻ and in CO₂.
parts.answer: +3 and +4

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of ethanedioic acid, H₂C₂O₄ (Mr 90.0), in mg per 100 g of spinach. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 533 mg per 100 g

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A 0.400 g sample of brass from a Peshawar metal workshop is dissolved in nitric acid; the solution is neutralised, and excess KI(aq) is added.
2Cu²⁺ + 4I⁻ → 2CuI + I₂
I₂ + 2S₂O₃²⁻ → 2I⁻ + S₄O₆²⁻
The iodine needs 20.20 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ Na₂S₂O₃.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Deduce the mole ratio Cu²⁺ : S₂O₃²⁻.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of copper in the brass. (Ar Cu = 63.5)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Starch is the indicator. State when it is added and the colour change at the end-point.
parts.answer: Near the end-point, when the solution is pale yellow/straw-coloured; blue-black to white/off-white (the CuI precipitate).
parts.working: B1 added near end-point. B1 blue-black disappears.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
6.95 g of hydrated iron(II) sulfate, FeSO₄·xH₂O, is dissolved in dilute sulfuric acid and made up to 250 cm³. 25.0 cm³ portions need 25.00 cm³ of 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ KMnO₄.
MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount of Fe²⁺ in the 250 cm³ solution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the Mr of the crystals and hence the value of x. (Mr FeSO₄ = 151.9, Mr H₂O = 18.0)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Old crystals of this salt often have a brown coating. Suggest what this is and how it would affect the calculated value of x.
parts.answer: Iron(III) compounds formed by air oxidation; less Fe²⁺ is titrated, so the calculated Mr and therefore x would be too high.
parts.working: B1 iron(III)/oxidised by air. B1 x too high.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A standard solution is made by dissolving 9.80 g of ammonium iron(II) sulfate, (NH₄)₂Fe(SO₄)₂·6H₂O, in dilute sulfuric acid and making it up to 250 cm³. 25.0 cm³ portions are pipetted into a flask, a redox indicator is added, and the solution is titrated with potassium dichromate(VI) of unknown concentration.
Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 6Fe²⁺ + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6Fe³⁺ + 7H₂O
titration | rough | 1 | 2 | 3
titre / cm³ | 26.00 | 25.55 | 25.65 | 26.10

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean titre using concordant results only.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of the K₂Cr₂O₇ solution, to 3 significant figures. (Mr of ammonium iron(II) sulfate = 392.0)
parts.answer: 0.0163 mol dm⁻³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Each burette reading has an uncertainty of ±0.05 cm³. Calculate the percentage error in the mean titre.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Run 3 is not used. Suggest one practical mistake that could cause a titre that is too large.
parts.answer: Over-running the end-point / air bubble in the burette jet / reading the burette at the wrong level.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Pyrolusite ore contains manganese(IV) oxide. A 0.400 g sample is warmed with 50.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ sodium ethanedioate in acid (an excess):
MnO₂ + C₂O₄²⁻ + 4H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 2CO₂ + 2H₂O
The excess ethanedioate is then titrated with 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ KMnO₄, needing 26.40 cm³:
2MnO₄⁻ + 5C₂O₄²⁻ + 16H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 10CO₂ + 8H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount of ethanedioate that remained after reaction with the MnO₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by mass of MnO₂ in the ore. (Mr MnO₂ = 86.9)
parts.working: M1 ethanedioate added = 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol. M1 reacted with MnO₂ = 3.68 × 10⁻³ = mol MnO₂ (1 : 1). A1 × 86.9 ÷ 0.400 × 100 = 79.9 %

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the change in oxidation number of manganese in each of the two reactions.

author: HomiLabs

stem: 25.0 cm³ of a 0.0400 mol dm⁻³ solution of violet V²⁺ ions is titrated with acidified 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ KMnO₄. 30.00 cm³ is needed. MnO₄⁻ is reduced to Mn²⁺.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount of electrons removed from each vanadium ion and deduce the final oxidation state of vanadium.
parts.answer: 3 electrons per V; +5

parts.label: b
parts.text: The vanadium product is VO₂⁺. Write the balanced ionic equation for the reaction.
parts.answer: 5V²⁺ + 3MnO₄⁻ + 4H⁺ → 5VO₂⁺ + 3Mn²⁺ + 2H₂O
parts.working: M1 V²⁺ + 2H₂O → VO₂⁺ + 4H⁺ + 3e⁻ (× 5) with MnO₄⁻ half-equation (× 3). A1 simplified (charge 11+ each side).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A solution contains a mixture of Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ ions.
Titration 1: 25.0 cm³ of the solution, acidified, needs 15.00 cm³ of 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ KMnO₄.
Titration 2: another 25.0 cm³ is warmed with excess zinc to reduce all the Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺, the zinc is filtered off, and the solution needs 24.00 cm³ of the same KMnO₄.
MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the concentrations of Fe²⁺ and of Fe³⁺ in the solution.
parts.working: M1 first titration measures Fe²⁺ only: 0.01500 × 0.0200 × 5 ÷ 0.0250 = 0.0600. M1 second measures total Fe: 0.0960. M1 Fe³⁺ = total − Fe²⁺. A1 0.0360

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why all the excess zinc must be removed before the second titration.
parts.answer: Zinc would react with (reduce) MnO₄⁻ / reduce Fe³⁺ back during titration, giving too large a titre.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the equation for the reduction of Fe³⁺ by zinc.
parts.answer: 2Fe³⁺ + Zn → 2Fe²⁺ + Zn²⁺

author: HomiLabs

stem: A student plans to determine the concentration of a KMnO₄ solution using ammonium iron(II) sulfate, (NH₄)₂Fe(SO₄)₂·6H₂O, as the primary standard.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to prepare 250 cm³ of a standard solution containing about 2.45 g of the solid. Include the apparatus and the steps that make the concentration accurate.
parts.answer: Weigh the weighing bottle with solid, tip the solid into a beaker, reweigh the bottle (weighing by difference); dissolve in dilute H₂SO₄ (with stirring); transfer the solution to a 250 cm³ volumetric flask with all the washings of the beaker and rod; make up to the mark with distilled water so that the bottom of the meniscus is on the line; stopper and invert several times to mix.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: weighing by difference; dissolve in dilute H₂SO₄ in beaker; transfer with washings to 250 cm³ volumetric flask; make up to mark (meniscus at eye level); invert/shake to mix.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The balance reads to ±0.005 g. Calculate the percentage error in the mass of solid used.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why dilute sulfuric acid, rather than distilled water alone, is used to dissolve the solid.
parts.answer: It reduces air oxidation of Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ (and prevents hydrolysis/precipitation of iron hydroxides), and supplies the H⁺ needed in the titration.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of potassium dichromate(VI) needed to make 250 cm³ of a 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ solution. (Mr K₂Cr₂O₇ = 294.2)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the half-equation for the reduction of dichromate(VI) ions in acid.
parts.answer: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the amount of Fe²⁺ that reacts with 20.0 cm³ of this solution.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Unlike KMnO₄, dichromate titrations need a redox indicator. Explain why.
parts.answer: The colour change from orange to green is not sharp enough to see the end-point clearly (dichromate is not self-indicating).

stem: Two students titrate 25.0 cm³ portions of the same iron(II) solution with the same KMnO₄ solution. Student A acidifies with dilute sulfuric acid and gets a mean titre of 18.20 cm³. Student B uses dilute hydrochloric acid instead and gets a mean titre of 19.35 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage difference between student B's titre and student A's titre.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why student B's titre is larger.
parts.answer: MnO₄⁻ also oxidises some Cl⁻ ions from HCl to Cl₂, so extra KMnO₄ is used.
parts.working: B1 Cl⁻ oxidised. B1 more MnO₄⁻ needed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the top of the meniscus is read for KMnO₄ in a burette.
parts.answer: The solution is so deeply coloured that the bottom of the meniscus cannot be seen.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Student A obtained titres of 18.20, 18.25 and 18.95 cm³. Identify the anomalous titre and suggest a possible cause.
parts.answer: 18.95 cm³; e.g. the end-point was overshot, or the flask was not swirled so the pink colour was missed.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Step 1: 25.0 cm³ of 0.0150 mol dm⁻³ K₂Cr₂O₇ is acidified and excess KI is added. The iodine released needs 22.75 cm³ of sodium thiosulfate solution.
Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 6I⁻ + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 3I₂ + 7H₂O;  I₂ + 2S₂O₃²⁻ → 2I⁻ + S₄O₆²⁻
Step 2: 10.0 cm³ of household bleach is diluted to 250 cm³. 25.0 cm³ of this is acidified and excess KI is added; the iodine needs 18.30 cm³ of the same thiosulfate.
ClO⁻ + 2I⁻ + 2H⁺ → Cl⁻ + I₂ + H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Deduce the mole ratio Cr₂O₇²⁻ : S₂O₃²⁻ and calculate the concentration of the thiosulfate, to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: M1 1 Cr₂O₇²⁻ → 3I₂ → 6S₂O₃²⁻. M1 mol Cr₂O₇²⁻ = 3.75 × 10⁻⁴. A1 × 6 ÷ 0.02275 = 0.0989

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the concentration of ClO⁻ in the original bleach.
parts.answer: 0.905 mol dm⁻³

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Transition element properties (variable oxidation states, catalysis)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term transition element.
parts.answer: A d-block element that forms one or more stable ions with an incomplete d subshell.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use electronic configurations to explain why zinc and scandium are d-block elements but not transition elements.
parts.answer: Zn forms only Zn²⁺, [Ar]3d¹⁰ (full d subshell); Sc forms only Sc³⁺, [Ar] (3d⁰, empty d subshell). Neither has an ion with a partly filled d subshell.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give three characteristic properties of transition elements or their compounds, other than variable oxidation states.
parts.answer: Any three: form coloured compounds/ions; act as catalysts; form complex ions; have paramagnetic compounds (unpaired electrons).
parts.working: 2 marks for three, 1 mark for two.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Transition element properties (variable oxidation states, catalysis)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of manganese in each: KMnO₄, K₂MnO₄, MnO₂, MnSO₄.
parts.working: 2 marks all four; 1 mark for two or three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why transition elements can show several different oxidation states.
parts.answer: The 3d and 4s electrons are close in energy, so different numbers of them can be lost or used in bonding.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the maximum oxidation state of chromium and explain it in terms of its electronic configuration.
parts.answer: +6; Cr is [Ar]3d⁵4s¹, so it has six electrons available (3d and 4s).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Transition element properties (variable oxidation states, catalysis)
stem:
Peroxodisulfate ions oxidise iodide ions: S₂O₈²⁻ + 2I⁻ → 2SO₄²⁻ + I₂
E°: S₂O₈²⁻ + 2e⁻ ⇌ 2SO₄²⁻ +2.01 V; Fe³⁺ + e⁻ ⇌ Fe²⁺ +0.77 V; I₂ + 2e⁻ ⇌ 2I⁻ +0.54 V

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why the uncatalysed reaction is slow even though it is energetically feasible.
parts.answer: Both reactants are negative ions, which repel each other, so the activation energy is high.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write two equations to show how Fe²⁺ ions catalyse the reaction, and calculate E°cell for each step.
parts.answer: S₂O₈²⁻ + 2Fe²⁺ → 2SO₄²⁻ + 2Fe³⁺, E°cell = +1.24 V; 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂, E°cell = +0.23 V
parts.working: B1 each equation. B1 each E°cell (positive, so each step feasible).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Fe³⁺ ions would catalyse the reaction equally well.
parts.answer: The steps occur in the reverse order: Fe³⁺ first oxidises I⁻, then the Fe²⁺ formed is oxidised by S₂O₈²⁻.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State whether this is homogeneous or heterogeneous catalysis.
parts.answer: Homogeneous (catalyst and reactants in the same phase, aqueous)

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Transition element properties (variable oxidation states, catalysis)
stem:
Data for calcium and iron (both in Period 4):
property | Ca | Fe
melting point / °C | 842 | 1538
density / g cm⁻³ | 1.55 | 7.87
atomic radius / nm | 0.197 | 0.126

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why iron has a much higher melting point than calcium.
parts.answer: Iron has more delocalised electrons (both 4s and 3d electrons) and smaller ions/atoms, so the metallic bonding (attraction between cations and delocalised electrons) is stronger.
parts.working: B1 more delocalised electrons incl. 3d. B1 stronger metallic bonding.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why iron is much denser than calcium.
parts.answer: Fe atoms have a greater mass but a smaller radius, so more mass is packed into the same volume.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Compare the colour of aqueous Ca²⁺ ions with that of aqueous Fe²⁺ ions and explain the difference.
parts.answer: Ca²⁺(aq) is colourless (no d electrons); Fe²⁺(aq) is pale green because it has a partly filled 3d subshell, allowing d–d electron transitions that absorb visible light.
parts.working: B1 colours. B1 partly filled d subshell/d–d transitions.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Transition element properties (variable oxidation states, catalysis)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Vanadium(V) oxide is the catalyst in the Contact process. In the first step V₂O₅ oxidises SO₂ to SO₃ and is itself reduced to V₂O₄; in the second step the catalyst is regenerated by oxygen. Write an equation for each step.
parts.answer: SO₂ + V₂O₅ → SO₃ + V₂O₄;  V₂O₄ + ½O₂ → V₂O₅

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the oxidation number of vanadium in V₂O₅ and in V₂O₄.
parts.answer: +5 and +4

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain which property of transition elements makes vanadium(V) oxide an effective catalyst here.
parts.answer: Vanadium can change easily between oxidation states (+5 and +4), so it can accept and then give back electrons/oxygen.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the type of catalysis.
parts.answer: Heterogeneous (solid catalyst, gaseous reactants)

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Transition element properties (variable oxidation states, catalysis)
stem:
The reaction S₂O₈²⁻ + 2I⁻ → 2SO₄²⁻ + I₂ can be catalysed by a transition-metal ion that cycles between two oxidation states.
E°: S₂O₈²⁻/SO₄²⁻ +2.01 V; I₂/I⁻ +0.54 V
Candidate couples: Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ +0.77 V; VO₂⁺/VO²⁺ +1.00 V; Cr³⁺/Cr²⁺ −0.41 V; Cu²⁺/Cu⁺ +0.15 V

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the two conditions that the E° of a couple must meet for it to catalyse the reaction.
parts.answer: E° must be less positive than +2.01 V (so S₂O₈²⁻ can oxidise the lower oxidation state) and more positive than +0.54 V (so the higher oxidation state can oxidise I⁻).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the data to identify which of the four couples could catalyse the reaction. Explain your answer for one couple that cannot.
parts.answer: Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ (+0.77) and VO₂⁺/VO²⁺ (+1.00) can. Cr³⁺/Cr²⁺ (−0.41) cannot: Cr³⁺ cannot oxidise I⁻ (E°cell = −0.41 − 0.54 = −0.95 V). Cu²⁺/Cu⁺ (+0.15) cannot: Cu²⁺ cannot oxidise I⁻ (−0.39 V).
parts.working: B1 Fe and V couples. B1 Cr and Cu rejected. B1 a correct negative E°cell given for one rejected couple.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Transition element properties (variable oxidation states, catalysis)
stem:
Acidified KMnO₄ is mixed with excess ethanedioate ions at 25 °C and the absorbance of MnO₄⁻ (proportional to its concentration) is recorded:
time / s | 0 | 30 | 60 | 90 | 120 | 150 | 180
absorbance | 1.00 | 0.97 | 0.90 | 0.70 | 0.38 | 0.15 | 0.05

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of decrease of absorbance between 0 and 30 s and between 60 and 120 s, in s⁻¹. Calculate how many times faster the second rate is.
parts.answer: 0.0010 s⁻¹ and 0.0087 s⁻¹; about 8.7 times faster

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the shape of the results.
parts.answer: At first the reaction is slow (high Ea, two anions repel). Mn²⁺ formed is a catalyst, so the rate increases as [Mn²⁺] rises (autocatalysis). Finally the rate falls as the reactants are used up.
parts.working: B1 slow start. B1 Mn²⁺ product catalyses (autocatalysis). B1 slows as reactant concentration falls.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe an experiment to confirm that Mn²⁺ is the catalyst.
parts.answer: Repeat with some MnSO₄ added at the start: there is no slow initial period.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Transition element properties (variable oxidation states, catalysis)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two reasons why transition elements and their compounds are often good catalysts.
parts.answer: They have variable oxidation states (can gain and lose electrons easily); they have partly filled d orbitals / vacant orbitals that allow reactants to be adsorbed (form temporary bonds) on the surface.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Classify each catalyst as homogeneous or heterogeneous:
(i) iron in the Haber process
(ii) Fe²⁺(aq) in the S₂O₈²⁻/I⁻ reaction
(iii) nickel in the hydrogenation of vegetable oils to make vanaspati ghee
(iv) V₂O₅ in the Contact process
parts.answer: (i) heterogeneous (ii) homogeneous (iii) heterogeneous (iv) heterogeneous
parts.working: 2 marks all four; 1 mark for three.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the full electronic configuration of: Fe, Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺, Cr, Cu⁺ and Mn²⁺.
parts.answer: Fe 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d⁶4s²; Fe²⁺ 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d⁶; Fe³⁺ 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d⁵; Cr 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d⁵4s¹; Cu⁺ 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d¹⁰; Mn²⁺ 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d⁵
parts.working: 4 marks for all six; 3 for five; 2 for four; 1 for two or three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why iron loses its 4s electrons before its 3d electrons when it forms ions.
parts.answer: Once the 3d orbitals are occupied, the 4s electrons are at higher energy (further from the nucleus/shielded), so they are removed first.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State how many d orbitals there are in the 3d subshell and the maximum number of electrons it can hold.
parts.answer: 5 orbitals; 10 electrons

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe in words the shapes of the 3dxy and 3dz² orbitals, including how they are arranged relative to the x, y and z axes.
parts.answer: 3dxy: four lobes (two dumb-bells) in the xy plane, pointing between the x and y axes. 3dz²: a dumb-bell along the z axis with a ring (doughnut) around the middle in the xy plane.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the two 3d orbitals whose lobes point along the axes.
parts.answer: 3dz² and 3dx²−y²

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the number of unpaired electrons in each gaseous ion: Ti³⁺, V³⁺, Cr³⁺, Mn²⁺, Fe²⁺, Ni²⁺, Cu²⁺, Zn²⁺.
parts.answer: Ti³⁺ 1; V³⁺ 2; Cr³⁺ 3; Mn²⁺ 5; Fe²⁺ 4; Ni²⁺ 2; Cu²⁺ 1; Zn²⁺ 0
parts.working: 3d counts 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10; fill singly before pairing (Hund's rule). 3 marks all eight; 2 for six or seven; 1 for four or five.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the ion in the list that has the same 3d configuration as Fe³⁺.
parts.answer: Mn²⁺ (both 3d⁵)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Paramagnetism increases with the number of unpaired electrons. Identify the most paramagnetic and the least paramagnetic ion in the list.
parts.answer: Most: Mn²⁺; least: Zn²⁺ (diamagnetic)

stem: Third ionisation energies / kJ mol⁻¹: Mn 3248; Fe 2957

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the electronic configurations of Mn²⁺ and Fe²⁺ in the form [Ar]3dⁿ.
parts.answer: Mn²⁺ [Ar]3d⁵; Fe²⁺ [Ar]3d⁶

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the third ionisation energy of manganese is greater than that of iron.
parts.answer: Mn's third electron is removed from a half-filled 3d⁵ subshell (all electrons unpaired); Fe's third electron is removed from 3d⁶ where one orbital holds a pair; repulsion between the paired electrons makes that electron easier to remove.
parts.working: B1 Mn: from 3d⁵ (half-filled, stable). B1 Fe: from a paired 3d orbital. B1 spin-pair repulsion lowers Fe's IE3.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the data to explain why aqueous Fe²⁺ is easily oxidised to Fe³⁺ in air, while Mn²⁺ is much harder to oxidise to Mn³⁺.
parts.answer: Less energy is needed to remove the third electron from Fe (291 kJ mol⁻¹ less than for Mn), and Fe³⁺ gains the stable 3d⁵ configuration.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: An ion M²⁺ has 25 electrons. Identify M, give the configuration of M²⁺ and the number of unpaired electrons.
parts.answer: M is cobalt (Z = 27); Co²⁺ [Ar]3d⁷; 3 unpaired electrons

parts.label: b
parts.text: An ion Y³⁺ has the same number of electrons as V²⁺. Identify Y and give the configuration of Y³⁺.
parts.answer: Y is chromium (Z = 24); Cr³⁺ [Ar]3d³
parts.working: M1 V²⁺ has 23 − 2 = 21 electrons, so Y has 24 protons. A1 Cr³⁺ [Ar]3d³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Copper(I) compounds such as CuCl are white, whereas copper(II) compounds are usually blue or green. Explain this in terms of electronic configuration.
parts.answer: Cu⁺ is 3d¹⁰: the d subshell is full, so no d–d transitions are possible and no visible light is absorbed. Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹ and can absorb light by promoting an electron between split d orbitals.
parts.working: B1 Cu⁺ 3d¹⁰ full, no transition. B1 Cu²⁺ 3d⁹ allows d–d transition.

stem: The first five ionisation energies of a Period 4 d-block element Z are (kJ mol⁻¹): 659, 1310, 2652, 4175, 9581.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio IE5 ÷ IE4 and use it to deduce the group of Z.
parts.answer: 2.29; Z has four outer (3d + 4s) electrons, so it is in Group 4
parts.working: B1 9581 ÷ 4175 = 2.29 (biggest jump). B1 four electrons removed easily → Group 4

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify Z and give the electronic configuration of the Z⁴⁺ ion.
parts.answer: Titanium; Ti⁴⁺ is 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶

parts.label: c
parts.text: Ti⁴⁺ compounds such as TiO₂ are white. Explain why.
parts.answer: Ti⁴⁺ has no d electrons (3d⁰), so no d–d transitions can absorb visible light.

author: HomiLabs
